\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We characterize the disjoint pairs of domains that generate essentially
incomplete first-order theories in the restriction idempotent completion
of a recursion category. The object on which the domains lie indexes
the nullary predicates, the only nonlogical symbols. The axioms are the
atomic sentences indexed by the first domain and the negated atomic
sentences indexed by the second. Under the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:free-first-order-adjunction}, a consistent theory so
generated is essentially incomplete if and only if no two complementary
domains contain the given domains, respectively. Here essential incompleteness
means that in every consistent deductively closed extension in the same
language, the join of the theorem and refutation subobjects is a proper subobject
of the sentence object. On pairs generating consistent theories, this
construction is left adjoint to the functor assigning to a consistent
theory its theorem and refutation subobjects.

Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness}, a
consistent theory is essentially incomplete if and only if its constant
family is essentially incomplete in the slice over its theorem object.
For Peano arithmetic (PA), the numerical interpretation of one total
morphism sends each index for a computably enumerable set of additional
axioms consistent with PA to the code of a sentence independent of the
resulting theory. The other applications concern
real closed ordered fields with constants for the entries of a Miller
sequence and propositional theories obtained from cosheaves on a
three-point space.
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}

Di Paola and Heller sought an algebraic account of generalized
incompleteness theorems in recursion categories
\cite[pp.~594--596, 629]{DPH}. We ask when a disjoint pair of domains
generates an internal first-order theory with no complete consistent
deductively closed extension in its language.
For a consistent generated theory this happens exactly when the two
domains are inseparable (Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-first-order-incompleteness}).

Let $\mathscr R$ be a recursion category. Splitting its restriction
idempotents makes the domains of partial morphisms into objects. Write
$\mathscr C=\Split(\mathscr R)$ for this completion and
$\mathcal D=\Tot(\mathscr C)$ for its category of total morphisms.
Assume that $\mathcal D$ is regular, that its finite coproducts are
disjoint and stable under pullback, and that every monomorphism in
$\mathcal D$ has a partial inverse in $\mathscr C$. A subobject $m:A\hookrightarrow X$ with partial inverse $r$ then
represents the restriction idempotent $mr:X\rightharpoonup X$.
Conversely, splitting a restriction idempotent on $X$ gives its
representing subobject (Section~\ref{subsec:restriction-idempotents}).
Two disjoint subobjects of $X$ are
\emph{inseparable} if no pair of complementary subobjects contains
them respectively. If $t:T\hookrightarrow S$ is the subobject of
derivable sentences and $\nu:S\to S$ is negation, the inverse image
$\nu^*T$ is the subobject of refutable sentences. The theory is consistent when
$T\wedge\nu^*T=\bot$ and complete when $T\vee\nu^*T=\top$
in $\operatorname{Sub}(S)$. A consistent theory $T$ is
\emph{essentially incomplete} if every deductively closed extension
$H\ge T$ in this language satisfies
\[
 H\wedge\nu^*H=\bot\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H\vee\nu^*H\ne\top
\]
(Section~\ref{subsec:theories-and-interpretation}).

Fix a variable object $V$ with decidable equality. For each
$X\in\mathcal D$, take the first-order language whose only nonlogical
symbols are nullary predicates indexed by $X$. Let $a,b$ be disjoint
subobjects of $X$ with inclusions $i_a:A\hookrightarrow X$ and
$i_b:B\hookrightarrow X$. Write $S_X$ for the sentence object of this
language and $\theta_X:X\to S_X$ for its atomic sentence constructor. Thus an index $x:W\to X$ gives
the sentence $\theta_Xx:W\to S_X$ over $W$. The index belongs to $a$
over $W$ precisely when $x=i_a y$ for some $y:W\to A$.
Write $\nu_X:S_X\to S_X$ for negation. The axiom subobject is
\[
 A_{a,b}=\im(\theta_Xi_a)\vee\im(\nu_X\theta_Xi_b)
 \quad\text{in }\operatorname{Sub}(S_X).
\]
For each $X$, assume that the syntax and variable-list algebras of
this language are initial in every parameter slice. For each first-order presentation
under consideration, assume an initial derivation algebra for every
axiom subobject of its sentence object (Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}).
Let $T_{a,b}$ be the image of the conclusion morphism for sentence
derivations from $A_{a,b}$. Under these hypotheses, if $T_{a,b}$ is
consistent, it is essentially incomplete exactly when $a,b$ are
inseparable. On pairs generating consistent theories, the construction
is left adjoint to the functor taking a consistent theory $H$ with
sentence object $S$ and negation $\nu$ to $(S,H,\nu^*H)$.
Section~\ref{sec:free-first-order-theories} defines the two categories
and their morphisms. Theorem~\ref{thm:free-first-order-adjunction} gives the adjunction.
A separator of $a,b$ supplies a Boolean valuation whose true sentences
form a consistent complete extension of $T_{a,b}$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-first-order-incompleteness}).
For the converse, let $t\hookrightarrow S$ be a consistent theory
and suppose a total $f:X\to S$ satisfies $a\le f^*t$ and
$b\le f^*(\nu^*t)$. The theorem and refutation subobjects of any
complete consistent closed extension of $t$ would pull back along
$f$ to complementary subobjects separating $a$ and $b$
(Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness}). For $T_{a,b}$ take $f=\theta_X$.

For a theory $u:U\hookrightarrow S$ on a sentence object $S$, define its
associated category to be the category of partial maps in $\mathcal D/U$.
It is a Turing category (Lemma~\ref{lem:partial-slice-turing}).
An inclusion of theories induces a fully faithful functor between their
associated categories (Theorem~\ref{thm:theory-extension}).
For each parameter object $P$ and each axiom subobject
$A\hookrightarrow P\times S$ over $P$, assume that the inference
endofunctor on $\mathcal D/(P\times\Phi)$ for the parameterized rules
has an initial algebra, where $\Phi$ is the formula object
(Section~\ref{subsec:essential-incompleteness-slice}).
Assume also that a fixed logical theorem $\lambda:1\to S$ factors
through every consistent closed theory. Then a consistent $u$ is
essentially incomplete if and only if every consistent closed extension of
$1_U\times u:U\times U\hookrightarrow U\times S$ in $\mathcal D/U$
is incomplete. An extension here is a subobject of $U\times S$ over
$U$ and may vary with the parameter.
The partial Boolean morphism
that is true on theorems and false on refutations in the constant family has a total
extension exactly when the original theorem and refutation subobjects are separable
(Theorem~\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness}).

To compare a recursion category $\mathscr R$ with an interpretation,
let $F:\mathscr R\to\mathcal A$ preserve restrictions, ranges,
zeros and binary restriction coproducts. Let $a_0,a_1$ be the diagonal domains on the Turing object $U$ defined in
Section~\ref{sec:lifting}. Let $P,N$ be disjoint domains on $FU$ with
$F(a_0)\le P$ and $F(a_1)\le N$. Suppose a partial morphism
$FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$ has summand inverse images $N,P$,
respectively, and lifts to $\mathscr R$. Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison}
gives a total morphism $g:U\to U$ with $(Fg)^*P=(Fg)^*N=0$. When $\mathcal A$ is split,
extend $F$ to $\widehat F:\Split(\mathscr R)\to\mathcal A$, choosing the
identity splitting of $F(1_U)$ so that $\widehat F(U,1_U)=FU$.
Let $t:S\rightharpoonup S$ be the theorem domain on a sentence object $S$ in
$\Split(\mathscr R)$, with negation $\nu:S\to S$. For a total sentence
morphism $\theta:(U,1_U)\to S$, take the two domains on $FU$ to be
\[
 P=(\widehat F\theta)^*\widehat F(t),\qquad
 N=\bigl(\widehat F(\nu\theta)\bigr)^*\widehat F(t).
\]
Suppose the interpreted theorem and refutation domains are disjoint,
$F(1_U)\ne0$, and inverse images along total morphisms in $\mathcal A$
preserve binary joins of restriction idempotents. Under the preceding
bounds and lifting hypothesis, Theorem~\ref{thm:logical-comparison}
then proves incompleteness of the internal theory and its interpretation.

The arithmetic realization uses the syntactic recursion categories of
Montagna and Di Paola--Montagna \cite{Montagna,DPM}. Montagna asked
how to relate the category for Peano arithmetic ($\PA$) to the
recursion category of partial recursive functions
\cite[pp.~114--115]{Montagna}. Section~\ref{sec:arithmetic} gives a computable bijection between
numerical derivations and the standard interpretations of syntactic
derivations, preserving the conclusion of each derivation. The completion of the syntactic category
$S_{\PA}$ represents computably enumerable (c.e.) extensions of $\PA$
by internal theories. Let $M$ be the standard arithmetic model $\N$ or
an ultrapower of that model. Interpreting program graphs in $M$ gives a
range functor $F_M:S_{\PA}\to\Pfn$, where $\Pfn$ is the category of
sets and partial functions. Its extension
$\widehat F_M:\Split(S_{\PA})\to\Pfn$ interprets the sentence theory.
For each consistent c.e.~extension of PA, choose a model $K$ of its axioms.
Soundness in $K$ and the comparison theorem show that both the
internal theory and its interpretation under $\widehat F_M$ are incomplete
(Theorem~\ref{thm:arithmetic-internal-comparison}).
For each such extension, the sets of standard codes of its provable
sentences and of its refutable sentences are recursively inseparable
(Corollary~\ref{cor:arithmetic}). Fix the PA axioms and let $\Gamma_e$ adjoin to them the
arithmetic sentences on whose codes program $e$ halts. In
$\Tot(\Split(S_{\PA}))$ there is one morphism from the numerical object to
the sentence object whose standard interpretation sends every $e$ with
$\Gamma_e$ consistent to the code of a sentence independent of $\Gamma_e$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:uniform-independent-sentences}). The associated-category
construction is applied separately to the first-order theory generated
by the arithmetic diagonal pair, whose nonlogical symbols are nullary
predicates (Corollary~\ref{cor:arithmetic-associated-categories}).

The second realization uses a sequence $a:\N\to[0,1]$ constructed by
Miller \cite{Miller2004}.
Bauer and Hanson used it to construct a parameterized realizability
topos with countable Dedekind reals \cite[Theorem~6.4]{BauerHanson}.
In the recursion category $\mathcal E_a$ of Section~\ref{sec:miller},
a partial function $f:\N\rightharpoonup\N$ is a morphism precisely when
one oracle program, run with any binary representation of $a$, halts at
$n$ exactly when $f(n)$ is defined and then returns $f(n)$.
Each representation computes a separator of
$\{n:a(n)<1/2\}$ and $\{n:a(n)>1/2\}$. No program computes the same
separator from every representation
(Corollary~\ref{cor:miller-cuts-inseparable}). In $\Split(\mathcal E_a)$
we extend the theory of real closed ordered fields by constants $c_n$
and all strict rational bounds on $c_n$ that hold at $a(n)$. Let $T_a$ be
the theory generated by these axioms. Every consistent extension of $T_a$
in this language is incomplete if it admits an axiom set that one oracle
program semidecides from every binary representation of $a$
(Theorem~\ref{thm:miller-incompleteness}). The constant family of each
consistent internal extension is essentially incomplete in its associated category
(Corollary~\ref{cor:miller-associated-categories}).

The third realization uses cosheaves on a three-point space. The
recursion category constructed from them is not equivalent as a
restriction category to the category of partial recursive functions.
In the total category of its Karoubi envelope we construct an initial
algebra of propositional formulas and an initial algebra of derivations
from the signed atomic axioms and the logical schemes by modus ponens.
Evaluating at either endpoint of the diagram $1\leftarrow0\to2$
gives a consistent propositional theory. Every
consistent extension in the same language with a c.e.~axiom set is
incomplete (Corollary~\ref{cor:cosheaf-essential-incompleteness}).
A conservative first-order extension of the internal propositional theory
supplies the third instance of
the associated-category construction
(Corollary~\ref{cor:fork-associated-theories}).
\subsection{Related work}

Rosolini's $P$-categories generalized dominical categories
\cite{RosoliniThesis,Rosolini}. Heller used them to define
prodominical categories \cite[Section~5]{Heller}.
We use the restriction categories of Cockett and Lack
\cite{CockettLack} (Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}).
Heller's existence theorem \cite[Sections~8--9]{Heller} and
Lengyel's existence theorems using faithful iteration functors
\cite{Lengyel2004,Corrections} concern the construction of recursion
categories. Di Paola and Montagna's syntactic examples raised the
question of extending Heller's theorem beyond locally connected categories
\cite{DPM}.

Di Paola and Heller assume throughout their Section~8 that the category
is a recursion category \cite[p.~621]{DPH}. For Theorem~8.15 they
require binary coproducts and, for each $f:Y\rightharpoonup Z$,
a section $s:Z\rightharpoonup Y$ satisfying $fs=\bar s$ and $fsf=f$.
Such a section gives $\ran(f)=fs=\bar s$: this restriction idempotent
fixes $f$, and $uf=vf$ implies $u(fs)=v(fs)$ for all parallel
$u,v:Z\rightharpoonup W$ \cite[p.~612, Definitions~6.1--6.2]{DPH}.
They also assume that $f+g$ is total whenever $f$ and $g$ are total
and that each canonical morphism
$(X\times Y)+(X\times Z)\to X\times(Y+Z)$ is an isomorphism
\cite[p.~615, Definition~7.1]{DPH}.

For a dominical category with binary coproducts and the stated sections,
let $\tau:X\times X\rightharpoonup X+X$ be a Turing morphism as in
\cite[p.~601, Definition~4.1]{DPH}. Thus for every
$p:X\times X\rightharpoonup X+X$ there is a total $k:X\to X$ such
that $p=\tau(k\times1_X)$. Put $h=\tau\Delta_X:X\rightharpoonup X+X$.
The domains $h^*(1_X+0_X)$ and $h^*(0_X+1_X)$ are disjoint.
If a complementary pair $c,d$ separated them, the diagonal construction
of \cite[pp.~625--626, Theorem~8.15]{DPH} would give a total $g:X\to X$ with
$g^*c=g^*d=0_X$. Thus $cg=dg=0_X$, and the range agreement law
(Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}) gives $c\ran(g)=d\ran(g)=0_X$.
For the copairing $[c,d]:X+X\rightharpoonup X$, commutativity of
restriction idempotents gives $\ran(g)[c,d]=0$. Since
$\ran[c,d]=c\vee d=1_X$, range agreement gives $\ran(g)=0_X$.
Then $g=0_X$, and totality gives $1_X=\bar g=0_X$. Hence the
diagonal domains are recursively inseparable if $1_X\ne0_X$.

Bernardi obtained categorical fixed-point
and inseparability results from precomplete equivalence relations,
including PA-provable equality of partial recursive functions among his
examples \cite[Sections~2--3, pp.~125--128]{Bernardi}.
Montagna obtained effectively inseparable pairs in his syntactic
category \cite[Remark~3.1]{Montagna}. The diagonal pair in
Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison} occurs in Lengyel's earlier comparison
\cite[Theorem~4.1]{Lengyel2006}. Appendix~\ref{app:lifting-counterexample}
gives a counterexample to that theorem as stated. Cockett attributes
to Lengyel the theorem that every nontrivial discrete Turing category
with finite joins of compatible morphisms stable under composition
has inseparable restriction idempotents
\cite[Sections~5.3 and 7.1, Theorem~7.8]{CockettComputability}.

Murwanashyaka, Pakhomov, and Visser prove a numerical antecedent of
Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-first-order-incompleteness}. Their theory of
an equivalence relation asserts the existence of a class of size $n+1$
for $n$ in one c.e.~set and denies it for $n$ in another. For disjoint
sets, the resulting theory is essentially undecidable exactly when the
sets are recursively inseparable \cite[Section~4.4, p.~1169]{MPV}. Here the indices form an
object of $\mathcal D$, and the first-order theory is free on the two
subobjects in the sense of Theorem~\ref{thm:free-first-order-adjunction}.

Di Paola and Heller also discussed the role of the formalized L\"ob
theorem among the axioms of diagonalizable algebras and the modal
provability logic $\mathrm{GL}$,
and the obstacles to extending modal fixed-point theorems to numerals
and quantification \cite[pp.~595--596]{DPH}. In categorical logic,
van Dijk and Gietelink Oldenziel give Joyal's arithmetic-universe
proofs of incompleteness and of the unprovability of consistency
\cite[Theorems~5.19--5.20]{vanDijkGO}. Their construction uses an
internal arithmetic universe in the initial arithmetic universe.

Cockett and Hofstra relate Turing categories to partial combinatory
algebras through idempotent splitting
\cite[Theorem~4.9]{CockettHofstra}. In a nontrivial Turing category with
a restriction zero and a provability predicate for the restriction order
on programs, Cockett constructs a restriction idempotent on the restriction
terminal object distinct from zero and the identity
\cite[Section~7.5, Theorem~7.14]{CockettComputability}.
In Theorem~\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness}, incompleteness of
an extension in the slice means that its theorem and refutation subobjects
fail to cover the sentence object of the constant family.
\section{Categorical preliminaries}\label{sec:preliminaries}
\subsection{Partial maps and restriction idempotents}\label{subsec:restriction-idempotents}

Composition is written $gf=g\circ f$, so $f$ is applied first.
A \emph{restriction category} is a category $\mathcal C$ with a
morphism $\bar f:X\rightharpoonup X$ for each $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$,
subject to the identities of Cockett and Lack~\cite[Section~2.1.1]{CockettLack},
\[
 f\bar f=f,\qquad
 \bar f\bar g=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \overline{g\bar f}=\bar g\bar f,\qquad
 \bar h f=f\overline{hf}.
\]
Here $g:X\rightharpoonup Z$ and $h:Y\rightharpoonup Z$.
The morphisms $\bar f$ are idempotent. They are called
\emph{restriction idempotents}, or \emph{domains} in
recursion-category terminology \cite[Section~5]{Heller}.
The morphism $f$ is \emph{total} when $\bar f=1_X$.
The \emph{category of total morphisms} $\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal C)$
has the objects of $\mathcal C$ and its total morphisms.
A \emph{restriction functor} $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ between
restriction categories satisfies $F(\bar f)=\overline{F(f)}$ for every
morphism $f$. A \emph{restriction equivalence} consists of restriction
functors in both directions whose composites are naturally isomorphic
to the respective identity functors.

Restriction idempotents on $X$ are ordered by $a\le b$ when $ba=a$.
Their meet is composition, their greatest element is $1_X$, and
$a\vee b$ denotes their least upper bound when it exists.
For parallel partial morphisms, the restriction order is
$f\le g$ when $f=g\bar f$.
Parallel morphisms $f,g:X\rightharpoonup Y$ are \emph{compatible} when
$f\bar g=g\bar f$. Their join, when it exists, is their least upper
bound in the restriction order.
A \emph{restriction zero} $0_{X,Y}:X\rightharpoonup Y$ is
absorbing under composition and satisfies
$\overline{0_{X,Y}}=0_{X,X}$. We abbreviate $0_{X,X}$ to $0_X$.
Restriction idempotents $a,b$ on $X$ are disjoint when $ab=0_X$.
They are complementary when also $a\vee b=1_X$.
A disjoint pair $a_0,a_1$ is \emph{inseparable} if no complementary
pair $c,c'$ satisfies $a_0\le c$ and $a_1\le c'$.

For $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ and a restriction idempotent $a$ on $Y$,
the \emph{inverse image} of $a$ is the restriction idempotent
$f^*a=\overline{af}$ on $X$. For restriction idempotents $a,b$ on $Y$,
the restriction identities give
\[
 f^*(ab)=(f^*a)(f^*b),\qquad
 f^*0_Y=0_X,\qquad f^*1_Y=\bar f.
\]
The middle equality assumes restriction zeros. For $g:Y\rightharpoonup Z$
and a restriction idempotent $c$ on $Z$, the composition law is
\[
 (gf)^*c=\overline{cgf}=\overline{\overline{cg}\,f}=f^*(g^*c).
\]
Thus inverse image is order-preserving (it preserves meets), and it
preserves the greatest restriction idempotent when $f$ is total.
The \emph{range} $\ran(f)$ of $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ is the least
restriction idempotent $r$ on $Y$ for which $rf=f$
\cite[Section~6]{Heller}. We require the agreement law
\[
 gf=hf\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 g\ran(f)=h\ran(f)
 \qquad(g,h:Y\rightharpoonup Z).
\]
For a partial function $f$, the restriction idempotent
$\bar f$ and the range $\ran(f)$ are the partial identities on its
domain of definition and image, respectively.

A \emph{restriction monomorphism} $m:A\to X$ is a total morphism
with a partial inverse $r:X\rightharpoonup A$ satisfying
$rm=1_A$ and $mr=\bar r$.
A restriction idempotent $e$ on $X$ \emph{splits} if
$e=mr$ for a total $m:A\to X$ and $r:X\rightharpoonup A$
with $rm=1_A$. The category is \emph{split} when every restriction
idempotent splits.
The \emph{restriction idempotent completion} of a restriction category
$\mathcal C$, denoted by $\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal C)$, is obtained
by splitting the restriction idempotents of $\mathcal C$.
Cockett--Lack denote this category by $K_r(\mathcal C)$
\cite[Section~2.3.3]{CockettLack}.
The objects of $\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal C)$ are pairs $(X,e)$, where $e$ is a
restriction idempotent on $X$. Its morphisms
$f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$ are morphisms
$f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ satisfying $f=dfe$.
The identity of $(X,e)$ is $e$, and $f$ is total there when
$\bar f=e$. Thus $(X,e)$ is the object through which $e$ splits.

The \emph{Karoubi envelope} $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathcal C)$ has as objects
pairs $(X,e)$ with $e:X\rightharpoonup X$ and $e^2=e$. A morphism
$(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$ is an $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ with $f=dfe$. The identity of
$(X,e)$ is $e$. The restriction of $f$ is represented by $\bar f e$,
so $f$ is total in the envelope precisely when $\bar f e=e$.
This is the construction $K_E(\mathcal C)$ of
\cite[Section~2.3.3, Proposition~2.26]{CockettLack} with $E$ the class
of all idempotents.

For a category $\mathcal E$ with pullbacks, let
$\operatorname{Par}(\mathcal E,\operatorname{Mono})$ be its category
of partial maps, where $\operatorname{Mono}$ denotes all monomorphisms
of $\mathcal E$ \cite[Section~3]{CockettLack}.
Its objects are those of $\mathcal E$. A morphism
$X\rightharpoonup Y$ is an isomorphism class of spans
$X\xleftarrow{m}D\xrightarrow{f}Y$ with $m$ monic, and composition
uses pullback. Its restriction is represented by
$X\xleftarrow{m}D\xrightarrow{m}X$.
We identify its total category with $\mathcal E$.
\subsection{Products, coproducts, and local connectedness}

A \emph{binary restriction product} $X\times Y$ has total
projections $\pi_1:X\times Y\to X$ and $\pi_2:X\times Y\to Y$.
For morphisms $f:Z\rightharpoonup X$ and $g:Z\rightharpoonup Y$,
there is a unique $\langle f,g\rangle:Z\rightharpoonup X\times Y$
with
\[
 \pi_1\langle f,g\rangle=f\bar g,\qquad
 \pi_2\langle f,g\rangle=g\bar f,\qquad
 \overline{\langle f,g\rangle}=\bar f\bar g.
\]
For $f:X\rightharpoonup X'$ and $g:Y\rightharpoonup Y'$, their product is
$f\times g=\langle f\pi_1,g\pi_2\rangle:X\times Y\rightharpoonup X'\times Y'$.
The total diagonal is
$\Delta_X=\langle1_X,1_X\rangle:X\to X\times X$.
A restriction category has a $P$-category structure if and only if
it has binary restriction products
\cite[Proposition 4.5]{CockettLackIII}.

Binary \emph{restriction coproducts} are categorical coproducts with
total injections $i_0:X\to X+Y$ and $i_1:Y\to X+Y$.
For morphisms $f:X\rightharpoonup Z$ and $g:Y\rightharpoonup Z$,
write $[f,g]:X+Y\rightharpoonup Z$ for their copairing.
For $f:X\rightharpoonup X'$ and $g:Y\rightharpoonup Y'$, write
$f+g=[i_0 f,i_1 g]:X+Y\rightharpoonup X'+Y'$.
The \emph{codiagonal} is
$\nabla_X=[1_X,1_X]:X+X\to X$.
For restriction idempotents $a,b$ on $X$, their copairing is
$[a,b]:X+X\rightharpoonup X$. A restriction idempotent $r$ on $X$
satisfies $r[a,b]=[a,b]$ precisely when $ra=a$ and $rb=b$, by the
coproduct property. The least such $r$ is therefore
$\ran[a,b]=a\vee b$ whenever ranges exist.

A range functor in the sense of Cockett, Guo, and Hofstra
\cite[p.~424]{CGHRangeI} preserves restrictions and ranges. Following
\cite[p.~7]{Lengyel2006}, we also require a \emph{range functor}
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ to preserve
restriction zeros and binary restriction coproducts. In particular, the canonical morphism
$\chi_{X,Y}=[F i_0,F i_1]:FX+FY\to F(X+Y)$
is an isomorphism, and
$F[f,g]\chi_{X,Y}=[Ff,Fg]$ for $f:X\rightharpoonup Z$ and
$g:Y\rightharpoonup Z$. For restriction idempotents $a,b$ on $X$, put
$h=F[a,b]:F(X+X)\rightharpoonup FX$ and $u=\chi_{X,X}$.
For every restriction idempotent $r$ on $FX$, one has
$rhu=hu$ if and only if $rh=h$, since $u$ is an isomorphism.
Thus $\ran(h)=\ran(hu)$, giving
\[
 F(a\vee b)=\ran(F[a,b])=\ran[F(a),F(b)]=F(a)\vee F(b).
\]
Since $F$ also preserves composition, zeros, and identities, it sends
complementary pairs to complementary pairs.
It need not preserve restriction products. Let $\Pfn$ denote the
category of sets and partial functions. For example, the functor
$F:\Pfn\to\Pfn$ given by $F(X)=X\times\{0,1\}$ and
$F(f)=f\times1_{\{0,1\}}$ preserves restrictions, images, zeros,
and coproducts. Its canonical morphism from $F(X\times Y)$ to
$FX\times FY$ sends $((x,y),a)$ to $((x,a),(y,a))$, and is
not surjective when $X,Y$ are nonempty.

A restriction idempotent $a$ on $X$ is \emph{connected} if, for
restriction idempotents $b,c$ on $X$, the equations $a=b\vee c$ and
$bc=0$ imply $b=0$ or $c=0$. The category is \emph{locally connected}
when its connected restriction idempotents are jointly epimorphic: for
$f,g:X\rightharpoonup Y$, the equations $fa=ga$ for every connected
restriction idempotent $a$ on $X$ imply $f=g$.
A \emph{partial monomorphism} $p:X\rightharpoonup Y$ satisfies
$pu=pv\Rightarrow\bar p u=\bar p v$ for all
$u,v:W\rightharpoonup X$.
A \emph{section} of $p$ is a morphism $s:Y\rightharpoonup X$
with $ps=\bar s$ and $psp=p$.
\emph{Weak choice} means that every partial monomorphism has such
a section. For partial functions, this is the existence of the
partial inverse of an injection on its domain.
\subsection{Recursion categories}

A restriction category with binary restriction products and zeros is
\emph{prodominical} if $f\times0_{A,B}=0_{X\times A,Y\times B}$ for
every $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ and all objects $A,B$. It is \emph{isotypical} if any
two of its objects are isomorphic.

A \emph{Turing morphism} on $U$ is a morphism
$\tau:U\times U\rightharpoonup U$ such that, for every object $X$
and every $f:X\times U\rightharpoonup U$, there is a total
parameter morphism $r:X\to U$ satisfying $f=\tau(r\times1_U)$.
A \emph{recursion category} is a prodominical isotypical
category with binary restriction products and a Turing morphism,
as in \cite[Section 9]{Heller}.

In a restriction category $\mathcal C$, a \emph{restriction terminal object}
$1$ has a unique total morphism $!_X:X\to1$ for each object $X$,
satisfying $!_Yf=!_X\bar f$ for every $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$.
A restriction category is \emph{cartesian} if it has binary
restriction products and a restriction terminal object.
A \emph{Turing category} is a cartesian restriction category with an
object $U$, called a \emph{Turing object}, such that every object $X$
admits a total morphism $m_X:X\to U$ and a morphism
$r_X:U\rightharpoonup X$ with $r_Xm_X=1_X$, and there is a
Turing morphism on $U$. This is the characterization of
Cockett--Hofstra~\cite[Theorem 3.4]{CockettHofstra}.
\section{Diagonal comparison and complementary conditionals}\label{sec:lifting}

The diagonal computation on a Turing object $U$ has two disjoint
domains $a_0,a_1$, one for each output summand. Let $F:\mathscr R\to\mathcal A$
be a range functor. The comparison theorem gives conditions under which
disjoint domains $P\geq F(a_0)$ and $N\geq F(a_1)$ satisfy
$P\vee N\ne1_{FU}$.

For a coproduct $Y+Z$, let
$\varepsilon_0=1_Y+0_Z$ and $\varepsilon_1=0_Y+1_Z$ be its summand
restriction idempotents. For the coproduct injections $i_j$, one has
$\varepsilon_j i_j=i_j$ and $\varepsilon_k i_j=0$ for $k\ne j$.
Thus $\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1$ vanishes on both injections.
Any upper bound $r$ of $\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1$ satisfies
$r i_j=r\varepsilon_j i_j=i_j$ for both $j$. The coproduct property
therefore gives $\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1=0_{Y+Z}$ and
$\varepsilon_0\vee\varepsilon_1=1_{Y+Z}$.
\subsection{The comparison theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Comparison theorem]\label{thm:comparison}
Let $\mathscr R$ be a recursion category with ranges and binary
restriction coproducts, let $\mathcal A$ be a restriction category with
ranges, restriction zeros, and binary restriction coproducts, and let
$F:\mathscr R\to\mathcal A$ be a range functor.
Choose a Turing morphism $\tau:U\times U\rightharpoonup U$ and an
isomorphism $b:U\to U+U$. Define
\[
 h=b\tau\Delta_U:U\rightharpoonup U+U,\qquad
 a_0=h^*(1_U+0_U),\qquad a_1=h^*(0_U+1_U).
\]
Let $P,N$ be disjoint restriction idempotents on $FU$ such that
$F(a_0)\le P$ and $F(a_1)\le N$. Suppose that
$s:FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$ satisfies
\[
 s^*(1_{FU}+0_{FU})=N,\qquad
 s^*(0_{FU}+1_{FU})=P,
\]
and that there is a morphism $\ell:U\rightharpoonup U+U$ with
$F\ell=\chi_{U,U}s$.
Then there is a total morphism $g:U\to U$ such that
\[
 (Fg)^*P=(Fg)^*N=0_{FU}.
\]
For any such $g$, if $F(1_U)\ne0$ and inverse image along $Fg$ preserves the join
$P\vee N$, then $P\vee N\ne1_{FU}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $u=b^{-1}\ell:U\rightharpoonup U$. Apply the Turing property
to $u\pi_2:U\times U\rightharpoonup U$, obtaining a total morphism
$g:U\to U$ with $\tau(g\times1_U)=u\pi_2$.
Since $g$ is total,
\[
 (g\times1_U)\langle1_U,g\rangle=\langle g,g\rangle=\Delta_Ug,
 \qquad \pi_2\langle1_U,g\rangle=g.
\]
Precomposing with $\langle1_U,g\rangle$ therefore gives
$\tau\Delta_Ug=ug$. Composing with $b$ gives $hg=\ell g$.

Write
$E=Fg:FU\to FU$ and
$H=\chi_{U,U}^{-1}Fh:FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$.
Applying $F$ to the preceding identity gives $HE=sE$.
For $i=0,1$, let $\varepsilon_i$ and $\varepsilon_i'$ be the $i$th summand
idempotents on $U+U$ and $FU+FU$, respectively. The coproduct comparison
satisfies $F(\varepsilon_i)\chi_{U,U}=\chi_{U,U}\varepsilon_i'$, so
$F(a_i)=H^*\varepsilon_i'$. Pullback along $E$ gives
$E^*F(a_i)=(HE)^*\varepsilon_i'=(sE)^*\varepsilon_i'$.
The two prescribed inverse images under $s$ give
\[
 E^*F(a_0)=E^*N,\qquad E^*F(a_1)=E^*P.
\]
The inequalities imply
\[
 E^*N=E^*F(a_0)\le E^*P,\qquad
 E^*P=E^*F(a_1)\le E^*N.
\]
The two inverse images are equal, and their meet is
$E^*(PN)=0_{FU}$. Hence both are zero.
If $P\vee N=1_{FU}$, totality of $E$ and preservation of this join
would give
\[
 1_{FU}=E^*1_{FU}=E^*(P\vee N)
       =E^*P\vee E^*N=0_{FU},
\]
contrary to $F(1_U)\ne0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Lifted separators]\label{cor:separator}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison} on
$\mathscr R$, $\mathcal A$, $F$, $\tau$, and $b$, suppose that
$F(1_U)\ne0$ and inverse images along total morphisms in $\mathcal A$ preserve
binary joins. A complementary pair $P,N$ on $FU$ satisfying
$F(a_0)\le P$ and $F(a_1)\le N$ admits no pair of morphisms
$s:FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$ and
$\ell:U\rightharpoonup U+U$ with
\[
 s^*(1_{FU}+0_{FU})=N,\qquad
 s^*(0_{FU}+1_{FU})=P,\qquad
 F\ell=\chi_{U,U}s.
\]
\end{corollary}
\subsection{Complementary conditionals}

\begin{corollary}[Inseparability from complementary conditionals]
\label{cor:source-conditionals}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison} on
$\mathscr R$, $\mathcal A$, $F$, $\tau$, and $b$, suppose that
$F(1_U)\ne0$ and inverse images along total morphisms in $\mathcal A$ preserve
binary joins of restriction idempotents.
Suppose that, for every complementary pair $c,c'$ on $U$, there
is a total morphism $\ell_c:U\to U+U$ satisfying
\[
 \ell_cc=i_1c,\qquad \ell_cc'=i_0c',
\]
where $i_0,i_1:U\to U+U$ are the coproduct injections.
Then the restriction idempotents $a_0,a_1$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison} are inseparable in $\mathscr R$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Put $\varepsilon_0=1_U+0_U$ and $\varepsilon_1=0_U+1_U$.
The diagonal domains are disjoint, since
\[
 a_0a_1=h^*(\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_1)=h^*0_{U+U}=0_U.
\]
Suppose $c,c'$ separate $a_0,a_1$. The defining equations of
$\ell_c$ give
\[
 (\varepsilon_0\ell_c)c=0=(i_0c')c,\qquad
 (\varepsilon_0\ell_c)c'=i_0c'=(i_0c')c'.
\]
Thus $\varepsilon_0\ell_c$ and $i_0c'$ agree after precomposition
with $[c,c']:U+U\rightharpoonup U$. Its range is
$c\vee c'=1_U$, so the agreement law gives $\varepsilon_0\ell_c=i_0c'$.
Interchanging the summands gives $\varepsilon_1\ell_c=i_1c$.
Taking restrictions yields $\ell_c^*\varepsilon_0=c'$ and
$\ell_c^*\varepsilon_1=c$.

Since $F$ preserves meets, joins, zeros, and identities,
$P=F(c)$ and $N=F(c')$ are complementary on $FU$.
For the canonical coproduct isomorphism
$\chi_{U,U}:FU+FU\to F(U+U)$, define
$s_c=\chi_{U,U}^{-1}F(\ell_c):FU\to FU+FU$.
Restriction preservation and the coproduct comparison give
\[
 s_c^*(1_{FU}+0_{FU})=N,\qquad
 s_c^*(0_{FU}+1_{FU})=P.
\]
Together with $F(\ell_c)=\chi_{U,U}s_c$, these identities contradict
Corollary~\ref{cor:separator}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:disjoint-joins}
Let $\mathcal C$ be a restriction category with restriction zeros and
binary restriction coproducts. Suppose every pair of parallel morphisms
whose restriction idempotents are disjoint has a join in the restriction
order.
For complementary restriction idempotents $c,c'$ on $X$, the morphism
\[
 \ell_c=(i_1c)\vee(i_0c'):X\rightharpoonup X+X
\]
is total and satisfies $\ell_cc=i_1c$ and $\ell_cc'=i_0c'$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The restrictions of $i_1c$ and $i_0c'$ are $c$ and $c'$ because
the injections are total. The upper-bound equations for the join
give $\ell_cc=i_1c$ and $\ell_cc'=i_0c'$.
Both $c$ and $c'$ lie below $\bar\ell_c$, so
$1_X=c\vee c'\le\bar\ell_c$ and $\ell_c$ is total.
\end{proof}

\section{Internal theories and essential incompleteness}\label{sec:internal-theories}
\subsection{Theories and their interpretation}\label{subsec:theories-and-interpretation}

Let $\mathscr R$ be a restriction category with ranges, restriction
zeros, and binary restriction coproducts. Put
$\mathscr S=\Split(\mathscr R)$ and $\mathcal D=\Tot(\mathscr S)$.
Assume that $\mathcal D$ is regular with disjoint, pullback-stable finite
coproducts and has the syntax of Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}.
Write $\Phi$ for the formula object ($\Fm$ in Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-syntax})
and $j:S\hookrightarrow\Phi$ for its sentence subobject. For an axiom
subobject $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S$, suppose the inference
endofunctor $H_A:\mathcal D/\Phi\to\mathcal D/\Phi$ of
Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations} has an initial algebra
with conclusion morphism $c_A:P_A\to\Phi$.
The pullback in $\mathcal D$
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 P_{A,S}\arrow[r]\arrow[d,"c_{A,S}"'] & P_A\arrow[d,"c_A"]\\
 S\arrow[r,hook,"j"'] & \Phi
\end{tikzcd}
\]
restricts conclusions to sentences. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-theory}, the regular image
$m_A:T_{A,S}\hookrightarrow S$ of $c_{A,S}$ is the inverse image along $j$ of the least deductively closed formula
subobject containing the axioms. Assume that $m_A$ is a restriction monomorphism in
$\mathscr S$: it has a partial inverse
$r_A:S\rightharpoonup T_{A,S}$ with
$r_A m_A=1_{T_{A,S}}$ and $m_A r_A=\bar r_A$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image} then gives the restriction
idempotent representing the sentence theory,
\[
 t_A=m_A r_A=\ran(c_{A,S}):S\rightharpoonup S.
\]
Negation preserves the empty free-variable list, so it restricts
to a total morphism $\nu:S\to S$ in $\mathcal D$.
The restriction idempotent $\nu^*t_A$ represents refutable sentences.
The sentence theory is \emph{consistent} when
$t_A\nu^*t_A=0_S$, and \emph{complete} when
$t_A\vee\nu^*t_A=1_S$.
A sentence subobject $u:U\hookrightarrow S$ is \emph{deductively closed}
if it contains every sentence derivable with $U$ as axioms. When the initial
derivation algebra for $U$ exists, this says that its sentence conclusion
$c_{U,S}:P_{U,S}\to S$ factors through $u$.
The theory $T_{A,S}$ is \emph{essentially incomplete} when it is consistent
and, for every deductively closed $U$ in the same language,
\[
 T_{A,S}\leq U,\quad U\wedge\nu^*U=\bot
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad U\vee\nu^*U\ne\top.
\]

Let $F:\mathscr R\to\mathcal A$ be a range functor, where
$\mathcal A$ is a split restriction category. For each restriction
idempotent $e$ on an object $X$ of $\mathscr R$, choose a splitting
\[
 F(e)=m_e r_e,\qquad
 m_e:E_e\to FX,\qquad r_e:FX\rightharpoonup E_e,\qquad
 r_e m_e=1_{E_e},
\]
with $m_e$ total. Choose the identity splitting when $e=1_X$.
These choices define a restriction functor
\[
 \widehat F:\mathscr S\longrightarrow\mathcal A,\qquad
 \widehat F(X,e)=E_e,\qquad
 \widehat F(f)=r_d F(f)m_e
\]
for $f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$. Its restriction to
$\mathscr R$, identified with the objects $(X,1_X)$, is $F$.
Indeed, the equations $f=dfe$ and $r_e m_e=1_{E_e}$ verify
identities and composition, while the restriction axioms give
$\overline{r_d F(f)m_e}=r_e F(\bar f)m_e$.

This extension preserves ranges. To see this, write
$a=\ran(f)\le d$, where the same restriction idempotent represents
the range in $\mathscr R$ and in $\mathscr S$.
Since $af=f$ and $a\le d$,
$(r_d F(a)m_d)\widehat F(f)=\widehat F(f)$.
If a restriction idempotent $q$ on $E_d$ satisfies
$q\widehat F(f)=\widehat F(f)$, the restriction axiom
$q r_d=r_d\overline{q r_d}$ gives
$m_d q r_d=F(d)\overline{q r_d}$, a product of restriction idempotents
on $FY$. Moreover, $(m_d q r_d)F(f)=F(f)$. Consequently
$F(a)=\ran(F(f))\le m_d q r_d$, and hence
$r_d F(a)m_d\le q$ since $r_d m_d=1_{E_d}$. Thus
$\ran(\widehat F(f))=\widehat F(\ran(f))$.
For a zero morphism $0:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$,
$\widehat F(0)=r_d F(0)m_e=0_{E_e,E_d}$ because $F$ preserves zeros.

The coproduct of $(X,e)$ and $(Y,d)$ in $\mathscr S$ is
$(X+Y,e+d)$. The canonical morphism
\[
 \kappa_{e,d}=r_{e+d}\chi_{X,Y}(m_e+m_d):
 E_e+E_d\longrightarrow E_{e+d}
\]
has inverse
$(r_e+r_d)\chi_{X,Y}^{-1}m_{e+d}$. The inverse equations follow
from $m_e r_e=F(e)$, $m_d r_d=F(d)$, and
$F(e+d)=\chi_{X,Y}(F(e)+F(d))\chi_{X,Y}^{-1}$.
Thus $\widehat F$ preserves binary restriction coproducts.
Since $a\vee b=\ran[a,b]$ for restriction idempotents $a,b$ on
the same object, preservation of coproducts and ranges gives
$\widehat F(a\vee b)=\widehat F(a)\vee\widehat F(b)$.

\begin{proposition}[Interpretation of a sentence theory]\label{prop:interpreted-theory}
Let $F:\mathscr R\to\mathcal A$ be a range functor with split
target, let $\widehat F:\Split(\mathscr R)\to\mathcal A$ be the
extension by chosen splittings, and let $t_A=m_A r_A=\ran(c_{A,S})$
be a sentence theory constructed above. Then
\begin{gather*}
 \widehat F(t_A)=\ran(\widehat F(c_{A,S})),\\
 \widehat F(m_A)\widehat F(r_A)=\widehat F(t_A),\qquad
 \widehat F(r_A)\widehat F(m_A)=1_{\widehat F(T_{A,S})}.
\end{gather*}
Suppose moreover that $\mathcal A=\Par(\mathcal E,\Mono)$ for a
regular category $\mathcal E$. If the total morphism
$\widehat F(c_{A,S})$ factors in $\mathcal E$ through a
monomorphism $v:V\hookrightarrow\widehat F S$, then
there is a unique $h:\widehat F(T_{A,S})\to V$ in $\mathcal E$
such that $v h=\widehat F(m_A)$. Put
\[
 d_V=[\widehat F S\xleftarrow{v}V\xrightarrow{v}\widehat F S]:
 \widehat F S\rightharpoonup\widehat F S.
\]
If $d_V(\widehat F\nu)^*d_V=0$, then
$\widehat F(t_A)(\widehat F\nu)^*\widehat F(t_A)=0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Range preservation gives the first equation, and functoriality
gives the two splitting equations. In $\Par(\mathcal E,\Mono)$,
every monomorphism of $\mathcal E$ has a partial inverse.
Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image} therefore identifies the range
of $\widehat F(c_{A,S})$ with the partial identity on its regular
image in $\mathcal E$. Its splitting by $\widehat F(m_A)$ and
$\widehat F(r_A)$ identifies $\widehat F(m_A)$ with that image.
Factorization through $v$ implies
$\widehat F(t_A)\le d_V$. Monotonicity of inverse image and meet
then gives
\[
 \widehat F(t_A)(\widehat F\nu)^*\widehat F(t_A)
 \le d_V(\widehat F\nu)^*d_V=0.
\]
\end{proof}

For an interpretation with validity subobject
$v:V\hookrightarrow\widehat F S$, soundness means that there is a morphism
$k:\widehat F(P_{A,S})\to V$ in $\mathcal E$ such that
$v k=\widehat F(c_{A,S})$. If validity and its inverse image under
negation are disjoint, the proposition then gives consistency of the
interpreted sentence theory.
\subsection{Incompleteness from semantic consistency}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:logical-comparison}
Let $\mathscr R,\mathcal A,F,U,\tau,b,a_0,a_1$ satisfy the
categorical hypotheses and definitions of
Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison}. Suppose that $\mathcal A$ is split,
that inverse images along total morphisms in $\mathcal A$ preserve binary joins
of restriction idempotents, and that $F(1_U)\ne0$.
Let $t_A=\ran(c_{A,S})$ represent a sentence theory in
$\Split(\mathscr R)$ as above, with total negation
$\nu:S\to S$, and let $\theta:(U,1_U)\to S$ be total in
$\Split(\mathscr R)$. With the identity splitting at $1_U$,
$\widehat F\theta:FU\to\widehat F S$. Put
\[
 t=\widehat F(t_A),\qquad
 P=(\widehat F\theta)^*t,\qquad
 N=(\widehat F\theta)^*(\widehat F\nu)^*t.
\]
Assume that $t(\widehat F\nu)^*t=0$, $F(a_0)\le P$, and
$F(a_1)\le N$.
Suppose there are partial morphisms
$s:FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$ and
$\ell:U\rightharpoonup U+U$ satisfying
\[
 s^*(1_{FU}+0_{FU})=N,\qquad
 s^*(0_{FU}+1_{FU})=P,\qquad
 F\ell=\chi_{U,U}s.
\]
Then there is a total $g:U\to U$ in $\mathscr R$ such that
\[
 (\widehat F(\theta g))^*t=0,\qquad
 (\widehat F(\theta g))^*(\widehat F\nu)^*t=0.
\]
In particular,
\[
 t\vee(\widehat F\nu)^*t\ne1_{\widehat F S},\qquad
 t_A\vee\nu^*t_A\ne1_S.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Preservation of meets and zero by inverse image gives
$PN=(\widehat F\theta)^*\bigl(t(\widehat F\nu)^*t\bigr)=0$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison} therefore supplies a total $g:U\to U$
with $(Fg)^*P=(Fg)^*N=0$. Since $\widehat F$ agrees with $F$ on
$\mathscr R$, composition of inverse images gives the two equalities.

If $t\vee(\widehat F\nu)^*t=1_{\widehat F S}$, inverse image along
the total morphism $\widehat F(\theta g):FU\to\widehat F S$ would
give
\[
 1_{FU}
 =(\widehat F(\theta g))^*\bigl(t\vee(\widehat F\nu)^*t\bigr)
 =0\vee0=0,
\]
contrary to $F(1_U)\ne0$.
If $t_A\vee\nu^*t_A=1_S$, applying $\widehat F$ and using
preservation of joins and inverse images would give
$t\vee(\widehat F\nu)^*t=1_{\widehat F S}$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}
\subsection{Inseparability in the source}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:domain-incompleteness}
Let $\mathcal C$ be a restriction category with restriction zeros and
binary joins of restriction idempotents preserved by inverse image along total morphisms.
Let $a,b$ be inseparable restriction idempotents on $U$. Suppose that
$\theta:U\to S$ and $\nu:S\to S$ are total, and that a restriction
idempotent $t_0$ on $S$ satisfies $a\le\theta^*t_0$ and
$b\le\theta^*\nu^*t_0$.
For every restriction idempotent $t\ge t_0$ on $S$ with $t\,\nu^*t=0_S$,
the pair $t,\nu^*t$ is inseparable. In particular,
$t\vee\nu^*t\ne1_S$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Suppose complementary restriction idempotents $e,e'$ on $S$ satisfy
$t\le e$ and $\nu^*t\le e'$. Put
$c=\theta^*e$ and $c'=\theta^*e'$. Inverse image preserves
meets and zero, so $cc'=\theta^*(ee')=0_U$.
Preservation of joins and totality of $\theta$ give
$c\vee c'=\theta^*(e\vee e')=\theta^*1_S=1_U$.
Monotonicity gives
$a\le\theta^*t_0\le\theta^*t\le c$ and
$b\le\theta^*\nu^*t_0\le\theta^*\nu^*t\le c'$.
Thus $c,c'$ would separate $a,b$, a contradiction.
If $t\vee\nu^*t=1_S$, the disjoint pair $t,\nu^*t$ would
itself be such a complementary separator.
\end{proof}

Visser proves essential undecidability when a recursive function maps
two recursively inseparable sets into the provable and the refutable
sentences, respectively \cite[Lemma~23]{VisserEHU}.
In synthetic computability, Kirst and Peters use a reduction of a
diagonal pair to provability and refutability to find an independent
sentence in each consistent extension with semidecidable provability
\cite[Definitions~7, 17 and Theorem~20]{KirstPeters}.
Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness} gives inseparability of
the theorem and refutation domains. In the split case, let
$j:J\hookrightarrow S$ represent their join $t\vee\nu^*t$.
Properness means that $1_S:S\to S$ does not factor through $j$.
If the total category has a terminal object $1$, a global point
outside the join is a morphism $s:1\to S$ that does not factor
through $j$. A proper subobject can contain every global element. For
example, let a nontrivial group $G$ act on itself by left
multiplication. The inclusion $1\hookrightarrow 1+G$ of $G$-sets is
proper, but every morphism $1\to 1+G$ factors through it because the
second summand has no fixed point.

An inseparable pair on an object of $\mathscr R$ remains inseparable
in $\Split(\mathscr R)$: the fully faithful inclusion
$U\mapsto(U,1_U)$ changes neither its endomorphisms nor its
restriction idempotents. Thus
Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness} applies to sentence
objects in $\Split(\mathscr R)$ even when the inseparable pair was
constructed in $\mathscr R$.

Section~\ref{sec:arithmetic} applies
Theorem~\ref{thm:logical-comparison} to a soundness factorization
and the lift in $S_{\PA}$ constructed in
Lemma~\ref{lem:arithmetic-proof-search}.
The numerical, Miller-sequence, and cosheaf realizations apply

\subsection{Generation and logical translations}
\label{sec:internal-adjunctions}

Continue with $\mathscr S=\Split(\mathscr R)$ and
$\mathcal D=\Tot(\mathscr S)$. Assume that $\mathcal D$ is regular
with disjoint, pullback-stable finite coproducts. Fix a first-order
syntax as in Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}. For every
axiom subobject of its sentence object, assume an initial algebra
of derivations as in Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}. For an object $X$ of $\mathcal D$, write
$\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathcal D}(X)$ for the ordered collection of
subobjects of $X$, with order given by factorization. If
$f:X\to Y$ is total, write $f^*B$ for the inverse image of
$B\hookrightarrow Y$, and $f_!A$ for the image of
$A\hookrightarrow X\xrightarrow{f}Y$.

Let $j:S\hookrightarrow\Phi$ be the sentence inclusion. For
$A\hookrightarrow S$, let $C(A)\hookrightarrow\Phi$ be the least
closed formula subobject supplied by
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-theory}, and put
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(A)=j^*C(A)=T_{A,S}.
\]
Write $\operatorname{Th}_{\mathcal D}(S)$ for the sentence theories,
ordered by inclusion. Equivalently, these are the subobjects $T$ with
$\operatorname{Gen}(T)=T$.

\begin{theorem}[Generation reflection]\label{thm:first-order-reflection}
Under the preceding hypotheses, $\operatorname{Gen}$ is extensive,
monotone, and idempotent. It is left adjoint to the inclusion
$\iota:\operatorname{Th}_{\mathcal D}(S)\hookrightarrow
\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathcal D}(S)$. Thus, for every axiom
subobject $A$ and sentence theory $T$,
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(A)\leq T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\leq T.
\]
For each theory $T$ choose a representative $i_T:|T|\hookrightarrow S$.
Let $J:\operatorname{Th}_{\mathcal D}(S)\to\mathcal D/S$ send $T$
to $i_T$ and $T\leq U$ to the unique factorization of $i_T$ through $i_U$. Then
$\Gamma(a:A\to S)=\operatorname{Gen}(\im a)$ defines a functor
$\Gamma:\mathcal D/S\to\operatorname{Th}_{\mathcal D}(S)$ with
$\Gamma\dashv J$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Axiom introduction gives $A\leq\operatorname{Gen}(A)$, and
leastness of $C(A)$ gives monotonicity. The closed formula
subobject $C(A)$ contains $j_!\operatorname{Gen}(A)$, whence
$C(\operatorname{Gen}(A))\leq C(A)$. Pullback along $j$ and
extensivity prove idempotence. For a theory $T$, monotonicity and $\operatorname{Gen}(T)=T$ give
$\operatorname{Gen}(A)\leq T$ if $A\leq T$. Extensivity gives the converse. If $k:(a:A\to S)\to(b:B\to S)$ lies over $S$, then $a=bk$,
so $\im a\leq\im b$. Applying generation gives $\Gamma(k)$.
A morphism in $\mathcal D/S$ from $a$ to $J(T)$ exists uniquely
exactly when $\im a\leq T$.
The equivalence identifies this hom-set with the hom-set from
$\Gamma(a)$ to $T$ in the theory order, naturally in both objects.
\end{proof}

A first-order presentation $P$ consists of the named-variable
syntax of Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}, the logical rules of
Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}, and a choice of initial
derivation algebra for each subobject $A\hookrightarrow S_P$ of its
sentence object. Choosing $A$ specifies the nonlogical axioms of a
theory in $P$. Write $\Tm_P,\Phi_P,S_P,j_P,\nu_P$ for the term
object, formula object, sentence object, sentence inclusion, and
sentence negation. Write $\operatorname{Gen}_P$ for generation.

Fix a common variable object $V$ for two such presentations $P,Q$.
A logical translation $\sigma:P\to Q$ consists of total morphisms
\[
 \sigma_{\Tm}:\Tm_P\to\Tm_Q,\qquad
 \sigma_{\Phi}:\Phi_P\to\Phi_Q,\qquad
 \sigma_S:S_P\to S_Q.
\]
The term morphism fixes variables, $\sigma_{\Tm}\eta_P=\eta_Q$,
where $\eta_P:V\to\Tm_P$ and $\eta_Q:V\to\Tm_Q$ are the variable constructors.
The formula morphism preserves equality, negation, implication, and quantification by the equations
\begin{align*}
 \sigma_\Phi\mathsf{eq}_P&=\mathsf{eq}_Q(\sigma_{\Tm}\times\sigma_{\Tm}),&
 \sigma_\Phi\neg_P&=\neg_Q\sigma_\Phi,\\
 \sigma_\Phi({\Rightarrow}_P)&=({\Rightarrow}_Q)(\sigma_\Phi\times\sigma_\Phi),&
 \sigma_\Phi{\forall}_P&={\forall}_Q(1_V\times\sigma_\Phi).
\end{align*}
The sentence morphism satisfies $j_Q\sigma_S=\sigma_\Phi j_P$.
Since $j_Q$ is monic and formula negation restricts to sentence
negation in each presentation, $\sigma_S\nu_P=\nu_Q\sigma_S$.

For substitution, put $E_P=V\times\Tm_P$, $E_Q=V\times\Tm_Q$ and
$e=1_V\times\sigma_{\Tm}:E_P\to E_Q$. Write
$a_{T,P}:\Tm_P\times E_P\to\Tm_P$ for term substitution and
$i_P:\Adm_P\hookrightarrow\Phi_P\times E_P$,
$a_{F,P}:\Adm_P\to\Phi_P$ for the admissibility inclusion and
formula substitution. Use the corresponding notation for $Q$.
We require $\sigma_{\Tm}a_{T,P}=a_{T,Q}(\sigma_{\Tm}\times e)$
and a morphism $s:\Adm_P\to\Adm_Q$ satisfying
\[
 i_Q s=(\sigma_\Phi\times e)i_P,\qquad
 a_{F,Q}s=\sigma_\Phi a_{F,P}.
\]
Thus each admissible substitution in $P$ translates to an admissible
substitution in $Q$ with the indicated value.

For $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, write $R_n^P$ for the object of logical
rule instances with $n$ premises, with premise and conclusion morphisms
\[
 p_n^P:R_n^P\to\Phi_P^n,\qquad q_n^P:R_n^P\to\Phi_P,
\]
and use the corresponding notation for $Q$.
Preservation of the logical rules means that there are morphisms
$\rho_n:R_n^P\to R_n^Q$ with
\[
 p_n^Q\rho_n=\sigma_{\Phi}^{n}p_n^P,\qquad
 q_n^Q\rho_n=\sigma_{\Phi}q_n^P.
\]
For $n=0$, $\rho_0$ sends instances of the seven logical axiom
schemes to logical axiom instances. For generalization and modus ponens
one may take $\rho_1=1_V\times\sigma_\Phi$ and
$\rho_2=\sigma_\Phi\times\sigma_\Phi$, respectively.
The three morphisms $\sigma_{\Tm},\sigma_\Phi,\sigma_S$ determine the
translation. The conditions on $s$ and $\rho_n$ require their existence.
Composition is componentwise. A nonlogical predicate
may be interpreted by a formula. Put
$\operatorname{Th}_P=\operatorname{Th}_{\mathcal D}(S_P)$.

\begin{theorem}[Translation Galois connection]\label{thm:translation-galois}
Let $\sigma:P\to Q$ be a logical translation between presentations
satisfying the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-reflection}. Inverse image along
$\sigma_S$ sends sentence theories to sentence theories, and
\[
 \sigma_\#:\operatorname{Th}_P\rightleftarrows
 \operatorname{Th}_Q:\sigma^*,\qquad
 \sigma_\#(T)=\operatorname{Gen}_Q(\sigma_!T),\qquad
 \sigma_\#\dashv\sigma^*.
\]
Here $\sigma_!$ and $\sigma^*$ abbreviate the image and inverse-image
operations for $\sigma_S$. Moreover,
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}_Q\sigma_!
   =\sigma_\#\operatorname{Gen}_P.
\]
For composable logical translations $\sigma:P\to Q$ and
$\rho:Q\to R$,
\[
 (\rho\sigma)_\#=\rho_\#\sigma_\#,\qquad
 (\rho\sigma)^*=\sigma^*\rho^*.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $T$ be a $Q$-theory. Put $D=C_Q(T)\hookrightarrow\Phi_Q$ and
$E=\sigma_\Phi^*D\hookrightarrow\Phi_P$. Closure of $D$ under the
$n$-premise rule means $(p_n^Q)^*(D^n)\leq(q_n^Q)^*D$ in
$\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathcal D}(R_n^Q)$. Pulling back along $\rho_n$
gives $(p_n^P)^*(E^n)\leq(q_n^P)^*E$. For $n=0$, the left side is
the whole object of logical axiom instances. Since
$j_P^*E=\sigma_S^* j_Q^*D=\sigma^*T$, also $j_{P,!}\sigma^*T\leq E$. Thus
$C_P(\sigma^*T)\leq\sigma_{\Phi}^*C_Q(T)$.
Pullback along $j_P$ gives
$\operatorname{Gen}_P(\sigma^*T)\leq\sigma^*T$;
extensivity gives equality. Now image and inverse image satisfy
$\sigma_!A\leq B$ exactly when $A\leq\sigma^*B$.
Combining this with Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-reflection}
proves the adjunction.

Apply closure preservation to
$T=\operatorname{Gen}_Q(\sigma_!A)$. The resulting inclusion
$\sigma_!\operatorname{Gen}_P(A)
\leq\operatorname{Gen}_Q(\sigma_!A)$, together with extensivity
and idempotence, proves the generation identity. Composition of
images and pullbacks then gives the two composition identities.
\end{proof}

Let $\mathsf{Ax}_V(\mathcal D)$ have pairs $(P,A)$ as objects,
where $P$ has variable object $V$ and $A\hookrightarrow S_P$ is an
axiom subobject. Its morphisms are logical translations
$\sigma:(P,A)\to(Q,B)$ satisfying $\sigma_!A\leq B$.
Let $\mathsf{Th}_V(\mathcal D)$ be its full subcategory on sentence
theories. Theorem~\ref{thm:translation-galois} also gives a
reflection
\[
 \mathsf{Ax}_V(\mathcal D)\rightleftarrows
 \mathsf{Th}_V(\mathcal D),\qquad
 (P,A)\longmapsto(P,\operatorname{Gen}_P(A)).
\]
The right adjoint is inclusion. The hom-set bijection leaves the
translation unchanged, since, for a target theory $T$,
$\sigma_!A\leq T$ exactly when
$\sigma_!\operatorname{Gen}_P(A)\leq T$.

\subsection{Change of the ambient category}
\label{sec:deduction-change-of-base}

Let $\mathscr S_i$ be split restriction categories and put
$\mathcal D_i=\Tot(\mathscr S_i)$ for $i=1,2$. Assume the
generation hypotheses above for a presentation in each
$\mathcal D_i$, with sentence object $S_i$. Write
$\operatorname{Th}_i=\operatorname{Th}_{\mathcal D_i}(S_i)$ and
let $\Gamma_i\dashv J_i$ be the functors of
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-reflection}. Let
$F:\mathscr S_1\to\mathscr S_2$ preserve restrictions and induce
a regular functor $G:\mathcal D_1\to\mathcal D_2$. A regular
functor preserves finite limits and regular epimorphisms. Fix a
total morphism $\sigma:GS_1\to S_2$ and define
\[
 L(A)=\im(\sigma G i_A),\qquad
 K(a:A\to S_1)=\sigma Ga:GA\to S_2.
\]
Here $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S_1$ represents the subobject $A$.
Thus $L:\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathcal D_1}(S_1)\to
\operatorname{Sub}_{\mathcal D_2}(S_2)$ is monotone. The functor
$K:\mathcal D_1/S_1\to\mathcal D_2/S_2$ sends a morphism $k$ over $S_1$
to $Gk$ over $S_2$.
For each $A$, let $c_{A,S_1}:P_{A,S_1}\to S_1$ be the pullback
of its conclusion morphism $c_A:P_A\to\Phi_1$ along the sentence
inclusion $j_1:S_1\hookrightarrow\Phi_1$.

\begin{proposition}[Comparison of deduction]\label{prop:deduction-comparison}
With these data, suppose that for every $A\hookrightarrow S_1$
there is a total morphism
\[
 p_A:GP_{A,S_1}\to P_{L(A),S_2},\qquad
 c_{L(A),S_2}p_A=\sigma Gc_{A,S_1}.
\]
Then $L^{\mathrm{th}}(T)=\operatorname{Gen}_2L(T)$ defines a
functor on theory orders satisfying
\[
 L^{\mathrm{th}}\operatorname{Gen}_1=\operatorname{Gen}_2L,
 \qquad \Gamma_2K=L^{\mathrm{th}}\Gamma_1.
\]
Consequently the left-adjoint square in
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large,row sep=large]
 \mathcal D_1/S_1\arrow[r,"K"]
   \arrow[d,shift right=.8ex,"\Gamma_1"'] &
 \mathcal D_2/S_2\arrow[d,shift right=.8ex,"\Gamma_2"']\\
 \operatorname{Th}_1\arrow[r,"L^{\mathrm{th}}"']
   \arrow[u,shift right=.8ex,"J_1"'] &
 \operatorname{Th}_2\arrow[u,shift right=.8ex,"J_2"']
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad \Gamma_i\dashv J_i
\]
commutes. Factorization through the generated theory gives a natural
transformation $KJ_1\to J_2L^{\mathrm{th}}$.
If $L\dashv R$ on subobject orders, $R$ sends theories to theories
and $L^{\mathrm{th}}\dashv R|_{\operatorname{Th}_2}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Factor $c_{A,S_1}$ through its image $\operatorname{Gen}_1(A)$.
Since $G$ preserves the regular epimorphism in this factorization,
\[
 L(\operatorname{Gen}_1(A))
 =\im(\sigma Gc_{A,S_1})
 =\im(c_{L(A),S_2}p_A)
 \leq\operatorname{Gen}_2(L(A)).
\]
Applying $\operatorname{Gen}_2$ gives one inequality in the first
identity by idempotence. The other follows from
$A\leq\operatorname{Gen}_1(A)$ by monotonicity of $L$ and
$\operatorname{Gen}_2$. Factoring $a$ through its image in the same
way gives $\im(K(a))=L(\im a)$, proving the second identity.
For each theory $T$, the unique factorization of $KJ_1(T)$ through
$J_2L^{\mathrm{th}}(T)$ defines the component of the comparison at $T$. Uniqueness proves naturality.
For a closed $B$, adjunction gives $LRB\leq B$, and hence
\[
 L\operatorname{Gen}_1(RB)
 \leq\operatorname{Gen}_2(LRB)\leq B.
\]
Thus $\operatorname{Gen}_1(RB)\leq RB$. Extensivity gives
equality, and the restricted adjunction follows from the
generation reflection.
\end{proof}

Suppose $G$ has a right adjoint $G^{\mathrm R}:\mathcal D_2\to\mathcal D_1$
with unit $\eta:1_{\mathcal D_1}\to G^{\mathrm R}G$. Put
$\sigma^\flat=G^{\mathrm R}\sigma\,\eta_{S_1}:S_1\to G^{\mathrm R}S_2$.
For $i_B:B\hookrightarrow S_2$, let $R(B)=(\sigma^\flat)^*(G^{\mathrm R} i_B)$.
The right adjoint $G^{\mathrm R}$ preserves monomorphisms.
For $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S_1$, a factorization
$k:GA\to B$ with $i_Bk=\sigma G i_A$ transposes to
$k^\flat=G^{\mathrm R}k\,\eta_A:A\to G^{\mathrm R}B$ satisfying
\[
 G^{\mathrm R} i_B\,k^\flat=\sigma^\flat i_A .
\]
Conversely this equation transposes back to the factorization through
$i_B$. By the pullback defining $R(B)$, it follows that
$L(A)\leq B$ exactly when $A\leq R(B)$.

To construct the derivation comparison, suppose
$\sigma_{\Phi}:G\Phi_1\to\Phi_2$ satisfies
$\sigma_\Phi G j_1=j_2\sigma$, where $j_i:S_i\hookrightarrow\Phi_i$.
Define $K_\Phi:\mathcal D_1/\Phi_1\to\mathcal D_2/\Phi_2$ by
$K_{\Phi}(q)=\sigma_{\Phi}Gq$ on objects and $K_\Phi(k)=Gk$ on
slice morphisms. Its right adjoint $R_\Phi$ sends $b:B\to\Phi_2$
to the pullback of $G^{\mathrm R}b$ along
$G^{\mathrm R}\sigma_{\Phi}\,\eta_{\Phi_1}:\Phi_1\to G^{\mathrm R}\Phi_2$.
On a morphism $k:(B,b)\to(B',b')$ over $\Phi_2$, $R_\Phi(k)$
is induced by $1_{\Phi_1}$ and $G^{\mathrm R}k:G^{\mathrm R}B\to G^{\mathrm R}B'$ on these pullbacks.
For each $A$, suppose the comparison of rule instances supplies a
natural transformation
\[
 \lambda:K_{\Phi}H_A\to H_{L(A)}K_{\Phi}.
\]
Its component at $q$ sends a rule instance with premise derivations
over $q$ to a target rule instance with premises over $K_\Phi(q)$
and the translated conclusion. Let
$\delta_{L(A)}:H_{L(A)}P_{L(A)}\to P_{L(A)}$ be the target initial algebra and
$\epsilon:K_{\Phi}R_{\Phi}\to1$ the counit. Transpose
\[
 K_{\Phi}H_AR_{\Phi}P_{L(A)}
 \xrightarrow{\lambda}H_{L(A)}K_{\Phi}R_{\Phi}P_{L(A)}
 \xrightarrow{H_{L(A)}\epsilon}H_{L(A)}P_{L(A)}
 \xrightarrow{\delta_{L(A)}}P_{L(A)}
\]
to give $R_{\Phi}P_{L(A)}$ a source algebra structure. Source initiality
gives a morphism from $P_A$ to this algebra. Its transpose has
underlying morphism $h:GP_A\to P_{L(A)}$ with
$c_{L(A)}h=\sigma_\Phi Gc_A$. Write $k_A:P_{A,S_1}\to P_A$ for the
pullback projection. Then
\[
 c_{L(A)}h\,Gk_A=\sigma_\Phi G j_1\,Gc_{A,S_1}
                 =j_2\sigma Gc_{A,S_1}.
\]
The pullback $P_{L(A),S_2}=P_{L(A)}\times_{\Phi_2} S_2$ therefore gives
$p_A$ with components $h\,Gk_A$ and $\sigma Gc_{A,S_1}$.

\subsection{Free first-order theories and inseparability}
\label{sec:free-first-order-theories}

Assume additionally that every monomorphism of $\mathcal D$ has a
partial inverse in $\mathscr S$. Subobjects then identify with
restriction idempotents. A consistent sentence theory is essentially incomplete if a total morphism
reduces an inseparable pair to its theorem and refutation subobjects
(Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness}).

Fix the decidable variable object $V$ of
Appendix~\ref{app:categorical-hypotheses}. Suppose that for every
$X\in\mathcal D$ the first-order language whose only nonlogical
symbols are nullary predicates indexed by $X$ has the syntax of
Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}, including initiality of the
syntax and variable-list algebras in every parameter slice. For every
axiom subobject of its sentence object, assume an initial derivation
algebra as in Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}. Write
$P_X$ for this presentation. Its terms are variables. A generalized index
$x:W\to X$ determines the atomic sentence $\theta_Xx:W\to S_X$,
where $\theta_X:X\to S_X$ is the atomic sentence constructor.
For $h:W'\to W$, the sentence at $xh$ is $(\theta_Xx)h$.
For disjoint subobjects $a,b\hookrightarrow X$, with inclusions
$i_a,i_b$, put
\[
 A_{a,b}=\im(\theta_Xi_a)\vee\im(\nu_X\theta_Xi_b),
 \qquad T_{a,b}=\operatorname{Gen}_{P_X}(A_{a,b}).
\]

Let $\mathsf{Pair}_c(\mathcal D)$ have triples $(X,a,b)$ as
objects, where $a\wedge b=0$ and $T_{a,b}$ is consistent. A
morphism $f:(X,a,b)\to(Y,c,d)$ is a total $f:X\to Y$ satisfying
$a\leq f^*c$ and $b\leq f^*d$.
Let $\mathsf{FO}_V(\mathcal D)$ have pairs $(P,T)$ as objects,
where $P$ has variable object $V$ and $T$ is a consistent
sentence theory. A morphism $(P,T)\to(Q,U)$ is a logical
translation $\sigma:P\to Q$ with $\sigma_!T\leq U$.
Define
\[
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}(X,a,b)=(P_X,T_{a,b}),\qquad
 J_{\mathrm{FO}}(P,T)=(S_P,T,\nu_P^*T).
\]
The functor $\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}$ sends $f$ to the interpretation
extending $\theta_Yf$, and $J_{\mathrm{FO}}$ sends $\sigma$ to
$\sigma_S$.

Voutsadakis gives an adjunction for relational signatures in which
morphisms substitute formulas for relation symbols
\cite[Theorem~7]{Voutsadakis}. Here an assignment $f:X\to S_P$ of
sentences to nullary predicates extends to a theory morphism
$(P_X,T_{a,b})\to(P,T)$ precisely when $a\leq f^*T$ and
$b\leq f^*\nu_P^*T$.

\begin{theorem}[Free first-order adjunction]
\label{thm:free-first-order-adjunction}
Let $\mathcal D=\Tot(\mathscr S)$ be regular with disjoint,
pullback-stable finite coproducts, where $\mathscr S$ is a split
restriction category and every monomorphism of $\mathcal D$ has a partial
inverse in $\mathscr S$. Fix a decidable variable object $V$. For every
$X\in\mathcal D$, assume that $P_X$ has the syntax and variable-list
algebras of Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}, initial in every
parameter slice, and an initial derivation algebra for each axiom
subobject. In $\mathsf{FO}_V(\mathcal D)$, each presentation $P$
has an initial derivation algebra for every $A\hookrightarrow S_P$,
and $T$ in an object $(P,T)$ is a consistent sentence theory of $P$.
Then
\[
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}:
 \mathsf{Pair}_c(\mathcal D)\rightleftarrows
 \mathsf{FO}_V(\mathcal D):J_{\mathrm{FO}},\qquad
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}\dashv J_{\mathrm{FO}}.
\]
The unit at $(X,a,b)$ has underlying morphism $\theta_X:X\to S_X$.
The counit $\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}J_{\mathrm{FO}}(P,T)\to(P,T)$
is the translation extending $1_{S_P}:S_P\to S_P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $f:X\to S_P$ assign a sentence to each nullary predicate, and
interpret variables by $V\to\Tm_P$. Initiality of the free syntax
gives a unique term and formula interpretation $\widehat f$.
Let $\ell:W_X\xrightarrow{\sim}W_P$ be the unique isomorphism
of the two initial variable-list algebras. Write
$\FV_X:\Phi_X\to W_X$ and $\FV_P:\Phi_P\to W_P$ for the
free-variable occurrence morphisms. Since $f$ takes values in
sentences, each interpreted nullary predicate has empty occurrence list.
At a quantifier, $\ell$ commutes with deletion of the bound variable;
at equality and implication it commutes with concatenation.
The occurrence folds therefore give
$\FV_P\widehat f_\Phi=\ell\FV_X$ on formulas and
$\FV_{\Tm_P}\widehat f_{\Tm}=\ell\FV_{\Tm_X}$ on terms.
Pullback along the empty-list inclusion gives the sentence morphism $\widehat f_S:S_X\to S_P$.

For substitution of $t$ for $x$ in $\forall y\,\varphi$, the branch
$y=x$ retains the quantified formula. On the branch $y\ne x$,
membership in the occurrence lists is preserved by $\ell$.
Hence the two interpretations give the same values for the tests
$x\in\FV_X(\varphi)$ and $y\in\FV_{\Tm}(t)$ that determine
capture in~\eqref{eq:quantifier-fold}. At a nullary predicate,
substitution fixes its interpreting sentence by the absent-variable
identity of Appendix~\ref{app:substitution}. At an equality $u=v$,
substitution acts on the two terms. Put $E_X=V\times\Tm_X$,
$E_P=V\times\Tm_P$ and $e=1_V\times\widehat f_{\Tm}:E_X\to E_P$.
Write $b_X:\Phi_X\times E_X\to 1+\Phi_X$ and
$b_P:\Phi_P\times E_P\to 1+\Phi_P$ for formula substitution with
failure in the first summand. The constructor equations and initiality
over $E_X$ give
\[
 (1_1+\widehat f_\Phi)b_X=b_P(\widehat f_\Phi\times e).
\]
Pulling back the success summand gives $s:\Adm_X\to\Adm_P$ with
the two substitution equations above. These equations translate the
instantiation and equality-substitution instances, and preservation
of the free-variable test translates quantifier distribution.
The other four logical schemes are preserved by their constructors.
Thus $\widehat f:P_X\to P$ is a logical translation.

Take $X=S_P$ and $f=1_{S_P}$, and denote the resulting translation
by $\epsilon:P_{S_P}\to P$. The theory $\epsilon_S^*T$ is closed by
Theorem~\ref{thm:translation-galois}. It is consistent because
$\epsilon_S$ commutes with negation and its inverse-image map preserves
meets and bottom. As $\epsilon_S\theta_{S_P}=1_{S_P}$, it contains
the positive axioms indexed by $T$ and the negative axioms indexed
by $\nu_P^*T$. Their generated theory is therefore consistent.
This proves that $J_{\mathrm{FO}}(P,T)$ is an object of
$\mathsf{Pair}_c(\mathcal D)$. For a theory morphism
$\sigma:(P,T)\to(Q,U)$, the bound $T\leq\sigma_S^*U$ and
$\sigma_S\nu_P=\nu_Q\sigma_S$ give
$\nu_P^*T\leq\sigma_S^*\nu_Q^*U$. Thus $\sigma_S$ is a morphism of pairs.

For a pair morphism $f:(X,a,b)\to J_{\mathrm{FO}}(P,T)$, the
defining inequalities put $\widehat f_!A_{a,b}$ inside $T$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:translation-galois} gives
$\widehat f_!T_{a,b}\leq T$.

Conversely, a theory morphism $\sigma:(P_X,T_{a,b})\to(P,T)$
restricts to $f=\sigma_S\theta_X:X\to S_P$. Preservation of negation
and the definition of the signed axioms give
\[
 a\leq f^*T,\qquad b\leq f^*\nu_P^*T.
\]
The extension satisfies $\widehat f_S\theta_X=f$, and uniqueness gives
$\widehat{\sigma_S\theta_X}=\sigma$. These equations make the two
assignments inverse. For a morphism of pairs $k$ with underlying
morphism $X'\to X$ and a theory translation $\rho:(P,T)\to(Q,U)$,
both sides of
\[
 \widehat{\rho_S f k}=\rho\,\widehat f\,\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}(k)
\]
take each generating predicate to the same sentence in $Q$.
Uniqueness of extension gives the equation, proving naturality in both
variables. The same uniqueness gives the functor laws for
$\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}$. For $J_{\mathrm{FO}}$ they follow from
composition of sentence morphisms.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:signed-first-order-incompleteness}
Under the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:free-first-order-adjunction}, let $a,b$ be
disjoint subobjects of $X$ and suppose $T_{a,b}$ is consistent.
Then $T_{a,b}$ is essentially incomplete if and only if $(a,b)$
is inseparable in $\mathscr S$, that is, if and only if no complementary
subobjects $C,D$ of $X$ satisfy $a\leq C$ and $b\leq D$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $U\geq T_{a,b}$ be any consistent closed theory of $P_X$.
Axiom introduction and monotonicity of inverse image give
\[
 a\leq\theta_X^*T_{a,b}\leq\theta_X^*U,\qquad
 b\leq\theta_X^*\nu_X^*T_{a,b}\leq\theta_X^*\nu_X^*U .
\]
If $U$ were complete, $U$ and $\nu_X^*U$ would be complementary.
Their inverse images under $\theta_X$ would separate $a,b$, as in
Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness}. Thus inseparability
implies essential incompleteness.

Conversely, let $m:C\hookrightarrow X$ and $n:D\hookrightarrow X$
be complementary subobjects containing $a$ and $b$, respectively.
Disjointness and extensivity make $[m,n]:C+D\to X$ monic, and
its image is the join of the two subobjects, hence all of $X$.
Thus $[m,n]$ is an isomorphism. Let $\Two=1+1$ with injections
$\mathbf{f},\mathbf{t}:1\to\Two$, in that order. The total morphism
$d=[\mathbf{t}!_C,\mathbf{f}!_D][m,n]^{-1}:X\to\Two$
is true on $a$ and false on $b$.
Interpret the terms in $1$, the nullary predicates by $d$, equality
by $\mathbf{t}:1\to\Two$ under $1\times1\cong1$, negation and
implication by their Boolean truth functions, and universal quantification
by the projection
$\pi_2:V\times\Two\to\Two$.
Free syntax gives a total valuation $v:\Phi_X\to\Two$.
In the substitution fold of Appendix~\ref{app:substitution}, consider
the pairs of an original formula and a substitution result. In
$\Phi_X\times(1+\Phi_X)$ take the coproduct of the failure summand
$\Phi_X\times1$ and the equalizer of $v\pi_1,v\pi_2:\Phi_X^2\to\Two$
in the success summand.
The atomic results lie in this subobject because a nullary predicate
retains its index and every equality has value $\mathbf t$. Negation and implication
preserve equality of values whenever their substituted arguments succeed.
At $\forall y\,\varphi$, substitution for $x$ returns the original
formula when $y=x$. When $y\ne x$, a successful result has the value
of the substituted body, hence of $\varphi$. Every failure belongs to
the first summand. Thus the subobject, with the full term carrier, is
closed under the substitution algebra in the parameter slice.
Initiality puts the fold in this subobject. On the success summand
$i:\Adm\hookrightarrow\Phi_X\times V\times\Tm_X$, with result
$a_F:\Adm\to\Phi_X$, this gives $v a_F=v\pi_{\Phi_X}i$.
Thus instantiation and
substitutivity of equality have value
$\mathbf{t}$. Reflexivity has that value by the interpretation of
equality, and quantifier distribution has it because quantification leaves
each truth value unchanged. The propositional schemes have value
$\mathbf{t}$, and modus ponens and generalization preserve truth.
Thus $U=(v j_X)^*\mathbf{t}\hookrightarrow S_X$ is closed. Negation
interchanges true and false, so $\nu_X^*U=(v j_X)^*\mathbf{f}$.
The two fibers are complementary, proving consistency and completeness.
Since $v j_X\theta_X=d$, the signed axioms lie in $U$, whence
$T_{a,b}\leq U$.
This contradicts essential incompleteness.
\end{proof}

\section{Theory extensions and recursion categories}
\label{sec:theory-extensions}

To an internal theory $t:T\hookrightarrow S$ we associate the category of
partial maps in the slice of the total category over $T$.
An inclusion of theories induces a fully
faithful functor between their associated categories. Under the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness}, the constant family is essentially
incomplete exactly when $t$ is. Evaluation at a logical theorem recovers
$t$ from this family.
\subsection{Categories associated with internal theories}

Let $\mathscr R$ be a recursion category, put
$\mathscr C=\Split(\mathscr R)$ and $\mathcal D=\Tot(\mathscr C)$,
and assume that $\mathcal D$ is regular with disjoint stable finite
coproducts. Assume also that every monomorphism $m:A\hookrightarrow X$
of $\mathcal D$ has a partial inverse $m^\dagger:X\rightharpoonup A$
with $m^\dagger m=1_A$ and $mm^\dagger=\overline{m^\dagger}$.
A monic span $X\xleftarrow{m}A\xrightarrow{f}Y$ in $\mathcal D$
represents $fm^\dagger$ in $\mathscr C$. Conversely, if
$h:X\rightharpoonup Y$ and $\bar h=mm^\dagger$, then $hm$ is total
and $h=(hm)m^\dagger$. Any two splittings of $\bar h$ give isomorphic
spans. For a second span $Y\xleftarrow{n}B\xrightarrow{g}Z$,
write $a:A\times_Y B\to A$ and $b:A\times_Y B\to B$ for the
pullback projections. The monomorphism $a$ represents the domain of
$n^\dagger f$. Indeed, a total $k:W\to A$ factors through $a$
if and only if $fk$ factors through $n$, equivalently if and only if
$n^\dagger f k$ is total. Hence $a a^\dagger=\overline{n^\dagger f}$.
Since $n^\dagger f a=b$, we have $n^\dagger f=b a^\dagger$ and
\[
 (g n^\dagger)(f m^\dagger)=(g b)(m a)^\dagger .
\]
The identity span represents the identity morphism, giving
$\mathscr C\simeq\Par(\mathcal D,\Mono)$.

For $T\in\mathcal D$, set
\[
 \mathscr C[T]=\Par(\mathcal D/T,\Mono).
\]
An object is a total morphism $p:X\to T$. A partial morphism from
$p:X\to T$ to $q:Y\to T$ is a span $X\xleftarrow{m}A\xrightarrow{f}Y$
with $m$ monic and $pm=qf$, up to isomorphism of its middle object
commuting with both legs.
Composition is by pullback. Its total category is $\mathcal D/T$.

\begin{lemma}[Turing structure in partial slices]
\label{lem:partial-slice-turing}
Under these assumptions, $\mathscr C$ and every $\mathscr C[T]$ are
Turing categories. If $Q$ is the original Turing object, with
$\tau:Q\times Q\rightharpoonup Q$, the Turing object in $\mathscr C[T]$
is $T\times Q\to T$. Under the product identification
$(T\times Q)\times_T(T\times Q)\cong T\times(Q\times Q)$, its
Turing morphism is
$1_T\times\tau:T\times(Q\times Q)\rightharpoonup T\times Q$ over $T$.
Let $\mathscr R[T]$ be the full restriction subcategory on the objects
$T\times X\to T$ for $X\in\mathscr R$. Then $\mathscr R[T]$ is a
recursion category and
\[
 \Split(\mathscr R[T])\simeq\mathscr C[T].
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The terminal object of $\mathcal D$ is restriction terminal in
$\mathscr C$. For $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$, split $\bar f=mr$.
The total morphism $fm$ satisfies $!_Yfm=!_Xm$, so composition with
$r$ gives $!_Yf=!_X\bar f$.

Every split object $(X,e)$ has a total embedding into $(X,1_X)$
and a partial retraction. An isomorphism $X\cong Q$ in $\mathscr R$
makes $(X,e)$ a retract of $Q$. The Turing morphism extends as in
Cockett--Hofstra~\cite[Section 3.5]{CockettHofstra}.
A morphism $(X,e)\times Q\rightharpoonup Q$ is represented in $\mathscr R$
by $f:X\times Q\rightharpoonup Q$ with $f(e\times1_Q)=f$.
Choose a total parameter $a:X\to Q$ with $f=\tau(a\times1_Q)$.
Then $f=\tau((ae)\times1_Q)$, and $ae:(X,e)\to Q$ is total since
$\overline{ae}=e$.
Thus $\mathscr C$ is Turing.

For $p:X\to T$, a total embedding $m_X:X\to Q$ gives a monomorphism
$m=\langle p,m_X\rangle:X\hookrightarrow T\times Q$. Its partial inverse
$m^\dagger:T\times Q\rightharpoonup X$ is a retraction over $T$.
The slice product of $p$ and $T\times Q\to T$ is
$X\times_T(T\times Q)\cong X\times Q$, with structure map $p\pi_1$.
Let $\varphi:(X\times Q,p\pi_1)\rightharpoonup(T\times Q,\pi_1)$
be a partial morphism over $T$. Its second component is
$f=\pi_2\varphi:X\times Q\rightharpoonup Q$ in $\mathscr C$.
Commutation over $T$ on the domain of definition gives
$\pi_1\varphi=p\pi_1\overline\varphi$.
Choose a total $a:X\to Q$ with $f=\tau(a\times1_Q)$. The total
parameter $\langle p,a\rangle:(X,p)\to(T\times Q,\pi_1)$ induces,
under the two slice product identifications, the morphism
\[
 \langle p\pi_1,\langle a\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle\rangle:
 X\times Q\longrightarrow T\times(Q\times Q).
\]
Its composite with $1_T\times\tau$ has second component $f$ and first
component $p\pi_1\bar\varphi$, so it equals $\varphi$.

An isomorphism $X\cong Y$ in $\mathscr R$ induces
$T\times X\cong T\times Y$ over $T$. The restriction product of two
such families is represented by $T\times(X\times Y)\to T$.
The zero span has domain the initial object of $\mathcal D/T$;
pullback stability of this initial object makes its product with any
partial map a zero span. Fullness supplies the parameter
$\langle p,a\rangle$ above whenever $p$ is a constant family.
For each $p:X\to T$, the graph embedding $m$ above satisfies
$m^\dagger m=1_X$ and $mm^\dagger=\overline{m^\dagger}$ over $T$.
Thus $m$ and $m^\dagger$ split the restriction idempotent
$\overline{m^\dagger}$ on $T\times Q\to T$ through $p$.
Since $\mathscr R[T]$ is full and $\mathscr C[T]$ is split,
the inclusion $\mathscr R[T]\hookrightarrow\mathscr C[T]$ induces
the claimed restriction equivalence.
\end{proof}

Fix a propositional or first-order deductive system in $\mathcal D$
as in Section~\ref{sec:internal-theories}, with sentence object $S$
and negation $\nu:S\to S$. In each slice $\mathcal D/P$, take the
syntax with constant family of sentences $P\times S\to P$ and the
logical rules with parameter $P$. Assume an initial derivation algebra
for every axiom subobject of this sentence family.
For a sentence theory $t:T\hookrightarrow S$, retain the sentence
family and theory
\[
 \widetilde S_T=(T\times S\xrightarrow{\pi_1}T),\qquad
 \widetilde t=1_T\times t:T\times T\hookrightarrow T\times S.
\]
The logical operations and rules retain the first coordinate.
Thus $\widetilde t$ is an internal theory in $\mathscr C[T]$.
\subsection{Functoriality under theory extension}

\begin{theorem}[Theory extensions and associated categories]
\label{thm:theory-extension}
Let $\mathscr R,\mathscr C,\mathcal D$ and the deductive system
satisfy the preceding assumptions. For internal theories
$t:T\hookrightarrow S$ and $u:U\hookrightarrow S$, let
$i:T\hookrightarrow U$ satisfy $t=ui$. Postcomposition defines a
fully faithful restriction functor
\[
 \Sigma_i:\mathscr C[T]\longrightarrow\mathscr C[U].
\]
Pullback defines $i^*:\mathscr C[U]\to\mathscr C[T]$, and the
underlying categories have adjunctions
\[
 \Sigma_i\dashv i^*\dashv\Sigma_i.
\]
If $i$ is proper, $\Sigma_i$ is not essentially surjective.
For composable theory inclusions $i,j$,
$\Sigma_j\Sigma_i=\Sigma_{ji}$.

The sentence and theorem comparison morphisms in $\mathcal D/U$
are $i\times1_S$ and $i\times i$. They give the commutative square
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 \Sigma_i(T\times T\to T)
   \arrow[r,"i\times i"]\arrow[d,hook,"\Sigma_i\widetilde t"'] &
 (U\times U\to U)\arrow[d,hook,"\widetilde u"]\\
 \Sigma_i\widetilde S_T\arrow[r,"i\times1_S"'] & \widetilde S_U.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Equivalently, $\widetilde S_T\cong i^*\widetilde S_U$ and
$\widetilde t\leq i^*\widetilde u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Postcomposition sends $p:X\to T$ to $ip:X\to U$ and retains each
span. Monicity of $i$ makes commutation over $U$ equivalent to
commutation over $T$ for spans between such objects. This proves full
faithfulness, restriction preservation, and the composition law.
The functor $i^*$ sends $q:Y\to U$ to the projection $T\times_U Y\to T$.
It sends $Y\xleftarrow{m}A\xrightarrow{f}Z$ over $U$ to
$T\times_UY\xleftarrow{i^*m}T\times_UA\xrightarrow{i^*f}T\times_UZ$
over $T$. The left leg remains monic, and pullback preserves the pullbacks
defining span composition.

For $p:X\to T$ and $q:Y\to U$, a span from $\Sigma_i p$ to $q$
factors its right leg uniquely through $T\times_UY$. This gives
\[
 \mathscr C[U](\Sigma_i p,q)\cong\mathscr C[T](p,i^*q).
\]
In the reverse direction let $Y\xleftarrow{m}A\xrightarrow{f}X$
represent $q\rightharpoonup\Sigma_i p$, so $qm=ipf$.
The pair $\langle pf,m\rangle:A\to T\times_UY$ is monic because its
composite with the projection to $Y$ is $m$. It is the left leg of a
span $i^*q\rightharpoonup p$. Conversely, composing a monic left leg
with $T\times_UY\hookrightarrow Y$ recovers a monic left leg over $U$.
These inverse assignments give
\[
 \mathscr C[T](i^*q,p)\cong\mathscr C[U](q,\Sigma_i p).
\]
Both assignments commute with pullback composition. They are natural,
and prove the adjunctions. Put $Y_T=T\times_U Y$, and write
$m:Y_T\hookrightarrow Y$ for the pullback of $i$. The unit of
$i^*\dashv\Sigma_i$ at $q$ is represented by the span
\[
 Y\xleftarrow{m}Y_T\xrightarrow{1_{Y_T}}Y_T
\]
over $U$. Thus the unit is $m^\dagger:q\rightharpoonup\Sigma_i i^*q$;
its restriction is $mm^\dagger$.

Suppose $1_U:U\to U$ is isomorphic in $\mathscr C[U]$ to
$\Sigma_i(p:X\to T)$. The isomorphism from $1_U$ to $ip$ has a
