total underlying morphism $b:U\to X$ since its inverse $a$ satisfies
$ab=1_U$ and hence $1_U=\overline{ab}\leq\bar b$. Since $b$ lies
over $U$, $i(pb)=1_U$. Monicity of $i$ now gives $(pb)i=1_T$.
Thus for proper $i$ the object $1_U$ lies outside the essential
image of $\Sigma_i$.
The comparison identity
$(1_U\times u)(i\times i)=(i\times1_S)(1_T\times t)$
follows from $ui=t$. Pullback of the sentence family gives $T\times S$,
and its theorem family contains $T\times T$ by $1_T\times i$.
\end{proof}

Using the equivalences of Lemma~\ref{lem:partial-slice-turing},
the functor $\Sigma_i$ can be written
\[
 \Split(\mathscr R[T])\xrightarrow{\Sigma_i}\Split(\mathscr R[U]).
\]
For $p:X\to T$ and $q:Y\to T$, monicity of $i$ gives
$ipx=iqy$ if and only if $px=qy$ for every $x:W\to X$, $y:W\to Y$.
Thus $X\times_T Y\to X\times_U Y$ is an isomorphism preserving the
two projections, so $\Sigma_i$ preserves binary restriction products.
Its value at the restriction terminal object $1_T:T\to T$ is $i:T\to U$,
which is restriction terminal precisely when $i$ is an isomorphism.
For $q:Y\to U$, the unit $m^\dagger$ above is total precisely when
$m:T\times_UY\to Y$ is an isomorphism, that is, when $q$ factors through $i$.
\subsection{Essential incompleteness in the associated category}\label{subsec:essential-incompleteness-slice}

Suppose a fixed logical theorem gives a total $\lambda:1\to S$
factoring through every theory under consideration. For
$u:U\hookrightarrow S$, write $\lambda_U:1\to U$ for its factorization.
Define
\[
 B_U:\mathscr C\to\mathscr C[U],\qquad
 B_U(X)=(U\times X\to U),\qquad B_U(f)=1_U\times f.
\]
Pullback along $\lambda_U$ sends $p:X\to U$ to
$E_U(p)=1\times_U X$ and pulls back both legs of a partial-map span.
Identifying $\mathcal D/1$ with $\mathcal D$ gives
$E_U:\mathscr C[U]\to\mathscr C$. The projections
$1\times_U(U\times X)\cong X$ give a natural isomorphism
$E_UB_U\cong1_{\mathscr C}$.
The isomorphism makes $B_U$ faithful. By construction $B_U$ preserves
restrictions, totality, and finite restriction products. It sends $\tau$ to $1_U\times\tau$, the Turing morphism
of Lemma~\ref{lem:partial-slice-turing}. It restricts to
$B_U:\mathscr R\to\mathscr R[U]$ on the original recursion category.

For a consistent theory $u$, let $\delta_u:S\rightharpoonup\Two$
have value $\mathbf t$ on the theorem subobject and $\mathbf f$ on
the refutation subobject $\nu^*u$. Their disjoint coproduct defines
this partial morphism, with restriction $u\vee\nu^*u$.
Subobjects are here identified with their restriction idempotents.
Put
\[
 \widetilde\delta_u=B_U(\delta_u):
 U\times S\rightharpoonup U\times\Two.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Incompleteness in an associated category]
\label{thm:associated-incompleteness}
Under the categorical and syntax hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:theory-extension}, suppose that a logical theorem $\lambda:1\to S$ factors through each
consistent internal sentence theory $u:U\hookrightarrow S$, and write
$\lambda_U:1\to U$ for its factorization. Then for every such $u$,
$u$ is essentially incomplete in $\mathscr C$ if and only if $\widetilde u=B_U(u)$ is
essentially incomplete in $\mathscr C[U]$. Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 u\text{ is incomplete}
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \widetilde\delta_u\text{ is not total},\\
 (u,\nu^*u)\text{ is inseparable in }\mathscr C
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \widetilde\delta_u\text{ has no total extension in }\mathscr C[U].
\end{aligned}
\]
If a consistent theory $t:T\hookrightarrow S$ admits a total reduction
of an inseparable pair to its theorem and refutation subobjects, every
consistent extension $u\geq t$ has an essentially incomplete theory
$\widetilde u$ in its associated category. The partial morphism $\widetilde\delta_u$ has no total extension.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use the restrictions to total morphisms
\[
 B:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D/U,\qquad E:\mathcal D/U\to\mathcal D
\]
of $B_U$ and $E_U$, respectively. Both are changes of base, along
$!_U:U\to1$ and $\lambda_U:1\to U$, with $\mathcal D/1\cong\mathcal D$.
They preserve finite limits. Regularity makes images stable under pullback,
and extensivity makes finite coproducts stable under pullback. Thus
both functors preserve consistency and completeness.

Let $j:S\hookrightarrow\Phi$ include sentences among formulas.
For a closed sentence theory $v\hookrightarrow S$, let
$C(v)\hookrightarrow\Phi$ be the formula subobject generated by $v$,
so $j^*C(v)=v$. Applying $B$ to its rule operations equips $B(C(v))$
with the operations in the slice and includes the axioms $Bv$.
Initiality for $Bv$ therefore places every derivable formula in $B(C(v))$.
Restriction along $Bj$ and axiom introduction give
$\operatorname{Gen}(Bv)=Bv$.

In the other direction let $W\hookrightarrow BS$ be a closed sentence
theory in $\mathcal D/U$. Write $e:EB\cong1_{\mathcal D}$ for the
projection isomorphism. On the original sentence and formula objects put
\[
 W_0=(e_S^{-1})^*E(W),\qquad C_0=(e_\Phi^{-1})^*E(C(W)).
\]
Naturality gives $(EBj)e_S^{-1}=e_\Phi^{-1}j:S\to EB\Phi$.
Since $(Bj)^*C(W)=W$ and $E$ preserves pullbacks, $j^*C_0=W_0$.
The logical rules of the slice retain the parameter. Applying $E$ to
their operations on $C(W)$ and transporting along $e$ gives their
operations on $C_0$. This transport preserves premises and conclusions
by naturality of $e$ at the rule morphisms and the finite-product
comparisons. Thus $C_0$ is closed under the original rules and contains
the axioms $W_0$ as sentences. Initiality for $W_0$ and restriction along
$j$ give $\operatorname{Gen}(W_0)\leq W_0$. The reverse inclusion is
axiom introduction.

A consistent complete closed extension of $u$ therefore gives one of
$B_U(u)$ by $B_U$. Conversely, let $W\hookrightarrow U\times S$ be any consistent
complete closed extension of $B_U(u)$ in $\mathcal D/U$. Under
the identification $E B(S)\cong S$, its fiber is
\[
 W_0=\langle\lambda_U !_S,1_S\rangle^*W\hookrightarrow S ,
\]
where the pullback is taken in $\mathcal D$ along the displayed morphism
$S\to U\times S$. It is closed, consistent and complete by the
preceding argument. The inclusion $B(u)\leq W$ gives $u\leq W_0$.
This proves the essential-incompleteness equivalence.

The same retraction proves that $\delta_u$ is total exactly when
$B_U(\delta_u)$ is total. By definition, $\delta_u$ is total exactly
when $u$ is complete. The true and false fibers of a total extension of $\delta_u$ separate $u$ and
$\nu^*u$. Conversely, a complementary separator of these subobjects defines a
total extension of $\delta_u$. Either functor
carries a total extension to a total extension. The retraction therefore
proves the second equivalence.
Finally, Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness} makes the theorem and
refutation subobjects of every consistent extension of $t$ inseparable.
Every consistent extension of $u$ also extends $t$, so $u$ is essentially
incomplete. The equivalence for constant families gives essential
incompleteness of $\widetilde u$, and inseparability of $u,\nu^*u$ excludes a
total extension of $\widetilde\delta_u$.
\end{proof}

In the numerical recursion category of partial recursive functions
(Section~\ref{subsec:numerical-realization}), let $A\subseteq\N$ be
infinite and computably enumerable.
Its partial identity $1_A$ splits through an object with carrier $A$.
To construct an isomorphism with $\N$, fix a program that halts on $x$
exactly when $x\in A$. Encode an input and a stage by a recursive
pairing and put
\[
 D=\{\langle x,s\rangle:\text{the program first halts on $x$ at stage $s$}\}.
\]
A simulation for $s$ steps decides membership in $D$. Each $x\in A$
occurs at exactly one such stage, so the first projection maps $D$
bijectively onto $A$. Since $D$ is infinite and recursive, its
increasing enumeration $d:\N\to D$ is total recursive. Thus
$e(n)=\pi_1(d(n))$ enumerates $A$ without repetitions. The inverse
search $r(x)=\min\{n:e(n)=x\}$ is partial recursive, with domain $A$.
As partial functions on $\N$ these maps satisfy
\[
     r e=1_{\N},\qquad e r=1_A .
\]
In the restriction splitting they give inverse total morphisms between
$\N$ and the object with carrier $A$. Postcomposition with these
morphisms identifies the slices over the two objects and hence their
categories of partial maps.
\section{The syntactic recursion category}\label{sec:syntactic}

Let $T$ be a consistent extension of $\PA$ in the language of arithmetic.
Its nonlogical symbols are the constants $0,1$, the binary operations
$+,\cdot$, and the binary relation $<$. Equality is logical. The numeral for $n\in\N$ is the closed term
given by $\bar 0=0$ and $\overline{n+1}=(\bar n+1)$.

In the syntactic recursion category $S_T$ of Montagna and
Di Paola--Montagna~\cite{Montagna,DPM}, we use formal product and
coproduct objects. Let $\mathsf O$ be the set of terms generated
by the constant $\omega$ and the binary operations $\times$ and $+$,
with syntactic equality. Assign a set $|X|$ to each
$X\in\mathsf O$ by
\[
 |\omega|=\N,\qquad
 |X\times Y|=|X|\times|Y|,\qquad
 |X+Y|=|X|\amalg|Y|,
\]
where $A\amalg B=(A\times\{0\})\cup(B\times\{1\})$.
Use the primitive-recursive pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle=2^a(2b+1)-1$ for products and the even and
odd codings for coproducts. These determine recursive bijections
$\gamma_X:|X|\to\N$ by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \gamma_\omega&=1_\N,\\
 \gamma_{X\times Y}(x,y)
   &=\langle\gamma_X(x),\gamma_Y(y)\rangle,\\
 \gamma_{X+Y}(x,0)&=2\gamma_X(x),\qquad
 \gamma_{X+Y}(y,1)=2\gamma_Y(y)+1.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The arithmetic formulas below use the single sort of PA.
The numerical pairing, its two projections, and division with
remainder by $2$ are primitive recursive; PA proves their defining
and inverse equations.

Use a deterministic form of Kleene's computation predicate as in
Montagna~\cite[p.~115, Note~1]{Montagna}. Let $E(e,x,h)$ be the primitive-recursive bounded evaluator for program
$e$ on input $x$. At stage $h$ it returns $0$ if no output has been
found and $y+1$ for output $y$.
Write $[a,x]$ for the pairing of the underlying program coding, with
primitive-recursive projections whose inverse equations are provable
in $\PA$. A halting trace has code $t=[h,y]$, where $h$ is its
first successful stage and $y$ its output. The projections are
$\mathsf{st}(t)=h$ and $\mathsf{out}(t)=y$. Thus
\[
 \mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 E(e,x,\mathsf{st}(t))=\mathsf{out}(t)+1
 \ \land\ \forall r<\mathsf{st}(t)\; E(e,x,r)=0.
\]
The graph of evaluation is
\[
 G(e,x,y)\equiv
 \exists t\,\bigl(\mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)\land\mathsf{out}(t)=y\bigr),
 \qquad G_e(x,y)=G(\bar e,x,y).
\]
Primitive-recursive symbols abbreviate their defining formulas in
PA, as in \cite[p.~644]{DPM}; the expanded graph formula is $\Sigma_1$.
For $X,Y\in\mathsf O$, let $\mathcal I(X,Y)=\N$.
An index $e\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ is interpreted using
$\gamma_X$ for inputs and $\gamma_Y$ for outputs.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:arithmetized-evaluation}
For this computation coding, there are an index $u\in\N$ and
primitive-recursive functions
$\operatorname{s},\operatorname{comp}:\N^2\to\N$
such that PA proves functionality
of $G$ and the universal closures of
\begin{align}
 G_u(\langle e,x\rangle,y)
   &\leftrightarrow G(e,x,y),
   \label{eq:arithmetized-universal}\\
 G(\operatorname{s}(e,a),x,y)
   &\leftrightarrow G(e,\langle a,x\rangle,y),
   \label{eq:arithmetized-specialization}\\
 G(\operatorname{comp}(f,e),x,z)
   &\leftrightarrow
     \exists y\,\bigl(G(e,x,y)\land G(f,y,z)\bigr).
   \label{eq:composition}
\end{align}
Regard $u$ as an element of $\mathcal I(\omega\times\omega,\omega)$.
For each fixed $e\in\N$, there is an index
$k_e\in\N$ for which PA proves
\[
 \forall a\forall p\,
 \bigl(G_{k_e}(a,p)\leftrightarrow
       p=\operatorname{s}(\bar e,a)\bigr).
\]
In particular, PA proves $\forall a\exists!p\,G_{k_e}(a,p)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Use the universal interpreter and formalized parameterization
\cite[p.~108; p.~115, Note~1]{Montagna}. For the program pairing,
the parameter function $s_0$ satisfies
$G(s_0(d,a),x,y)\leftrightarrow G(d,[a,x],y)$ in $\PA$.
On input $\langle e,x\rangle$, let $u$ decode $e,x$ and apply the
interpreter to $[e,x]$. Choose a program $v$ that, on input
$[e,[a,x]]$, computes $\langle a,x\rangle$ and runs $e$ on that input.
The inverse equations for the two pairings give in $\PA$
\[
 G_v([e,[a,x]],y)\longleftrightarrow G(e,\langle a,x\rangle,y).
\]
Two applications of the parameter equation now give
\eqref{eq:arithmetized-specialization} for the primitive-recursive
function $\operatorname{s}(e,a)=s_0(s_0(v,e),a)$.
Choose an index $c$ whose program, on input
$\langle\langle f,e\rangle,x\rangle$, searches successive codes
of pairs $(t,t')$ for which
\[
 \mathsf{Tr}(e,x,t)\land\mathsf{Tr}(f,\mathsf{out}(t),t').
\]
At the first such pair it returns $\mathsf{out}(t')$. Put
$\operatorname{comp}(f,e)=\operatorname{s}(c,\langle f,e\rangle)$,
which is primitive recursive. PA proves that the code of any
witnessing pair bounds the search, and that a successful search
supplies witnesses to both graphs, with intermediate value
$\mathsf{out}(t)$. Two traces for the same input have the same least successful stage
and the same value of $E$ there. Thus $\PA$ proves functionality of
$G$, and all witnessing pairs give the same output, proving~\eqref{eq:composition}.
For $k_e$, use an index for the primitive-recursive function
$a\mapsto\operatorname{s}(e,a)$; its defining equation and
totality are provable in PA.
\end{proof}

The objects of $S_T$ are the terms in $\mathsf O$. Its morphisms
$X\rightharpoonup Y$ are the equivalence classes in
$\mathcal I(X,Y)$ under
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform}
 e\equiv_T f
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T\vdash \forall x\forall y\,
       \bigl(G_e(x,y)\leftrightarrow G_f(x,y)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Write $[e]_T$ for the class of $e\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$.

For $e\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ and $f\in\mathcal I(Y,Z)$, define
$[f]_T[e]_T=[\operatorname{comp}(f,e)]_T$.
Substitution of T-provably equivalent graphs in
\eqref{eq:composition} proves independence of representatives.
Choose an index $i$ for the identity program, so that
$\PA\vdash\forall x\forall y\,(G_i(x,y)\leftrightarrow y=x)$.
Its class in $\mathcal I(X,X)/{\equiv_T}$ is $1_X$.
The identity and associativity equations follow by substituting
the graph of $i$ and reassociating the existential quantifiers
in~\eqref{eq:composition}.

Montagna's objects are the sets generated from $\N$ by
Cartesian products and the displayed disjoint unions
\cite[p.~105]{Montagna}. Let $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ denote that
presentation of the unprimed category, using the computation
formulas and the induced numerical codings fixed above
\cite[p.~646]{DPM}. For this set presentation take von Neumann
naturals and Kuratowski ordered pairs. Each $|X|$ is infinite, by
the bijection $\gamma_X$. The element $0=\varnothing$ belongs to
$\N$ and is no ordered pair, so $\N$ is neither a product nor a
tagged union of these sets. The second projection of $A\times B$
is the infinite set $B$, whereas that of $A\amalg B$ is $\{0,1\}$.
The two projections recover the factors of a product, and the two
tag fibres recover the summands of a tagged union. Induction
therefore shows that $|X|=|Y|$ implies $X=Y$. In particular, each
object of the set presentation has a unique coding $\gamma_X$
given by the displayed recursion. There is a functor
\[
 \Pi_T:S_T\longrightarrow S_T^{\mathrm{set}},\qquad
 \Pi_T(X)=|X|,\qquad \Pi_T([e]_T)=[e]_T^{\mathrm{set}}.
\]
Every object of $S_T^{\mathrm{set}}$ is $|X|$ for a term
$X\in\mathsf O$, and the map on each hom-set is a bijection
because both presentations use \eqref{eq:uniform} with the same
numerical codings. Thus $\Pi_T$ is an equivalence. For $T=\PA$,
the target is Montagna's unprimed category $S$ with these choices
of computation formulas and codings.

The pointwise relation used in the primed systems identifies
$e,f\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$ when, for every standard input code $n$,
\[
 T\vdash\forall y\,
   \bigl(G_e(\bar n,y)\leftrightarrow G_f(\bar n,y)\bigr).
\]
Montagna's $S'$ is the case
$T=\PA$ of Di Paola and Montagna's $S'_T$ \cite{Montagna,DPM}.
\emph{Pointwise provable equality and the failure of composition}
\cite[Corollary 2]{Composition} proves that the proposed composition
is not independent of representatives for any consistent c.e.\
extension $T$ of $\PA$. Thus these primed systems do not define
categories with that composition.

For $X\in\mathsf O$ and a $\Sigma_1$ arithmetic formula $C(x)$,
where $x$ is the numerical code variable for $X$, choose
an index $j_C$ for which
\[
 \PA\vdash\forall x\forall y\,
 \bigl(G_{j_C}(x,y)\leftrightarrow(C(x)\land y=x)\bigr).
\]
Such an index searches increasing bounds for a witness to $C(x)$
and returns $x$ when a witness is found
\cite[p.~109, equation~$(*)$]{Montagna}. Write
$[C]_T=[j_C]_T:X\rightharpoonup X$.
For two such formulas,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:domain-order}
 [C]_T\le[D]_T
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 T\vdash\forall x\,(C(x)\longrightarrow D(x)).
\end{equation}
Conjunction and disjunction give meets and joins of restriction
idempotents. For $[e]_T:X\rightharpoonup Y$, its restriction
$\overline{[e]_T}$ and range $\ran([e]_T)$ are represented respectively by
\[
 \exists y\,G_e(x,y),\qquad
 R_e(y):=\exists x\,G_e(x,y).
\]
For a restriction idempotent $[C]_T:Y\rightharpoonup Y$, the
equation $[C]_T[e]_T=[e]_T$ holds if and only if
$T$ proves $G_e(x,y)\to C(y)$ universally, equivalently when
$T$ proves $R_e(y)\to C(y)$ universally.
Write $g=[p]_T,h=[q]_T:Y\rightharpoonup Z$.
If $g[e]_T=h[e]_T$, the
composition equation and PA-provable functionality of $G_e$ give
\[
 T\vdash\forall y\forall z\,
 \bigl(R_e(y)\longrightarrow
       (G_p(y,z)\leftrightarrow G_q(y,z))\bigr).
\]
A witness $x$ to $R_e(y)$ can be used in the equality of
the composite graphs, and functionality identifies the intermediate
output with $y$. Hence $g[R_e]_T=h[R_e]_T$ in $S_T$.
The search program $j_{R_e}$ depends only on $e$, so its class
represents the range over every extension of $T$.

For $[e]_T:W\rightharpoonup X$ and $[f]_T:W\rightharpoonup Y$,
a program $h$ runs both computations and pairs their outputs.
For $[p]_T:X\rightharpoonup Z$ and $[q]_T:Y\rightharpoonup Z$,
a program $k$ reads the input tag and runs the indicated program.
Their graphs satisfy the following equivalences in $\PA$:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 G_h(w,\langle x,y\rangle)&\longleftrightarrow G_e(w,x)\land G_f(w,y),\\
 G_k(2x,z)&\longleftrightarrow G_p(x,z),\\
 G_k(2y+1,z)&\longleftrightarrow G_q(y,z).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Together with the numerical projections and tagged injections,
these give the restriction pairing $[h]_T:W\rightharpoonup X\times Y$
and the copairing $[k]_T:X+Y\rightharpoonup Z$.
Put $\tau_T=[u]_T:\omega\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$.
For $f=[e]_T:X\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$, put
$r=[k_e]_T:X\to\omega$. Lemma~\ref{lem:arithmetized-evaluation}
proves that $r$ is total and gives a PA-proof of
\[
 G_e(\langle a,x\rangle,y)\leftrightarrow
 \exists p\,
 \bigl(G_{k_e}(a,p)\land G_u(\langle p,x\rangle,y)\bigr)
\]
for all numerical codes $a,x,y$.
The composition and product graph equations therefore give
$f=\tau_T(r\times1_\omega)$ in $S_T$.
Thus $\tau_T$ is a Turing morphism. The class of $i$ in
$S_T(X,\omega)$ represents $\gamma_X$ on the decoded sets.
The same program in $S_T(\omega,X)$ represents $\gamma_X^{-1}$.
Both composites have identity graph by~\eqref{eq:composition}.
The product of any morphism with a nowhere-defined program has
empty graph. Hence $S_T$ is a recursion category.

\subsection{The total restriction splitting}
\label{subsec:syntactic-total-splitting}

To construct syntax and theories in
$\mathcal B_T=\Tot(\Split(S_T))$, we present its objects by
arithmetic predicates. Robinson and Rosolini~\cite[pp.~108--109]{RobinsonRosolini}
present syntactic partial maps by functional $\Sigma_1$ formulas
up to provable graph equality.

Let $\mathcal P_T$ have as objects the $\Sigma_1$ arithmetic formulas
$C(x)$ with free variable $x$. A morphism from $C$ to $D$
is represented by a $\Sigma_1$ formula $\Gamma(x,y)$ for which $T$
proves
\begin{align}
 &\forall x\forall y\,
   \bigl(\Gamma(x,y)\longrightarrow C(x)\land D(y)\bigr),
                                               \label{eq:syntactic-support}\\
 &\forall x\,
   \bigl(C(x)\longrightarrow\exists!y\,\Gamma(x,y)\bigr).
                                               \label{eq:syntactic-totality}
\end{align}
Two representing formulas define the same morphism when $T$ proves
their universal equivalence. The identity on $C$ is represented by
$C(x)\land y=x$, and composition is represented by
$(\Delta\Gamma)(x,z)\equiv
\exists y\,(\Gamma(x,y)\land\Delta(y,z))$.
These formulas are $\Sigma_1$ and satisfy
\eqref{eq:syntactic-support}--\eqref{eq:syntactic-totality}; first-order
logic proves the identity and associativity equations. We write
$\Gamma:C\to D$ for the morphism represented by $\Gamma(x,y)$.
Identity relations give isomorphisms between provably equivalent
carrier predicates.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:syntactic-functional-search}
For every $\Sigma_1$ formula $\Gamma(x,y)$ there is an index
$a_\Gamma$ such that PA proves
\begin{gather*}
 \forall x\forall y\,
   \bigl(G_{a_\Gamma}(x,y)\longrightarrow\Gamma(x,y)\bigr),\\
 \forall x\,
   \bigl(\exists y\,G_{a_\Gamma}(x,y)
          \longleftrightarrow\exists y\,\Gamma(x,y)\bigr).
\end{gather*}
If $T$ proves that $\Gamma$ is functional, then
\[
 T\vdash\forall x\forall y\,
       \bigl(G_{a_\Gamma}(x,y)\longleftrightarrow\Gamma(x,y)\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $\Gamma(x,y)$ in the PA-provably equivalent form
$\exists w\,R(x,y,w)$, with $R$ primitive recursive. Search the
codes $n=0,1,\ldots$ in increasing order for
$R(x,\pi_0n,\pi_1n)$, and return $\pi_0n$ at the first $n$ satisfying
this predicate. Here $\pi_0,\pi_1$ are the projections of the fixed numerical
pairing.

PA proves by induction on the number of tests that a halting run
returns $\pi_0n$ for the least $n$ satisfying $R(x,\pi_0n,\pi_1n)$. Conversely,
if such an $n$ exists, its least value supplies a finite
halting computation. Formalized least-number search and the
computation coding therefore prove the first two assertions.
If $T$ also proves functionality, any pair satisfying $\Gamma$
has the same output as this search. Hence $T$ proves the universal equivalence of $G_{a_\Gamma}(x,y)$ and
$\Gamma(x,y)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:syntactic-total-category}
There is an equivalence $\mathcal P_T\simeq\mathcal B_T$.
The category $\mathcal B_T$ is regular, with finite coproducts
that are disjoint and stable under pullback. Every monomorphism
of $\mathcal B_T$ has a partial inverse in $\Split(S_T)$.
For $\Gamma:C\to D$ in the predicate presentation, its regular
image is represented by the inclusion
\[
 R_\Gamma(y)\equiv\exists x\,\Gamma(x,y)
 \quad\hookrightarrow\quad D(y).
\]
In particular, every subobject of a predicate $D$ is isomorphic
over $D$ to an inclusion of a $\Sigma_1$ predicate.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Send a carrier $C$ to $(\omega,[C]_T)$ and a represented morphism
$\Gamma:C\to D$ to $[a_\Gamma]_T$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search}, its graph is
$T$-provably equivalent to $\Gamma$. Conditions
\eqref{eq:syntactic-support}--\eqref{eq:syntactic-totality} imply
\[
 [a_\Gamma]_T=[D]_T[a_\Gamma]_T[C]_T,
 \qquad\overline{[a_\Gamma]_T}=[C]_T.
\]
These are the support and totality equations for a morphism
$(\omega,[C]_T)\to(\omega,[D]_T)$ in $\mathcal B_T$.
The arithmetized composition equation proves functoriality.

Conversely, a total morphism from $(\omega,[C]_T)$ to
$(\omega,[D]_T)$ has a graph satisfying
\eqref{eq:syntactic-support}--\eqref{eq:syntactic-totality} in $T$.
Equality of these morphisms is universal $T$-provable graph
equivalence. The functor is therefore full and faithful.
For an object $(X,e)$ of $\Split(S_T)$, let $j:X\to\omega$ be
the coding isomorphism and put $e'=jej^{-1}$. The morphism
$je:(X,e)\to(\omega,e')$ is an isomorphism with inverse $ej^{-1}$.
If $b$ represents $e'$, put $C(x)\equiv\exists y\,G_b(x,y)$.
The equation $e'=\bar e'$ says that $T$ proves
\[
 G_b(x,y)\longleftrightarrow(C(x)\land y=x)
\]
universally. Hence $e'=[C]_T$, proving the equivalence.

We prove the remaining claims in $\mathcal P_T$.
The predicate $x=0$ is terminal: the unique morphism to it from
$C$ has graph $C(x)\land y=0$.
A product of $C$ and $D$ is represented by
$C(\pi_0z)\land D(\pi_1z)$ with its numerical projections.
If $\Gamma:A\to C$ and
$\Delta:A\to D$, their pairing has graph
\[
 \exists x\exists y\,
   \bigl(\Gamma(a,x)\land\Delta(a,y)\land z=\langle x,y\rangle\bigr).
\]
The PA-provable pairing identities give its universal property.
For parallel morphisms $\Gamma,\Delta:C\to D$, the equalizer is
the inclusion into $C$ of
\[
 E(x)\equiv C(x)\land
             \exists y\,(\Gamma(x,y)\land\Delta(x,y)).
\]
If $\Lambda:A\to C$ equalizes $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$,
equality of the composite graphs and functionality of $\Lambda$
give a $T$-proof that $\Lambda(a,x)$ implies $E(x)$.
The same graph therefore defines its unique factorization through
$E$. This proves finite completeness. In particular, the pullback
of $\Gamma:C\to E$ and $\Delta:D\to E$ is represented by
\[
 P(w)\equiv C(\pi_0w)\land D(\pi_1w)\land
       \exists y\,(\Gamma(\pi_0w,y)\land\Delta(\pi_1w,y)),
\]
with the two numerical projections.

Call a represented morphism $\varepsilon:C\to D$
\emph{provably surjective} when
\[
 T\vdash\forall y\,
       \bigl(D(y)\longrightarrow\exists x\,\varepsilon(x,y)\bigr).
\]
Every such morphism has a section. Apply the first two assertions
of Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search} to the relation
$\varepsilon(x,y)$ with input $y$ and output $x$. The program returns the preimage from the first witness it finds.
Its graph is PA-provably functional. In $T$, surjectivity and
support give domain $D$ and values in $C$, so the program
defines $\sigma:D\to C$. The correctness of
the search and functionality of $\varepsilon$ give
$\varepsilon\sigma=1_D$.

Such a split epimorphism is the coequalizer of its kernel pair.
Let $k_0,k_1:K\rightrightarrows C$ be the kernel-pair
projections, and let $\beta:C\to Z$ satisfy
$\beta k_0=\beta k_1$. Since
$\varepsilon=\varepsilon\sigma\varepsilon$, the pair
$(1_C,\sigma\varepsilon)$ induces a morphism $C\to K$.
Thus $\beta=\beta\sigma\varepsilon$, so
$\beta\sigma:D\to Z$ is the required factorization. If
$\lambda\varepsilon=\beta$, then
$\lambda=\lambda\varepsilon\sigma=\beta\sigma$, proving
uniqueness.

Every $\Gamma:C\to D$ factors through $R_\Gamma$ by the same
graph, followed by the identity inclusion of $R_\Gamma$ into $D$.
The first morphism is provably surjective, hence regular epic by
the preceding argument, and the inclusion is monic.
Conversely, a regular epimorphism factors through its predicate
image as above; extremality of regular epimorphisms forces the
image inclusion to be an isomorphism, which implies its provable
surjectivity. Thus regular epimorphisms are precisely the provable
surjections, and they all split. A pullback of a split epimorphism
$\varepsilon:C\to D$ along $\Gamma:Z\to D$ has the section
$\langle\sigma\Gamma,1_Z\rangle:Z\to C\times_D Z$.
Consequently regular epimorphisms are stable under pullback.
This proves regularity and the asserted image formula.

The false predicate is initial. If $C$ admits a morphism to it,
totality gives $T\vdash\forall x\,\neg C(x)$, so $C$ is
isomorphic to the false predicate; thus the initial object is
strict. A coproduct is represented by the predicate
\[
 (C+D)(z)\equiv
   \exists x\,(z=2x\land C(x))\;\lor\;
   \exists y\,(z=2y+1\land D(y)),
\]
with the even and odd injections. Copairing selects the first graph
on even inputs and the second on odd inputs. The parity identities prove
the coproduct equations and disjointness of its injections.
For $\Gamma:A\to C+D$, put
\[
 A_C(a)\equiv\exists x\,\Gamma(a,2x),\qquad
 A_D(a)\equiv\exists y\,\Gamma(a,2y+1).
\]
These are the pullback carriers of the two injections, up to the
isomorphism that forgets the uniquely determined output coordinate.
Totality and functionality of $\Gamma$ prove in $T$ that
\[
 A(a)\longleftrightarrow A_C(a)\lor A_D(a),\qquad
 \neg(A_C(a)\land A_D(a)).
\]
The morphism $A_C+A_D\to A$ sends both summand representatives
to their underlying element of $A$.
Its inverse has graph
\[
 (A_C(a)\land z=2a)\;\lor\;(A_D(a)\land z=2a+1).
\]
The partition equations prove both inverse identities. Hence finite
coproducts are disjoint and stable under pullback.

Let $\Gamma:C\to D$ be monic and form its kernel pair. Its carrier is
\[
 K(w)\equiv C(\pi_0w)\land C(\pi_1w)\land
    \exists y\,(\Gamma(\pi_0w,y)\land\Gamma(\pi_1w,y)).
\]
Monicity implies equality of the two kernel-pair projections.
Consequently, $T$ proves $K(w)\to\pi_0w=\pi_1w$ universally.
Using the numerical pairing, this gives
\[
 T\vdash\forall x\forall x'\forall y\,
  \bigl(\Gamma(x,y)\land\Gamma(x',y)\longrightarrow x=x'\bigr).
\]
Regard the monomorphism in $\Split(S_T)$ through the preceding
equivalence. The transposed relation $\Gamma(x,y)$, with input $y$ and
output $x$, is therefore $T$-provably functional. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search} it defines a partial
morphism $r:D\rightharpoonup C$ in $\Split(S_T)$ whose domain
predicate is $R_\Gamma$. Totality and functionality of $\Gamma$,
together with the displayed injectivity statement, prove
\[
 r\Gamma=1_C,\qquad
 \Gamma r=[R_\Gamma]_T=\bar r.
\]
Here $[R_\Gamma]_T$ denotes the partial identity on the predicate
$R_\Gamma$, regarded as a partial endomorphism of the split object
presented by $D$. The corestriction $C\to R_\Gamma$ is an isomorphism,
with the same transposed relation as its total inverse.
\end{proof}

In particular, there is a restriction equivalence
\[
 \Par(\mathcal B_T,\Mono)\simeq\Split(S_T).
\]
A span $C\xleftarrow{m}E\xrightarrow{g}D$ is sent
to $gm^{-1}$, where $m^{-1}$ is the partial inverse.
Conversely, a partial morphism is represented by its domain
inclusion and its total restriction to that domain. For a program index $e$ representing the partial morphism, its domain
predicate is $\exists y\,G_e(x,y)$. By the pullback calculation in Section~\ref{sec:theory-extensions},
composition of spans agrees with composition in $\Split(S_T)$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-total-category}, $\mathcal B_T$ is regular
with disjoint stable finite coproducts, and its monomorphisms have
partial inverses in $\Split(S_T)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:partial-slice-turing}
therefore makes $\Split(S_T)$ a Turing category with Turing object
$(\omega,1_\omega)$ and Turing morphism represented by $\tau_T=[u]_T$.
The restriction equivalence supplies a restriction
terminal object, represented by the singleton predicate $x=0$.
Binary restriction products are
$(X,e)\times(Y,d)=(X\times Y,e\times d)$.
For every object $(X,e)$, the total morphism
$e:(X,e)\to(X,1_X)$ has retraction
$e:(X,1_X)\rightharpoonup(X,e)$, and $(X,1_X)\cong(\omega,1_\omega)$
by the coding isomorphism.

Ranges extend to $\Split(S_T)$ by the same representatives.
For a morphism $f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$, the equation
$df=f$ implies $\ran_{S_T}(f)\leq d$. This range is therefore
a restriction idempotent on $(Y,d)$, with the same leastness
and agreement properties. Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image}
applies because every monomorphism of $\mathcal B_T$ has a
partial inverse.

\subsection{Syntax and lists}
\label{sec:st-parameterized-syntax}

We use primitive-recursive codes for finite sequences with length,
entry, and concatenation operations whose defining equations are
provable in $\PA$. Each finite sequence has one code; the empty
sequence and adjoining an entry are injective constructors with
disjoint images. For example, encode the empty sequence by $0$
and $(a,w)$ by $1+\langle a,w\rangle$. The tail code is smaller
than the nonempty sequence code, so bounded traversal defines the
sequence operations and induction in $\PA$ proves their equations.
All arithmetical implications and equivalences in this subsection
are understood to be universally quantified.

\begin{lemma}[Finite membership conditions]
\label{lem:st-finite-sigma1}
Let $C(x)$ be $\Sigma_1$, and let $a$ code a finite sequence with
entries $a_i$. The assertion that all entries satisfy $C$ is equivalent
in $\PA$ to a $\Sigma_1$ formula. Let $m$ be a positive integer and let
$D_0(x),\ldots,D_{m-1}(x)$ be $\Sigma_1$ formulas. Fix a $\Sigma_1$
graph formula $L(x,w)$ for a primitive-recursive program whose values on
$\N$ lie in $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$. Define the entry condition
\[
 C_L(x)\equiv\bigvee_{j=0}^{m-1}\bigl(L(x,\bar j)\land D_j(x)\bigr).
\]
The assertion that all entries satisfy $C_L$ is also equivalent in $\PA$
to a $\Sigma_1$ formula.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $C(x)$ as $\exists v\,C_0(x,v)$ with $C_0$ primitive recursive.
For a sequence code $a$, use a coded sequence of witnesses:
\[
 \exists b\,\bigl(\operatorname{len}(b)=\operatorname{len}(a)
   \land\forall i<\operatorname{len}(a)\,
                  C_0(a_i,b_i)\bigr).
\]
Reading the entries proves the reverse implication. For the forward implication,
induction in $\PA$ on the length constructs a sequence of witnesses by
appending one witness at a time.
The finite disjunction defining $C_L$ is $\Sigma_1$, so the first
assertion applies to $C_L$.
\end{proof}

Fix a nonnegative integer $d$ and objects
$V,\Sigma_0,\ldots,\Sigma_d,\Pi_0,\ldots,\Pi_d$
of $\mathcal B_T$, represented by $\Sigma_1$ carrier formulas with
the same letters. Numerical equality gives decidable equality on
$V$: on the source $V\times V$, the Boolean test is true precisely
when its two numerical coordinates are equal. The diagonal and its
complement are therefore represented by the predicates
$V(x)\land V(y)\land x=y$ and
$V(x)\land V(y)\land x\ne y$, respectively.

Assign distinct natural numbers to the constructors for variables,
$k$-ary function and relation symbols ($0\leq k\leq d$), equality,
negation, implication, and universal quantification.
Encode a node by its constructor number and, when required, its
numerical symbol or variable label, using the fixed finite-sequence
coding. The word for a tree consists of the words for its children, in order,
followed by one entry for the root.

Recover the tree by primitive recursion through this sequence,
maintaining a finite sequence of completed subtrees. At a constructor
of arity $k$, replace the last $k$ subtrees by the tree obtained by
applying that constructor, in their order. The operation is defined
only when these subtrees have the required term or formula sorts.
A nullary constructor appends a one-node tree. A sequence represents
a tree exactly when this recursion is defined and ends with one tree.
A variable has arity zero, a $k$-ary function or relation has arity $k$,
equality and implication have arity two, and negation and universal
quantification have arity one. A universal quantifier also has a
variable label.

The sequence operations are primitive recursive. They recover each
constructor's ordered children uniquely. Sequence length is a
primitive-recursive size function, and every child has smaller size.
Induction on sequence length proves these assertions in $\mathrm{PA}$.

The predicate $\operatorname{Tm}(t)$ requires that $t$ parse as a term,
that its variable labels satisfy $V$, and that each function label of
arity $k$ satisfy $\Sigma_k$. The formula
$\operatorname{Fm}(a)$ has the analogous conditions for formulas,
including membership in $\Pi_k$ for relation labels and in $V$ for
quantifier labels. Lemma~\ref{lem:st-finite-sigma1} makes these
formulas $\Sigma_1$ by existentially quantifying membership witnesses.
For example, let $w$ be a word whose parse tree has a relation
symbol $r$ of arity $k$ at its root and ordered term subtrees
with words $t_1,\ldots,t_k$. Then $\PA$ proves, under this
parsing hypothesis,
\[
  \operatorname{Fm}(w)\ \longleftrightarrow\
  \Pi_k(r)\land\bigwedge_{j=1}^k\operatorname{Tm}(t_j).
\]
Indeed, the label test at the root is $\Pi_k(r)$, and every
remaining label lies in exactly one of the parsed children.
The same argument gives the carrier equations for the other
constructors. Conversely, concatenating words that each parse
as a tree of the required sort, then appending the root node,
recovers those children in order.
Write
\[
 \Tm=(\omega,[\operatorname{Tm}]_T),\qquad
 \Fm=(\omega,[\operatorname{Fm}]_T)
\]
for the corresponding objects of $\mathcal B_T$.

\begin{proposition}[Syntax initiality with parameters]
\label{prop:st-syntax-initiality}
Let $d$ be a nonnegative integer and let $V,\Sigma_k,\Pi_k$ be
objects of $\mathcal B_T$ for $0\leq k\leq d$. Powers below
denote finite products. The endofunctor
$K:\mathcal B_T^2\to\mathcal B_T^2$ defined by
\[
 K(X,Y)=\left(
 V+\coprod_{k=0}^{d}\Sigma_k\times X^k,
 X^2+\coprod_{k=0}^{d}\Pi_k\times X^k+Y+Y^2+V\times Y
 \right)
\]
has an initial algebra in $\mathcal B_T^2$, with carriers
$\Tm$ and $\Fm$. This algebra is stable
under parameters in the sense of Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}: for every object $P$,
its pullback to $(\mathcal B_T/P)^2$ is initial for $K_P$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
On a pair of morphisms $(f:X\to X',g:Y\to Y')$, the functor $K$
acts by the identity on the symbol and variable coefficients, by $f$
on term factors, and by $g$ on formula factors. At $(\Tm,\Fm)$, the
constructor decomposition equivalences give the carrier conditions for
the primitive-recursive operations on these summands. These operations
are therefore morphisms of $\mathcal B_T$ and define a $K$-algebra.

Fix an object $P$ and a $K_P$-algebra with
carriers $\xi:X\to P$ and $\upsilon:Y\to P$. Choose graph indices for their projections and for the
finitely many algebra operations. Write
$\Xi(x,p)$ and $\Upsilon(y,p)$ for the projection graphs. The source of a function operation is represented, for example, by
the predicate
\[
       P(p)\land\Sigma_k(s)\land
       \bigwedge_{i=1}^k\bigl(X(x_i)\land\Xi(x_i,p)\bigr).
\]
The algebra operation
is $T$-provably total on this predicate and has values $x$ satisfying
$X(x)\land\Xi(x,p)$. The other operations have the corresponding
fiber-product sources and preserve their projection to $P$.

Define relations $\operatorname{Ev}_{\mathrm{Tm}}(p,t,x)$ and
$\operatorname{Ev}_{\mathrm{Fm}}(p,a,y)$ by finite sequences with
one entry for each node. Each entry consists of a value in $X$ or
$Y$, according to the node's sort, and a code of a halting computation
of the algebra operation at that node. Its inputs
are its label, the values already assigned to its children, and
the fixed parameter $p$. At a term node with value $u$, require
$X(u)\land\Xi(u,p)$; at a formula node with value $v$, require
$Y(v)\land\Upsilon(v,p)$. For $\operatorname{Ev}_{\mathrm{Tm}}(p,t,x)$
require $P(p)\land\operatorname{Tm}(t)$ and root value $x$.
For $\operatorname{Ev}_{\mathrm{Fm}}(p,a,y)$ require
$P(p)\land\operatorname{Fm}(a)$ and root value $y$.

The carrier and projection conditions are $\Sigma_1$, and the tests on
halting traces are primitive recursive. By Lemma~\ref{lem:st-finite-sigma1},
existential quantification over the evaluation sequence gives a $\Sigma_1$
formula for each relation.

Simultaneous induction in $T$ on node count $n$ proves that every
valid input of size at most $n$, with every parameter satisfying $P$,
has exactly one evaluation value of the required sort over that
parameter. At a variable or nullary constructor,
the corresponding algebra operation is total on the input
predicate. At any other constructor, its unique decomposition gives
children of smaller size. The induction hypothesis supplies their
values with the required common projection. They therefore form
an input in the source of the algebra operation at the root.
Its totality supplies an output in the correct fiber. Concatenating
the child sequences and appending the root computation supplies
the required evaluation sequence. Functionality of the operation graphs,
together with the induction hypothesis, proves uniqueness of the
value.

This induction takes place in $T$, using PA induction and the totality and
projection equations of the algebra. By Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search}
the two evaluation relations define total morphisms over $P$
\[
 h_{\mathrm{Tm}}:P\times\Tm\longrightarrow X,
 \qquad
 h_{\mathrm{Fm}}:P\times\Fm\longrightarrow Y.
\]
Decomposing an
evaluation sequence at its root proves, in $T$, their algebra-morphism
equations: evaluation of a constructor is the corresponding algebra
operation applied to the evaluated children. Thus these morphisms form
a $K_P$-algebra morphism in the slice.

Let $(h'_{\mathrm{Tm}},h'_{\mathrm{Fm}})$ be any other such algebra
morphism. Its totality and its algebra-morphism equations are
theorems of $T$. A second simultaneous induction on size proves
that its values equal the evaluation values. At a constructor,
use its algebra-morphism equation, replace the child values by the
induction hypothesis, and use functionality of the algebra
operation. Both pairs of graphs are supported on the same source
predicates. The resulting universal graph equivalences are
therefore equality of the two pairs of morphisms in
$\mathcal B_T$. This proves uniqueness for every $P$. Taking $P$
to be terminal proves initiality in $\mathcal B_T^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Use the codes of finite sequences and the predicate
\[
 \operatorname{List}_V(w)\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
 w\text{ is a sequence code}\ \land\
       \forall i<\operatorname{len}(w)\,V(w_i).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:st-finite-sigma1} gives a $\Sigma_1$ presentation.
The empty sequence and the operation of prepending an entry are
primitive recursive, and $\mathrm{PA}$ proves their carrier
conditions and the unique nil-or-cons decomposition.

For an algebra in $\mathcal B_T/P$ on an arbitrary projection
$\xi:X\to P$, its nil operation is a morphism $P\to X$ over
$P$, and its cons operation has source
$(P\times V)\times_P X$. Evaluate a list from its final entry
back to its first entry, starting with the nil value in the fiber
over $p$. A finite sequence records these values and the
codes of halting computations of the two algebra operations. Lemma~\ref{lem:st-finite-sigma1} combines the finitely many carrier and
computation conditions into a $\Sigma_1$ condition on the evaluation sequence.
Existential quantification over its code gives a $\Sigma_1$ evaluation
relation. Induction in $T$ on length proves
its totality, functionality, and preservation of the projection to
$P$. Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search} makes it a morphism.
The nil and cons equations follow by splitting the evaluation sequence,
and induction in $T$ on length proves uniqueness of any morphism
satisfying these equations.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Free variables and substitution}
\label{sec:st-substitution-realization}

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:st-substitution-realization}
On the preceding codes, the list operations, free-variable morphisms,
term substitution, and the formula-substitution morphism with codomain
$1+\Fm$ of Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories} are represented by algorithms whose
defining equations and preservation of the specified carriers are
provable in $\PA$. Restricting each graph to its source predicate
gives a morphism of $\mathcal B_T$. These are the morphisms
constructed there by parameterized initiality. In particular, the
subobject $\Adm$ is the free-for substitution domain on
these named-variable codes, represented by a complemented
subobject in $\mathcal B_T$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Concatenation, membership, and deletion on sequence codes are
primitive recursive. Membership compares numerical variable labels;
deletion removes every entry equal to the specified label.
Induction in $\mathrm{PA}$ on sequence length proves their nil and
cons equations and the two membership identities displayed in
Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}. Concatenation and deletion return
lists of variables, and membership returns a Boolean value.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:st-list-initiality}, these equations determine
the three list operations.

Write $L_V$ for the list object of Proposition~\ref{prop:st-list-initiality}.
The free-variable maps $\FV_{\Tm}:\Tm\to L_V$ and
$\FV_{\Fm}:\Fm\to L_V$ read the nodes in children-before-parent order. A variable contributes
the singleton list. Function symbols, relation symbols, equality, and
implication concatenate the child lists in argument order. Negation
retains its child list, and quantification deletes the bound variable. This is a primitive-recursive traversal
on finite codes. Induction in $\mathrm{PA}$ on node count proves
that its output satisfies $\operatorname{List}_V$ and proves the
constructor equations. These are the equations of the
$K$-algebra on lists, so
Proposition~\ref{prop:st-syntax-initiality} identifies this algorithm
with $\FV_{\Tm}$ and $\FV_{\Fm}$.

For substitution, use a traversal which retains at each node both
its original subtree and its computed result. Its parameters are
a variable code $x$ satisfying $V(x)$ and a term code $t$
satisfying $\operatorname{Tm}(t)$. Put $E=V\times\Tm$.
The result maps, with the expression first, have types
\[
 a_T:\Tm\times E\longrightarrow\Tm,\qquad
 b_F:\Fm\times E\longrightarrow1+\Fm .
\] Write
$\fail_{\Fm}:1\to1+\Fm$ and $\ok_{\Fm}:\Fm\to1+\Fm$ for the
coproduct injections. The first summand represents inadmissible
substitution. The second contains the substituted formulas.
Negation uses $1_1+\neg:1+\Fm\to1+\Fm$.
For implication, define
$\widehat{\Rightarrow}:(1+\Fm)^2\to1+\Fm$ to restrict to
$\ok_{\Fm}\mathord{\Rightarrow}$ on the $\Fm\times\Fm$ summand
and to $\fail_{\Fm}$ composed with the unique morphism to $1$
on each of the other three summands.
For quantification, define
$\widehat\forall:V\times(1+\Fm)\to1+\Fm$ to restrict to
$\ok_{\Fm}\forall$ on $V\times\Fm$ and to $\fail_{\Fm}$ composed
with the unique morphism to $1$ on $V\times1$.
These are the morphisms used in Appendix~\ref{app:substitution}.
At a term variable $v$, the result is $t$ if $v=x$ and is the
original variable term otherwise. At a function symbol, apply the
constructor to the substituted children. At an atomic formula,
apply its constructor to the substituted terms, followed by
$\ok_{\Fm}$. At negation and implication, apply the morphisms
just defined to the values computed for the immediate subformulas.

At a quantified formula $\forall y\,\varphi$, let $z$ be the
computed value in $1+\Fm$ for its body. The algorithm returns
\[
 \begin{cases}
  \ok_{\Fm}(\forall y\,\varphi),&y=x,\\
  \widehat\forall(y,z),&y\ne x\text{ and }
       \bigl(x\notin\operatorname{FV}(\varphi)
             \text{ or }y\notin\operatorname{FV}(t)\bigr),\\
  \fail_{\Fm},&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here $x\notin\FV(\varphi)$ means that the numerical list
contains no entry equal to $x$, and the other occurrence assertions have the
same meaning. The first branch uses the original body, even if
the value computed for that body lies in the first summand. These branches give
the quantified-constructor equation in Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}.

The traversal is primitive recursive: it runs through the finite
node sequence, retaining finite lists of original subtrees and
computed values, using only primitive-recursive coding operations.
Induction in $\mathrm{PA}$ proves that the term result is a valid
term and that every value in the second summand is the image of a valid formula.
The same induction proves that the first component is the original
subtree and verifies all the constructor equations of the
$K_{V\times\Tm}$-algebra used in Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}.
Uniqueness in Proposition~\ref{prop:st-syntax-initiality} identifies
the result morphisms with $a_T$ and $b_F$.

Let $D(\varphi,x,t)$ be the source predicate
$\operatorname{Fm}(\varphi)\land V(x)\land\operatorname{Tm}(t)$.
Let $b(\varphi,x,t)$ be the numerical tag of the result of the
traversal, with $1$ for success and $0$ for failure. Set $b=0$ if $\varphi$ does not parse as a formula or $t$ as a term. The traversal
parses constructor tags and tests equality of numerical labels, so
$b$ is primitive recursive independently of signature membership. On the source $D$, induction in $\PA$
identifies success with the free-for condition. Thus the two
inverse images of the summands of $1+\Fm$ are represented by
\[
 \operatorname{Adm}(\varphi,x,t)\equiv D(\varphi,x,t)\land b(\varphi,x,t)=1,
 \qquad D(\varphi,x,t)\land b(\varphi,x,t)=0 .
\]
They are complements in the subobject order of $\Fm\times V\times\Tm$.
For a quantified formula on this source the free-for condition is
\[
 y=x\quad\text{or}\quad
 \bigl(y\ne x\ \land\
   (x\notin\operatorname{FV}(\varphi)
        \text{ or }y\notin\operatorname{FV}(t))\ \land\
   \operatorname{Adm}(\varphi,x,t)\bigr).
\]
The formula in the second summand satisfies the substitution equation on
each such branch.

\subsection{Derivations and theories}
\label{subsec:syntactic-theories}

Let $\operatorname{fv}_{\Fm}(z)$ denote the numerical free-variable
list function. Since $0$ codes the empty list,
the predicate
$\operatorname{Sent}(z)\equiv
\operatorname{Fm}(z)\land\operatorname{fv}_{\Fm}(z)=0$
presents the sentence object
$S=(\omega,[\operatorname{Sent}]_T)$. Its inclusion into $\Fm$
is represented by the identity on sentence codes. This is the
pullback of the empty-list morphism along $\FV_{\Fm}$ required
by Definition~\ref{def:sentence-object}.
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:syntactic-derivation-initiality}
Let $T\supseteq\PA$, let $F$ be an object of $\mathcal B_T$, and
fix morphisms
\[
 p_n:R_n\longrightarrow F^n,\qquad
 q_n:R_n\longrightarrow F\qquad(0\leq n\leq N),
\]
where $N$ is a fixed nonnegative integer.
The inference endofunctor $H$ of
Appendix~\ref{app:closed-subobjects} has an initial algebra in
$\mathcal B_T/F$.  Its underlying object and conclusion morphism
are represented by $\Sigma_1$ formulas.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-total-category}, choose isomorphisms
$i:F'\to F$ and $j_n:R'_n\to R_n$ from objects represented by
$\Sigma_1$ formulas $F(z)$ and $R_n(r)$. Take program indices
$u_n,v_n$ for the morphisms
\[
 (i^{-1})^n p_n j_n:R'_n\longrightarrow (F')^n,\qquad
 i^{-1}q_n j_n:R'_n\longrightarrow F',
\]
respectively. Postcomposition with $i$ identifies $\mathcal B_T/F'$
with $\mathcal B_T/F$. Under this identification, the $j_n$ induce
a natural isomorphism between the inference endofunctor for the
transported rules and $H$. We use these representatives below. The
nullary product is represented by the singleton code $0$.

Fix codes for finite ordered trees in which a node of arity
$n\leq N$ has a numerical label $r$. Write
$\operatorname{node}_n(r,d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ for the constructor.
These constructors can be chosen injective,
with pairwise disjoint images, and so that each $d_j$ is smaller
than the resulting code.  For example, use
$1+\langle n,\langle r,\operatorname{tuple}_n(d_1,\ldots,d_n)
\rangle\rangle$, with fixed-length tuple codes, taking the empty
tuple code to be $0$.  The pairing of Section~\ref{sec:syntactic}
is at least each of its components, so this inequality is provable
in $\PA$.
Course-of-values primitive recursion then defines a
primitive-recursive predicate $\operatorname{Tree}(d)$ and a
primitive-recursive list of the node occurrences of a tree.  At
each occurrence the list records the arity, numerical label, and
indices of its immediate children.  The list is ordered so that
children precede their parent.  Its constructor equations and
the unique decomposition of a tree are provable in $\PA$ by
induction on its numerical code.

Let $P(d)$ assert that $d$ is a tree and that each node, with label $r$,
arity $n$, and immediate subtrees $d_1,\ldots,d_n$, satisfies $R_n(r)$
and admits an $n$-tuple $(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ such that
\[
 G_{u_n}(r,\langle z_1,\ldots,z_n\rangle)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 G_{v_{m_j}}(r_j,z_j)\quad(1\leq j\leq n).
 \tag{\(*\)}
\]
Here $m_j$ and $r_j$ are the arity and label of the root of
$d_j$.  For $n=0$, the condition in \((*)\) is
$G_{u_0}(r,0)$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:st-finite-sigma1} makes $P$ a $\Sigma_1$
formula, with witnesses for node membership and computations existentially
quantified.

For a tree $d$ whose root has arity $n$ and label $r$, put
$C(d,z)\equiv P(d)\land G_{v_n}(r,z)$.
This abbreviates the finite disjunction over $0\leq n\leq N$
using the primitive-recursive root projections.
The $T$-provable totality of $q_n$ on $R_n$ shows that
$T$ proves $P(d)\to\exists!z\,C(d,z)$ and
$C(d,z)\to F(z)$.
The formula $C$ is $\Sigma_1$ and its functionality is already
provable in $\PA$, by the functionality of the deterministic
program graphs.  Witness search therefore supplies an index
$e_c$ for which
\[
 \PA\vdash\forall d\forall z\,
             \bigl(G_{e_c}(d,z)\leftrightarrow C(d,z)\bigr).
\]
Its class represents a morphism $c:(\omega,[P]_T)\to F$ in
$\mathcal B_T$.

The constructor equations for the node list give, in $T$,
\begin{align}
 &P\bigl(\operatorname{node}_n(r,d_1,\ldots,d_n)\bigr)
                                                        \label{eq:syntactic-derivation-domain}\\
 &\quad\longleftrightarrow
 R_n(r)\land\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}P(d_j)\land
 \exists z_1\cdots z_n\,
 \left(G_{u_n}(r,\langle z_1,\ldots,z_n\rangle)
       \land\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}C(d_j,z_j)\right).
 \notag
\end{align}
For $n=0$, the last conjunct means $G_{u_0}(r,0)$.
The right-hand side is a predicate presenting
$B_n(P,c)$.  Consequently the constructors define a total
morphism $\delta:H(P,c)\to(P,c)$ in $\mathcal B_T/F$:
its conclusion is $q_n(r)$ on this summand.

Let $\alpha:H(Q,q)\to(Q,q)$ be any algebra in this slice.
Represent $Q$ by $Q(y)$, $q$ by an index $b$, and $\alpha$ by
an index $a$. The graph $G_a$ is $T$-provably total on the
carrier of $H(Q,q)$.

For $0\leq n\leq N$, let $\operatorname{tag}_n:\N^{n+1}\to\N$
be the primitive-recursive function obtained from the fixed tuple
and coproduct encodings for the $n$th summand of $H(Q,q)$.
Define $E_a(d,y)$ to assert that $d$ is a tree and there is a
finite list of values, one for each node occurrence, whose root
value is $y$, with the following property.  At a node of arity
$n$ and label $r$, if its children's values are
$y_1,\ldots,y_n$ and its own value is $y'$, then
\[
 G_a\bigl(\operatorname{tag}_n(r,y_1,\ldots,y_n),y'\bigr).
\]
This definition is $\Sigma_1$ by
the argument for finite sequences above.  The functionality of $G_a$
proves the functionality of $E_a$ in $\PA$: compare two value
lists in their children-before-parent order and use induction on
the position in the list.
Decomposing and concatenating value lists proves in $\PA$ that,
for trees $d_1,\ldots,d_n$,
\begin{align}
 &E_a\bigl(\operatorname{node}_n(r,d_1,\ldots,d_n),y\bigr)
                                                        \label{eq:syntactic-derivation-fold}\\
 &\quad\longleftrightarrow
 \exists y_1\cdots y_n\,
 \left(\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}E_a(d_j,y_j)
       \land G_a(\operatorname{tag}_n(r,y_1,\ldots,y_n),y)
 \right).
 \notag
\end{align}

Induction on the numerical tree code now proves in $T$ that
each $d$ satisfying $P(d)$ has an evaluation $y$ in $Q$, and
that its image under $q$ equals its conclusion under $c$.
For the induction step, the induction hypotheses give values
$y_j$ for the immediate subtrees, with
$q(y_j)=c(d_j)$.  Equation~\eqref{eq:syntactic-derivation-domain}
therefore places $(r,y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ in $B_n(Q,q)$, and hence
its code $\operatorname{tag}_n(r,y_1,\ldots,y_n)$ in $H(Q,q)$,
the domain of $\alpha$. Its $T$-provable totality supplies
$y$, and its equation as a slice morphism supplies
$q(y)=q_n(r)=c(d)$.  Equation~\eqref{eq:syntactic-derivation-fold}
supplies the evaluation at $d$.  The same argument covers
$n=0$, with no induction hypotheses.
Thus $T$ proves
\[
 P(d)\longrightarrow\exists!y\,E_a(d,y),
 \qquad
 P(d)\land E_a(d,y)\longrightarrow Q(y),
\]
and, for all $d,y,z$, proves
\[
 P(d)\land E_a(d,y)
 \longrightarrow\bigl(G_b(y,z)\leftrightarrow C(d,z)\bigr).
\]
Witness search for the $\Sigma_1$ relation
$P(d)\land E_a(d,y)$ gives a partial-recursive graph uniformly
equivalent to it in $\PA$.  It defines a total slice morphism
$h:(P,c)\to(Q,q)$.  Equation~\eqref{eq:syntactic-derivation-fold}
gives the algebra-morphism equation
$h\delta=\alpha H(h)$.

If $g:(P,c)\to(Q,q)$ is another algebra morphism, its
algebra-morphism equation gives the same recursion equation
on the domain in~\eqref{eq:syntactic-derivation-domain}.
Induction on $d$, using the unique root decomposition, proves
in $T$ that its graph on $P(d)$ is equivalent to $E_a(d,y)$.
Outside $P$ both morphisms have empty domain, by their source
restriction equations.  Their graphs are therefore uniformly
$T$-provably equivalent.  Hence $g=h$, proving initiality.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:syntactic-generated-theory}
Let $T$ be a consistent extension of $\PA$ and put
$\mathcal B_T=\Tot(\Split(S_T))$. Fix a nonnegative integer $d$
and variable and signature objects $V,\Sigma_k,\Pi_k$ of
$\mathcal B_T$ for $0\leq k\leq d$.
The syntax, list, and substitution constructions above realize
the first-order structure of Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}
in $\mathcal B_T$. For every axiom subobject $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S$
of its sentence object, the inference endofunctor $H_A$ has an
initial algebra with conclusion morphism $c_A:P_A\to\Fm$.
Its image is the least subobject of $\Fm$ containing the logical
and nonlogical axioms and closed under generalization and modus
ponens. The sentence pullback of this image is the least sentence
theory containing $A$.

Use the sentence predicate above, and choose the derivation
predicate $P_A(p)$ and conclusion index $e_A$ furnished by the
construction. Put $\operatorname{Th}_A(z)\equiv\exists p\,G_{e_A}(p,z)$.
Then the restriction idempotent
\[
 t_A=[\operatorname{Sent}(z)\land\operatorname{Th}_A(z)]_T:
                  \omega\rightharpoonup\omega
\]
belongs to $S_T$, and its splitting represents that sentence theory.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-total-category} supplies regularity,
disjoint stable finite coproducts, and partial inverses for
monomorphisms. Numerical equality gives decidable equality on $V$.
Propositions~\ref{prop:st-syntax-initiality} and
\ref{prop:st-list-initiality} give the required initial algebras,
stable under every parameter object.
Proposition~\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization} identifies
their free-variable and substitution morphisms with the specified
numerical operations.

Every rule object in Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}
is a finite product, coproduct, or pullback of these objects and
$A$. Its premise and conclusion morphisms are composites of the
realized constructors and substitution morphisms. They are
therefore morphisms of $\mathcal B_T$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-derivation-initiality} applies with $N=2$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-theory} and the sentence-theory
construction following it give the two leastness assertions.

The morphism $[e_A]_T:\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$
has restriction $[P_A]_T$ and range $[\operatorname{Th}_A]_T$.
The graph $G_{e_A}(p,z)\land\operatorname{Sent}(z)$
is $\Sigma_1$ and PA-provably functional. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search} it has a program
index $e_{A,S}$ with PA-provably equivalent graph.
Put $D_{A,S}(p)\equiv\exists z\,
(G_{e_A}(p,z)\land\operatorname{Sent}(z))$.
The program $e_{A,S}$ represents the total conclusion map
$c_{A,S}:(\omega,[D_{A,S}]_T)\to
(\omega,[\operatorname{Sent}]_T)=S$.
The range of $[e_{A,S}]_T:\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$ in $S_T$ is $t_A$.
Since $t_A\leq[\operatorname{Sent}]_T$, the same program class
for this partial identity defines $\ran(c_{A,S}):S\rightharpoonup S$
in $\Split(S_T)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image}, it
splits through the regular image of $c_{A,S}$.
Thus its splitting is the asserted sentence theory.
\end{proof}

For a c.e.\ axiomatization of $T$ in the arithmetic signature, choose
a $\Sigma_1$ formula $\operatorname{Ax}_T(z)$ whose solutions in
$\N$ are the codes of its axioms. Then
$\operatorname{Sent}(z)\land\operatorname{Ax}_T(z)$ presents an
axiom subobject $A\hookrightarrow S$ in $\mathcal B_T$.
The idempotent $t_A$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:syntactic-generated-theory}
represents the sentence theory generated by this presentation.
\section{Interpretation and soundness}\label{sec:models}

The restriction product of $X$ and $Y$ in $\Pfn$ has underlying set
$X\times Y$. The pairing of $f:W\rightharpoonup X$ and
$g:W\rightharpoonup Y$ sends $w$ to $(f(w),g(w))$ on
$\operatorname{dom}(f)\cap\operatorname{dom}(g)$. The coproduct
is the disjoint union $X\amalg Y$.

Fix a model $M\models T$. Assign a set $X_M$ to each term
$X\in\mathsf O$ by
\[
 X_M=|M|\quad(X=\omega),\qquad
 (X\times Y)_M=X_M\times Y_M,\qquad
 (X+Y)_M=X_M\amalg Y_M.
\]
The recursive coding for each $X\in\mathsf O$ induces a bijection
$\gamma_X^M:X_M\to|M|$: use the identity for $\omega$, the
interpreted pairing for products, and the interpreted even and odd
codings for the two coproduct summands. The PA-provable coding
identities give the inverses. For $e\in\mathcal I(X,Y)$
and elements $x\in X_M$, $y\in Y_M$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:model-functor}
 \begin{aligned}
 F_M(X)&=X_M,\\
 F_M([e]_T)(x)=y
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 M\models G_e\bigl(\gamma_X^M(x),\gamma_Y^M(y)\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The standard index $e$ in $G_e$ is interpreted as its numeral in $M$.
Traces and intermediate values in this formula range over $M$,
including its nonstandard elements.

\begin{proof}
Functionality is provable in $\PA$, so the interpreted graph is a
partial function. Equation \eqref{eq:uniform} makes the assignment
independent of the representative. Equation \eqref{eq:composition},
interpreted in $M$, quantifies over an intermediate arithmetic code.
The bijection $\gamma_Y^M$ converts that code into the intermediate
element of $Y_M$, proving preservation of composition. The identity
graph gives the identity function on $X_M$.

For $[e]_T:X\rightharpoonup Y$ the domain is
$\{x\in X_M:M\models\exists b\,G_e(\gamma_X^M(x),b)\}$.
Every witness $a\in|M|$ to $R_e(\gamma_Y^M(y))$ is the code
of $(\gamma_X^M)^{-1}(a)$, so
\[
 \{y\in Y_M:M\models R_e(\gamma_Y^M(y))\}
 =\operatorname{im}(F_M[e]_T),
\]
where $R_e(b)\equiv\exists a\,G_e(a,b)$. Hence $F_M$ preserves ranges.
False predicates, conjunction, and disjunction
give zeros, intersections, and unions. The PA-provable product and
coproduct graph equations give the corresponding operations on
partial functions.
\end{proof}
\subsection{Lifting complementary conditionals}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:switch}
Let $c,c'$ be complementary restriction idempotents on $X$ in $S_T$.
There is a total morphism $s:X\to X+X$ with
\[
 sc=i_1c,\qquad sc'=i_0c'.
\]
For every $M\models T$, the morphism $\chi_{X,X}^{-1}F_Ms$ is the
unique section of $\nabla_{F_MX}(F_Mc'+F_Mc)$, where
$\chi_{X,X}:F_MX+F_MX\to F_M(X+X)$ is the coproduct isomorphism.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose $\Sigma_1$ predicates $C(x)$ and $C'(x)$ representing
$c$ and $c'$.
The theory $T$ proves universally their disjointness and coverage.
For $j=0,1$, put $\iota_j(x)=2x+j$. The graph
$z=\iota_j(x)$ represents the coproduct injection
$i_j:X\to X+X$ on numerical codes.
The $\Sigma_1$ relation
\[
 R(x,z)\equiv
 (C(x)\land z=\iota_1(x))\lor(C'(x)\land z=\iota_0(x))
\]
is $T$-provably functional and total.
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-functional-search} supplies an index $e_s$
whose graph is $T$-provably equivalent to $R$. Thus $s=[e_s]_T$
is total in $S_T$, and its graph gives $sc=i_1c$ and $sc'=i_0c'$.

Interpret this graph equivalence in $M\models T$.
Under the coproduct isomorphism $\chi_{X,X}^{-1}$, $F_M(s)$ sends
$x$ to its image under the second coproduct injection when
$M\models C(\gamma_X^M(x))$ and under the first when
$M\models C'(\gamma_X^M(x))$.
These conditions partition $X_M$, so
$\chi_{X,X}^{-1}F_M(s)$ is the partial inverse of
$\nabla_{X_M}(F_M(c')+F_M(c))$. The latter partial function is injective
on its domain and has range $X_M$, so its partial inverse is its
unique section.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:model-pair}
For every $M\models T$, the functor $F_M$ satisfies the hypotheses of
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals}. Thus, for a Turing morphism
$\tau:\omega\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$ and an isomorphism
$b:\omega\to\omega+\omega$ in $S_T$, the restriction idempotents
\[
 (b\tau\Delta_\omega)^*(1_\omega+0_\omega),\qquad
 (b\tau\Delta_\omega)^*(0_\omega+1_\omega)
\]
are inseparable in $S_T$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
In $\Pfn$, inverse images along total morphisms preserve binary joins of restriction
idempotents. Proposition~\ref{prop:model} supplies the range functor,
Lemma~\ref{lem:switch} supplies the total source conditionals, and
$F_M(1_\omega)\ne0$ because $|M|$ is nonempty.
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} applies.
\end{proof}
\subsection{The total interpretation functor}

For a model $M\models T$, split each interpreted restriction
idempotent in $\Pfn$ by its domain inclusion. Restricting the resulting
functor $\widehat F_M:\Split(S_T)\to\Pfn$ to total morphisms gives
\[
 G_M:\mathcal B_T\longrightarrow\mathbf{Set},
 \qquad \mathcal B_T=\Tot(\Split(S_T)).
\]
Explicitly, put $D_e=\operatorname{dom}F_M(e)\subseteq X_M$ for a
split object $(X,e)$. A morphism
$f:(X,e)\rightharpoonup(Y,d)$ satisfies $f=dfe$.
Thus $\widehat F_M(X,e)=D_e$, and
$\widehat F_M(f):D_e\rightharpoonup D_d$ sends $x$ to $F_M(f)(x)$
where this value is defined. For a total split morphism,
$\bar f=e$, so the domain is all of $D_e$. This restriction of
$F_M(f)$ is the function $G_M(f):D_e\to D_d$.
Let $J_T:\mathcal P_T\to\mathcal B_T$ denote the equivalence
constructed in Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-total-category}. Thus
$J_T(C)=(\omega,[C]_T)$. Splitting by domain inclusions gives
\[
 G_MJ_T(C)=C(M):=\{a\in |M|:M\models C(a)\},
\]
and $G_MJ_T(R):C(M)\to D(M)$ is the function whose graph
is the interpretation of the functional graph $R:C\to D$ in $M$.

\begin{proof}
It suffices to work along the equivalence $J_T$.
The terminal predicate $x=0$ is interpreted as a singleton.
The numerical pairing bijection identifies the interpretation of
the product predicate with $C(M)\times D(M)$. For functional graphs
$R,R':C\to D$, the equalizer predicate
\[
 C(x)\land\exists y\,
             \bigl(R(x,y)\land R'(x,y)\bigr)
\]
is interpreted as the equalizer of the two functions. Hence $G_M$
preserves finite limits. The even and odd coding bijections identify
the interpreted coproduct predicate with the disjoint union;
the false predicate is interpreted as the empty set. Finally,
the regular image of $R:C\to D$ has predicate
$\exists x\,R(x,y)$. Its interpretation is the image
of the interpreted function, since the quantified variable ranges
over all of $|M|$.
\end{proof}
\subsection{Soundness on standard codes}

Fix the arithmetic signature and the variable object
$V=(\omega,1_\omega)\in\mathcal B_{\PA}$, so that
$G_{\N}V=\N$. Use the syntax of
Section~\ref{sec:st-parameterized-syntax} and the proof-tree
algebra of Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-derivation-initiality}. Write $j:S\hookrightarrow\Fm$ for the sentence inclusion. Let $\Gamma$ be
a computably enumerable set of arithmetic sentences. Choose a
$\Sigma_1$ formula $\operatorname{Ax}_\Gamma(z)$ whose solutions
in $\N$ are the codes of the sentences in $\Gamma$, and let $i_A:A=A_\Gamma\hookrightarrow S$
be the subobject with carrier predicate
$\operatorname{Sent}(z)\land\operatorname{Ax}_\Gamma(z)$. Write
\[
 c_A:P_A\longrightarrow\Fm,\qquad
 c_{A,S}:P_{A,S}\longrightarrow S
\]
for the conclusion morphism and its pullback to sentences.
The standard interpretation of $i_A$ is the inclusion of the
codes of the sentences in $\Gamma$.

For $s\in G_{\N}S$, let $\varphi_s$ be the sentence with formula code
$G_{\N}(j)(s)$. Let $K\models\Gamma$ be a nonempty first-order
structure for the arithmetic signature, with equality interpreted
as identity. Define a subobject in $\mathbf{Set}$ by
\[
 \iota_K:\operatorname{Th}(K)\hookrightarrow G_{\N}S,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Th}(K)=\{s\in G_{\N}S:K\models\varphi_s\}.
\]
The arithmetic model $\N$ interprets the code objects and their
morphisms; the structure $K$ interprets the decoded arithmetic
formulas.

Let $i_{\Adm}:\Adm\hookrightarrow\Fm\times V\times\Tm$
be the admissibility inclusion in $\mathcal B_{\PA}$.
Composing $G_{\N}(i_{\Adm})$ with the product
comparison gives an injection of sets
\[
 a_{\N}:G_{\N}\Adm\hookrightarrow
             G_{\N}\Fm\times\N\times G_{\N}\Tm.
\]
Write $\ulcorner t\urcorner\in G_{\N}\Tm$ and
$\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner\in G_{\N}\Fm$ for the codes of a finite term
$t$ and formula $\varphi$, respectively.

\begin{lemma}[Semantic substitution]\label{lem:semantic-substitution}
Let $\sigma:\N\to |K|$ be an assignment of values to variables.
For $x\in\N$ and $a\in|K|$, write
$\sigma[x\mapsto a]:\N\to|K|$ for the assignment obtained
by changing the value of $x$ to $a$. For finite terms $r,t$,
\[
 \llbracket r[x:=t]\rrbracket^K_\sigma
 =\llbracket r\rrbracket^K_{
          \sigma[x\mapsto\llbracket t\rrbracket^K_\sigma]}.
\]
For a finite formula $\varphi$, if
$(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner,x,\ulcorner t\urcorner)$ lies in
the image of $a_{\N}$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:semantic-substitution}
 K,\sigma\models\varphi[x:=t]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 K,\sigma[x\mapsto\llbracket t\rrbracket^K_\sigma]
             \models\varphi.
\end{equation}
The substitution morphisms of
Proposition~\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization}, interpreted by
$G_{\N}$, give the codes of $r[x:=t]$ and, when admissible,
$\varphi[x:=t]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
First, term values and formula truth depend only on the values
assigned to their free variables. For a variable this is the
definition of its value. The induction steps for function and
relation symbols, equality, negation, and implication follow from
their semantic clauses. For $\forall y\,\psi$, assignments agreeing
on its free variables yield, after changing $y$ to the same
$b\in|K|$, assignments agreeing on the free variables of $\psi$.
The induction hypothesis for $\psi$ therefore proves the assertion
for the quantified formula. The free-variable lists computed in
Proposition~\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization} record the free occurrences
used in this induction.

Induction on $r$ proves the term identity. At a variable it is the
two-case definition of substitution; at a function application it
follows by applying the interpretation of the function symbol to
the induction hypotheses for its arguments. The atomic cases of
\eqref{eq:semantic-substitution} follow from this term identity.
Negation and implication follow from their truth clauses and the
induction hypotheses.

Consider $\varphi=\forall y\,\psi$ and put
$a=\llbracket t\rrbracket^K_\sigma$. If $y=x$, substitution leaves
$\varphi$ unchanged. The values of
$\sigma[x\mapsto b]$ and
$\sigma[x\mapsto a][x\mapsto b]$ agree for every $b$, proving
the required equivalence. Suppose $y\ne x$. If $x$ is not free
in $\psi$, substitution leaves $\psi$ unchanged, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization}; dependence on free variables gives the equivalence. Otherwise admissibility
requires that $y$ is not free in $t$ and that substitution into
$\psi$ is admissible. For every $b\in|K|$, independence of the value of $t$ from $y$ gives
$\llbracket t\rrbracket^K_{\sigma[y\mapsto b]}=a$. Since $x\ne y$,
\[
 \sigma[y\mapsto b][x\mapsto a]
   =\sigma[x\mapsto a][y\mapsto b].
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis to $\psi$ at
$\sigma[y\mapsto b]$ and then quantify over $b$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Soundness on standard codes]
\label{prop:standard-code-soundness}
Let $\Gamma$ be a computably enumerable set of arithmetic sentences,
with axiom subobject $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S$ in
$\mathcal B_{\PA}$, and let $K\models\Gamma$.
There is a unique function
\[
 e_K:G_{\N}P_{A,S}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Th}(K)
 \quad\text{such that}\quad
 \iota_K e_K=G_{\N}c_{A,S}.
\]
If $\nu:S\to S$ is sentence negation, then the subobjects
$\iota_K$ and $(G_{\N}\nu)^*\iota_K$ of $G_{\N}S$ have empty
intersection.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Call a finite formula valid in $K$ if it holds under every
assignment $\N\to|K|$. We check validity for the seven logical
axiom schemes of Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}.
The truth tables for negation and implication give validity of
\eqref{eq:hilbert-one}--\eqref{eq:hilbert-three}.

For universal instantiation, if $\forall x\,\varphi$ holds at
$\sigma$, then $\varphi$ holds at
$\sigma[x\mapsto\llbracket t\rrbracket^K_\sigma]$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:semantic-substitution} gives
$\varphi[x:=t]$ at $\sigma$, since the parameters of universal
instantiation are restricted to admissible substitutions.
For universal distribution, suppose
$\forall x(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)$ and $\varphi$ hold at
$\sigma$. The side condition says that $x$ is not free in
$\varphi$. Thus $\varphi$ holds at $\sigma[x\mapsto b]$ for
every $b\in|K|$, and the universally quantified implication gives
$\psi$ there. This proves $\forall x\,\psi$ at $\sigma$.
Reflexivity holds because the two occurrences of a term have the
same value. Finally, if $u=t$ holds at $\sigma$, the assignments
obtained by assigning $x$ the values of $u$ and $t$ are equal.
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:semantic-substitution} to both admissible
substitutions proves the equality-substitution axiom.

Every nonlogical axiom is a sentence satisfied by $K$, and hence
is valid under every assignment. Modus ponens preserves validity
by the truth clause for implication. Generalization preserves
validity because validity of $\varphi$ includes its truth at
$\sigma[x\mapsto b]$ for every assignment $\sigma$ and every
$b\in|K|$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-derivation-initiality}, each element
of $G_{\N}P_A$ is the code of a finite derivation tree. The
rule instance at each node satisfies its defining predicate, and
the conclusions of its immediate subderivations are its premises.
Induction on the tree shows that its root
formula is valid in $K$. Restriction to the pullback
$G_{\N}P_{A,S}$ gives a sentence satisfied by $K$.
Consequently $G_{\N}c_{A,S}$ takes values in $\operatorname{Th}(K)$; its
corestriction is $e_K$. The inclusion $\iota_K$ is monic, proving
uniqueness.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:st-substitution-realization} and the
interpretation of the constructors, $G_{\N}\nu$ sends a sentence code to
the code of its negation. A sentence and its negation cannot
both hold in $K$. This proves the empty-intersection assertion.
\end{proof}
\subsection{Ultrapowers of the interpretation functor}

Work in the set-theoretic metatheory with choice. Fix a
nonempty set $I$ and a proper ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on $I$.
For a set $X$, let
\[
 \mathscr U(X)=X^I/{\sim_{\mathcal U}},
 \qquad
 (x_i)\sim_{\mathcal U}(y_i)
 \Longleftrightarrow\{i:x_i=y_i\}\in\mathcal U.
\]
Here $X^I$ is the set of functions from $I$ to $X$. For a
function $f:X\to Y$, put
$\mathscr U(f)[x_i]=[f(x_i)]$.

\begin{proof}
The empty set and singleton are preserved. Coordinatewise pairing
gives a bijection
$\mathscr U(X\times Y)\cong\mathscr U(X)\times\mathscr U(Y)$.
Let $E\hookrightarrow X$ be the equalizer of $f,g:X\to Y$.
An element $[x_i]\in\mathscr U(X)$ equalizes
$\mathscr U(f)$ and $\mathscr U(g)$ precisely when
$J=\{i:x_i\in E\}$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. In that case
$J$ is nonempty, so choose $e\in E$ and replace $x_i$ by $e$
outside $J$. This gives a representative in $E^I$. Conversely,
every representative in $E^I$ equalizes the two functions.
The induced map from $\mathscr U(E)$ is injective by the
definition of $\sim_{\mathcal U}$. Hence equalizers, and
therefore finite limits, are preserved.

For a family in $X\amalg Y$, exactly one of the sets of indices
at which its value lies in the first or second coproduct summand
belongs to $\mathcal U$. Retain that summand on this set and
fill the other coordinates with one
element of the same summand. The summand is nonempty because
the retained set is nonempty. This proves surjectivity of
\[
 \mathscr U(X)\amalg\mathscr U(Y)
       \longrightarrow\mathscr U(X\amalg Y).
\]
The two summands are disjoint, and equality within either summand
is given by $\sim_{\mathcal U}$. Thus this
map is bijective. Finally, every surjection of sets has a section,
so its image under $\mathscr U$ is surjective. Since $\mathscr U$ preserves finite limits, it also preserves
monomorphisms. It therefore takes the image factorization of a function
to the image factorization of its ultrapower.
\end{proof}

Let $M=\N^I/\mathcal U$ be the arithmetic ultrapower.
By \L o\'s's theorem~\cite[Theorem~3.1]{Keisler}, $M\models\PA$.

\begin{lemma}[Comparison with the arithmetic ultrapower]
\label{lem:ultrapower-comparison}
There is a natural isomorphism of functors
\[
 \eta:\mathscr U G_{\N}\xRightarrow{\ \cong\ }G_M:
             \mathcal B_{\PA}\longrightarrow\mathbf{Set}.
\]
On a predicate object $J_{\PA}(C)$ it is the map
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ultrapower-predicate-comparison}
 \eta_{J_{\PA}(C)}:
 \mathscr U(C(\N))\longrightarrow C(M),
 \qquad [c_i]\longmapsto[c_i].
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \L o\'s's theorem, $\eta_{J_{\PA}(C)}$ is well defined and
injective. If $a=[a_i]\in C(M)$, then
$J=\{i:\N\models C(a_i)\}$ belongs to $\mathcal U$.
Choose $c\in C(\N)$ from one coordinate in $J$, and replace
$a_i$ by $c$ outside $J$. The resulting family belongs to
$C(\N)^I$ and represents $a$, proving surjectivity.

Let $f:C\to D$ in $\mathcal P_{\PA}$ have graph $R(x,y)$. Write
$f_{\N}:C(\N)\to D(\N)$ and $f_M:C(M)\to D(M)$ for the functions
it defines. For $c_i\in C(\N)$ put $d_i=f_{\N}(c_i)$. Since
$\N\models R(c_i,d_i)$ for every $i$, \L o\'s's theorem gives
$M\models R([c_i],[d_i])$. Functionality in $M$ yields
\[
 f_M([c_i])=[f_{\N}(c_i)]\quad\text{in }D(M).
\]

To define the comparison on $\mathcal B_{\PA}$, for each
object $B$ choose an isomorphism
$u_B:J_{\PA}(C_B)\xrightarrow{\cong}B$, as supplied by
Lemma~\ref{lem:syntactic-total-category}, and set
\[
 \eta_B=G_M(u_B)\,
       \eta_{J_{\PA}(C_B)}\,
       \mathscr U(G_{\N}(u_B^{-1})):
       \mathscr U(G_{\N}B)\longrightarrow G_MB.
\]
For $f:B\to B'$, full faithfulness gives a unique
$g:C_B\to C_{B'}$ with $J_{\PA}(g)=u_{B'}^{-1}fu_B$.
Apply naturality on predicates to $g$, compose on the left with
$G_M(u_{B'})$ and on the right with $\mathscr U(G_{\N}(u_B^{-1}))$.
This gives
\[
 G_M(f)\eta_B=\eta_{B'}\mathscr U(G_{\N}(f)):
       \mathscr U(G_{\N}B)\longrightarrow G_MB'.
\]
Taking $f=1_B$ and using two presentations of $B$ in this calculation
gives equality of the two formulas for $\eta_B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Soundness in the arithmetic ultrapower]
\label{thm:ultrapower-soundness}
Let $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S$ and $K$ satisfy the hypotheses of
Proposition~\ref{prop:standard-code-soundness}, and let
$\nu:S\to S$ be syntactic negation in $\mathcal B_{\PA}$.
Let $I$ be nonempty,
let $\mathcal U$ be a proper ultrafilter on $I$, and put
$M=\N^I/\mathcal U$. Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \iota_{K,\mathcal U}
   &=\eta_S\mathscr U(\iota_K):\mathscr U(\operatorname{Th}(K))\hookrightarrow G_MS,\\
 e_{K,\mathcal U}
   &=\mathscr U(e_K)\eta_{P_{A,S}}^{-1}:
       G_MP_{A,S}\longrightarrow \mathscr U(\operatorname{Th}(K)).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ultrapower-soundness-factorization}
 \iota_{K,\mathcal U}e_{K,\mathcal U}=G_Mc_{A,S},
\end{equation}
and $\iota_{K,\mathcal U}$ has empty intersection with its inverse
image along $G_M\nu$. Consequently the interpreted theorem
subobject and its inverse image along $G_M\nu$ have empty
intersection. Equivalently, for the restriction idempotent
$t_A=\ran(c_{A,S})$ in $\Split(S_{\PA})$,
\[
