 A_i=\{e:\tau_a(e,e)\mathord\downarrow=m
                   \text{ for some }m\equiv i\pmod2\},
 \qquad i=0,1.
\end{equation}

\subsection{The index sets below and above \texorpdfstring{$1/2$}{1/2}}
\label{sec:miller-cuts}

Define $L_a=\{n:a(n)<\tfrac12\}$ and
$R_a=\{n:a(n)>\tfrac12\}$.
Their partial identities belong to $\mathcal E_a$ by the two
finite-prefix tests in Lemma~\ref{lem:miller-unanimity}, with $c=1/2$.

\begin{proof}
For $e,m,t\in\N$, let $H_{e,m,t}$ be the finite union of halting
cylinders enumerated by stage $t$ for the computation
$\Phi_e^q(e)\mathord\downarrow=m$. Choose these finite unions increasing
in $t$, and put $K_{e,m,t}=\rho(2^{\N}\setminus H_{e,m,t})\subseteq Q$.
Each $K_{e,m,t}$ is a finite union of closed dyadic boxes computable
from $e,m,t$. Compactness of $P_z$ gives
\begin{align*}
 U_e^i
 &:=\{z\in Q:\tau_z(e,e)\mathord\downarrow=m
                      \text{ for some }m\equiv i\pmod2\}\\
 &=\bigcup_{\substack{m\equiv i\pmod2\\t\in\N}}
       (Q\setminus K_{e,m,t}).
\end{align*}
In particular, $U_e^0$ and $U_e^1$ are disjoint effectively open sets.

The product topology on $Q$ is induced by the metric
\[
 d_Q:Q\times Q\to[0,1],\qquad
 d_Q(z,w)=\sum_{n\geq0}2^{-n-1}|z(n)-w(n)|.
\]
For a nonempty box restricting finitely many coordinates to closed
rational intervals $I_n$, the distance from $z$ to the box is the
finite sum
$\sum_n2^{-n-1}\operatorname{dist}(z(n),I_n)$ over those coordinates.
Distance to a nonempty finite union is the minimum of these distances.
Define $\delta_{e,m,t}:Q\to[0,1]$ by
$\delta_{e,m,t}(z)=d_Q(z,K_{e,m,t})$ when $K_{e,m,t}$ is nonempty, and
$\delta_{e,m,t}(z)=1$ when it is empty. In each box formula, replacing
$z(n)$ by $b_{n,N}(p)$ changes the distance by at most
$2^{-N}\sum_n2^{-n-1}=2^{-N}$, since distance to an interval is
$1$-Lipschitz. Taking a finite minimum preserves this error bound.
Thus the distances are computable uniformly in $e,m,t$ from each
$p\in P_z$. They are continuous, and $\delta_{e,m,t}(z)>0$ exactly
when $z\notin K_{e,m,t}$.
For each $i$, take a fixed recursive enumeration
$(m_j,t_j)_{j\geq0}$ of all pairs with $m_j\equiv i\pmod2$, and define
\[
 g_e^i:Q\to[0,1],\qquad
 g_e^i(z)=\sum_{j\geq0}2^{-j-1}\delta_{e,m_j,t_j}(z).
\]
Since $0\le\delta_{e,m,t}\le1$, the tail from $j=N$ onward is at most
$2^{-N}$. Approximating each of the first $N$ distances to within $2^{-N}$
gives a rational approximation to $g_e^i(z)$ with error at most
$2^{1-N}$. This proves computability from every $p\in P_z$, and uniform
convergence gives continuity. The sum belongs to $[0,1]$ and is positive
exactly on $U_e^i$. The computable continuous function
\[
 r_e:Q\to[1/4,3/4],\qquad
 r_e(z)=\frac12+\frac{g_e^1(z)-g_e^0(z)}4
\]
is below $1/2$ exactly on $U_e^0$, and
is above $1/2$ exactly on $U_e^1$.

Given $e,k$ and $p\in2^{\N}$, take $N=k+1$ in the two
approximations to $g_e^i(\rho(p))$. Substituting them in the formula for
$r_e$ gives a rational with error at most $2(2^{1-N})/4=2^{-N}$.
Search the rational enumeration for its index. This gives one oracle
program $\Psi$ with
\[
 \bigl|q_{\Psi^p(e,k)}-r_e(\rho(p))\bigr|<2^{-k}
 \qquad(e,k\in\N,\ p\in2^{\N}).
\]
The oracle parameter theorem gives a total recursive $h$ such that
$\Phi_{h(e)}^p(k)=\Psi^p(e,k)$. For $p\in P_a$ these computations
represent the same real $r_e(a)$, so the Miller property gives
$a(h(e))=r_e(a)$.
Together with $a\in U_e^i\Longleftrightarrow e\in A_i$, this proves
the asserted inverse-image equalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
If complementary restriction idempotents in $\mathcal E_a$ separated
$1_{L_a},1_{R_a}$, their inverse images under $h$ would separate
$1_{A_0},1_{A_1}$, contrary to
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} as applied above.
For $p\in P_a$, put $C_p=\{n:p(\langle n,0\rangle)=0\}$. A binary
expansion beginning with $0$ represents a number at most $1/2$,
and one beginning with $1$ represents a number at least $1/2$. Hence
\[
 L_a\subseteq C_p\subseteq\N\setminus R_a
 \qquad(p\in P_a).
\]
One program decides $C_p$ by reading the first digit. At $a(n)=1/2$
the two expansions $0.0111\ldots$ and $0.1000\ldots$ give different
answers. If a single set $C$ separating the cuts were decided by one
program for every $p\in P_a$, the complementary partial identities
$1_C$ and $1_{\N\setminus C}$ would separate the cuts in $\mathcal E_a$.
\end{proof}

If $J_p\tau_a$ were a Turing morphism, Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals},
applied to $I_p:\mathrm{Rec}^{p}\to\mathcal K_p$ and its
$p$-recursive conditionals associated with complementary restriction
idempotents, would make $1_{A_0},1_{A_1}$ inseparable in
$\mathrm{Rec}^{p}$. The $p$-decidable set $h^{-1}(C_p)$ separates
$A_0,A_1$. Hence $J_p\tau_a$ is not a Turing
morphism, although $\mathrm{Rec}^{p}$ has a Turing morphism.

\subsection{A theory of real closed fields}
\label{subsec:miller-field-theory}

A subset $D\subseteq X$ is \emph{$\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable} if
its partial identity $1_D$ belongs to $\mathcal E_a$. In the chosen
coding this says
\[
 (\exists e\in\N)(\forall p\in P_a)\quad
 \operatorname{dom}(\Phi_e^p)=\iota_X(D).
\]
Indeed, a computation with this domain computes the partial identity
if it returns its input whenever it halts.

We use the presentation of $\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a)$
in which such a subset $D\subseteq X$ represents $(X,1_D)$.
For another $\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable subset $E\subseteq Y$,
a morphism $D\rightharpoonup E$ is represented by
a morphism $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ of $\mathcal E_a$ satisfying
$f=1_Ef1_D$; it is total when $\bar f=1_D$.
Put $\mathcal D_a=\operatorname{Tot}(\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a))$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:miller-theory-realization}
The category $\mathcal D_a$ is regular, with finite coproducts that
are disjoint and stable under pullback. Every monomorphism of
$\mathcal D_a$ has a partial inverse in
$\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a)$, and there is a restriction equivalence
\[
 \operatorname{Par}(\mathcal D_a,\operatorname{Mono})
       \simeq\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a).
\]
For $V=\N$ and a recursive signature of bounded finite arity, the
syntax and list algebras of Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}
exist in $\mathcal D_a$ and are stable under parameters.
For every axiom subobject of the sentence object, the inference
endofunctor of Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-theory} has an initial
algebra of finite derivations.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A singleton is terminal. Products have carriers $C\times D$, and the
equalizer of $f,g:C\to D$ has carrier $\{x\in C:f(x)=g(x)\}$.
Parallel semidecision and numerical equality semidecide these carriers.
The empty carrier and disjoint unions give finite coproducts.
For $f:C\to D+E$, write $i_D,i_E$ for the coproduct injections and put
\[
 C_D=f^{-1}(i_D(D)),\qquad C_E=f^{-1}(i_E(E)).
\]
Each carrier is semidecidable by running $f$ and reading its summand.
They are disjoint. The inclusions induce an isomorphism
$C_D+C_E\to C$ whose inverse sends $x$ to the summand determined by
$f(x)$. Thus pulling back the coproduct injections along $f$ gives a
coproduct decomposition of $C$.

For $f:C\to D$, dovetail the computations of $f(x)$ over all coded
inputs $x$. This semidecides $f(C)$ and gives the image factorization
$C\twoheadrightarrow f(C)\hookrightarrow D$. For a surjection
$e:C\to D$, the kernel pair has carrier
\[
 C\times_D C=\{(x,x')\in C\times C:e(x)=e(x')\}.
\]
Let $p_1,p_2:C\times_D C\to C$ be its projections. If $h:C\to Z$
satisfies $hp_1=hp_2$, then there is a unique $k:D\to Z$ with
\[
 k(y)=h(x)\quad\text{whenever } e(x)=y.
\]
Indeed, on input $y$, dovetail the computations of $e(x)$ until one
returns $y$, then return $h(x)$. The search succeeds exactly on $D$.
Different binary representations of $a$ may yield different witnesses
$x$, but $hp_1=hp_2$ makes the returned value independent of the
witness. Thus $k$ is a morphism of $\mathcal D_a$, and $e$ is the coequalizer
of its kernel pair. Conversely, if $f$ is a regular epimorphism, its
extremality makes the inclusion $f(C)\hookrightarrow D$ an
isomorphism, so $f$ is surjective. For any $g:B\to D$, the projection
$B\times_D C\to B$ is surjective when $e$ is. Hence regular
epimorphisms are stable under pullback, proving regularity.

Singleton morphisms detect failure of injectivity, so the monomorphisms
of $\mathcal D_a$ are the injections. For an injection $m:C\to D$,
the same preimage search computes the partial morphism
$m^\dagger:D\rightharpoonup C$ with
\[
 m^\dagger m=1_C,\qquad mm^\dagger=1_{m(C)}.
\]
For $y\in m(C)$ the witness is unique. The span
$C\xleftarrow{m}B\xrightarrow{g}D$ represents the partial morphism
$gm^\dagger:C\rightharpoonup D$. Conversely, a partial morphism
$u:C\rightharpoonup D$ is represented by
$C\hookleftarrow\operatorname{dom}(u)
\xrightarrow{u|_{\operatorname{dom}(u)}}D$.
For $v:D\rightharpoonup E$, the domain of $vu$ is the inverse image of $\operatorname{dom}(v)$
under the total restriction of $u$ to $\operatorname{dom}(u)$.
This is the pullback used to compose the spans. The two assignments
therefore give the stated restriction equivalence.

Equality on the variable object $V=\N$ is decidable. Encode terms and formulas
as finite labeled ordered trees with distinct numerical labels for
the constructors, and lists of variable names as finite sequences. Recursive parsing
and the recursive symbol carriers make these carriers and their
constructors recursive. Fix an arbitrary object $P$ of $\mathcal D_a$
and a $K_P$-algebra on two objects over $P$. On input $(w,t)$ or
$(w,\varphi)$, first semidecide $w\in P$ and check the tree, then
evaluate it from its leaves to its root using the algebra operations
in the fiber over $w$. Each operation preserves that fiber.
Induction on the tree proves termination and gives the same result
for every $p\in P_a$, because each algebra operation has a common
domain and value. Thus evaluation defines total morphisms from
$P\times\mathsf{Tm}$ and $P\times\mathsf{Fm}$. They satisfy the algebra
equations, and induction
proves uniqueness. This proves syntax initiality in every slice
over $P$. Evaluation of finite lists, retaining the same parameter
$w$, proves the corresponding assertion for the list algebra.

The free-variable morphism of Appendix~\ref{app:syntax-theories}
computes finite lists of occurrences. The formula-substitution morphism
has codomain $1+\mathsf{Fm}$, with injections
$\fail_{\mathsf{Fm}}:1\to1+\mathsf{Fm}$ and
$\ok_{\mathsf{Fm}}:\mathsf{Fm}\to1+\mathsf{Fm}$.
Its value belongs to the first summand when substitution is inadmissible
and to the second summand otherwise. Its defining recursion
compares the bound and substituted variables and uses the finite
membership tests in~\eqref{eq:quantifier-fold}. These computations
are recursive functions. The pullback in
Proposition~\ref{prop:categorical-substitution} therefore gives the
recursive free-for domain and substitution on that domain. The
sentence carrier, where the free-variable list is empty, is recursive.

Let $A$ be the semidecidable image of an axiom subobject in the
sentence carrier. Use the seven logical schemes, modus ponens,
and generalization of Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}.
A finite derivation tree records its rule instance and ordered
children at every node. Tree shape, logical instance conditions,
and agreement of child conclusions with the required premises are
recursive tests. Run these tests together with the finitely many
semidecision procedures for membership of nonlogical axiom leaves.
These tests semidecide the same carrier $D_A$ of valid derivations
for every $p\in P_a$. Reading the root gives a total conclusion morphism
$c_A:D_A\to\mathsf{Fm}$, and adjoining a labeled root gives an
$H_A$-algebra.

For any $H_A$-algebra, first semidecide that the input is a valid
derivation, then evaluate it from its leaves to its root. Induction
shows that each intermediate value has the prescribed conclusion,
so the next algebra operation is applied on its domain. The
evaluation terminates on every valid derivation. The operations'
common domains and values make its domain and result independent
of $p\in P_a$, so it is a morphism of $\mathcal D_a$ over
$\mathsf{Fm}$. Its recursive equations make it an algebra morphism;
induction on derivations proves uniqueness. Thus the derivation
algebra is initial.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:miller-parameterized-deduction}
Let $X$ be an object of $\mathcal D_a$. The first-order language
with variables $\N$, equality, and a nullary predicate for each
label in $X$ has the syntax and list algebras of
Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax}, stable under parameters.
For this language and for every recursive signature covered by
Proposition~\ref{prop:miller-theory-realization}, finite derivation
algebras are also stable under parameters. More precisely, if $P$
is an object of $\mathcal D_a$, $\mathsf{Fm}$ is the formula object,
$S$ is the sentence object, and
$A\hookrightarrow P\times S$ is an axiom subobject over $P$, the
corresponding inference endofunctor on
$\mathcal D_a/(P\times\mathsf{Fm})$ has an initial algebra.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Represent $X$ and $P$ by $\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable numerical
carriers. In the nullary language the term and formula functor of
Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax} reduces to
\[
 K(Y,Z)=(\N,\;Y^2+X+Z+Z^2+\N\times Z).
\]
Its formula constructors are equality, a predicate with label in $X$,
negation, implication and universal quantification. To recognize a
formula tree, check its shape and run the membership tests for its
finitely many predicate labels in parallel. This gives a semidecision
uniform in $p\in P_a$. Occurrence lists and substitution are computed
on these trees as in Proposition~\ref{prop:miller-theory-realization}.

Let $\iota$ denote the constructor algebra, and let $\iota_P$ be its
pullback to the slice over $P$. For a $K_P$-algebra
$\alpha:K_P(Y,Z)\to(Y,Z)$, evaluate each constructor at the given
parameter $w\in P$. If $t$ is a valid term or formula tree, induction
on $t$ shows that evaluation terminates in the fiber over $w$ and gives
the same value for every $p\in P_a$. Testing $w\in P$ and validity
before evaluation gives a pair of total morphisms over $P$,
\[
 h:(P\times\Tm,P\times\Fm)\longrightarrow(Y,Z),
 \qquad h\iota_P=\alpha K_P(h).
\]
The equation determines $h$ on every constructor, hence on every tree.
For lists the same recursion on the empty list and on cons gives the
unique algebra morphism from $P\times\List\N$ in the slice.

For either language put $F_P=P\times\Fm$. Let $L$ be the coproduct of the seven parameter objects for the logical
axiom schemes. Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be the objects of generalization and
modus ponens instances of Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}. For
$A\hookrightarrow P\times S$ the rule objects are
\[
 R_0^P=(P\times L)+A,\qquad R_1^P=P\times R_1,\qquad
 R_2^P=P\times R_2.
\]
Giving every premise and the conclusion of each rule the same parameter
$w$ defines the inference endofunctor $H$ on $\mathcal D_a/F_P$. A derivation at $w$ is
a finite tree of these rule instances in which the ordered child
conclusions agree with the premises at each node.
For a nonlogical axiom leaf labelled $\varphi$, the test is
$(w,\varphi)\in A$. Run all leaf tests, the syntax and rule-instance
tests, and the test $w\in P$ in parallel. Agreement of codes is
decidable. Thus the carrier $D_A$ of valid pairs $(w,t)$ is
$\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable. Reading the root defines
$c_A:D_A\to F_P$ by $c_A(w,t)=(w,\varphi)$ for root conclusion
$\varphi$. Adjoining a rule above its premises gives
$\delta:H(D_A,c_A)\to(D_A,c_A)$.

For an object $\pi_B:B\to F_P$ of the slice and an algebra
$\beta:H(B,\pi_B)\to(B,\pi_B)$, evaluate each
valid tree from the leaves to the root using $\beta$. Inductively,
each child value lies over its premise at $w$, so the rule and its
child values belong to the domain of the corresponding operation of
$\beta$. For every $p\in P_a$ it returns the same value over the rule
conclusion. With the test for membership in $D_A$
this gives a total morphism $e:D_A\to B$ satisfying
\[
 \pi_B e=c_A,\qquad e\delta=\beta H(e).
\]
The second equation forces the value at each leaf and at each node
once its children have been evaluated. Induction gives uniqueness,
so $(D_A,c_A,\delta)$ is initial.
\end{proof}

Consider the language of ordered fields with additional constants
$(c_n)_{n\in\N}$. Its symbol carriers are recursive and its arities
are at most two, so Proposition~\ref{prop:miller-theory-realization}
applies. Write $S$ for the object of sentence codes. Let
$\Gamma_a\subseteq S$ consist of a recursive axiomatization of
real closed ordered fields together with the sentences
\begin{equation}\label{eq:miller-theory}
 q<c_n\quad\text{if }q<a(n),\qquad
 c_n<q\quad\text{if }a(n)<q,
 \qquad(q\in\mathbb Q, n\in\N).
\end{equation}
For each $q=u/v$ with $u\in\mathbb Z$ and $v$ a positive integer,
the two bounds stand for the sentences
$\underline{u}<\underline{v}\,c_n$ and
$\underline{v}\,c_n<\underline{u}$, respectively, where $\underline{j}$
is the ring term for the integer $j$.
From any $p\in P_a$, enumerate the recursive field axioms and
dovetail the two strict-inequality tests of
Lemma~\ref{lem:miller-unanimity} over all $n,u,v$ with $v>0$.
Whenever a test succeeds, enumerate its sentence. For each $p\in P_a$
this enumerates exactly $\Gamma_a$, so $\Gamma_a$ is
$\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable. Let $T_a$ be the sentence theory
generated by $\Gamma_a$. The real field with $c_n$ interpreted as $a(n)$
is a model of $T_a$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:miller-incompleteness}
Let $a$ be a Miller sequence with property~\eqref{eq:miller-property}.
In the language of ordered fields with constants $c_n$ for $n\in\N$,
let $T_a$ be the deductive closure of the axioms for real closed
ordered fields together with the rational bounds in~\eqref{eq:miller-theory}.
For every consistent extension of $T_a$ in the same language with
an $\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable axiom set, the partial identities on its
theorem and refutation sets are inseparable in
$\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a)$.
In particular, every such extension is incomplete.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The recursive set $S$ of sentence codes is an
object of $\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a)$. Negation and insertion
of a constant into an inequality give recursive total morphisms
\[
 \nu:S\to S,\qquad
 \nu(\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner)=\ulcorner\neg\varphi\urcorner,
 \qquad
 \theta:\N\to S,\qquad
 \theta(n)=\ulcorner 2c_n<1\urcorner.
\]
For a theory $T$ with an $\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable axiom set,
let $A_T\hookrightarrow S$ be its axiom subobject. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:miller-theory-realization}, the inference
endofunctor $H_{A_T}$ has an initial derivation algebra. Pulling its
conclusion morphism $c_{A_T}:D_{A_T}\to\mathsf{Fm}$ back along the sentence
inclusion $S\hookrightarrow\mathsf{Fm}$ gives
$\mathrm{Prf}_T=D_{A_T}\times_{\mathsf{Fm}}S$ with projection
$c_T:\mathrm{Prf}_T\to S$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-theory} identifies its image with the
sentence theory generated by $A_T$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:miller-theory-realization} supplies a partial
inverse for this image monomorphism in
$\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a)$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image} therefore identifies
$t_T=\ran(c_T)$ with the partial identity on the theorem set in
$\operatorname{Split}(\mathcal E_a)$.
The inverse image $\nu^*t_T$ is the partial identity on the set of
sentence codes whose negations are provable in $T$.

Let $T\supseteq T_a$ be a consistent extension with
$\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable axioms. Every member of $\Gamma_a$ is derivable in $T$. Replacing the uses of those
axioms in a finite derivation gives $t_{T_a}\le t_T$. For $n\in L_a$, the
sentence $2c_n<1$ belongs to $\Gamma_a$. For $n\in R_a$, the
axiom $1<2c_n$ and asymmetry of the strict order give
$\neg(2c_n<1)$.
Thus
\[
 1_{L_a}\le\theta^*t_{T_a}\le\theta^*t_T,\qquad
 1_{R_a}\le\theta^*\nu^*t_{T_a}\le\theta^*\nu^*t_T .
\]
The cuts remain inseparable in the splitting by
Corollary~\ref{cor:miller-cuts-inseparable}, since the restriction
idempotents and their order on $(\N,1_{\N})$ are those of $\mathcal E_a$.
Consistency gives $t_T\nu^*t_T=0_S$. Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness}
applied to $\theta$ now gives inseparability of $t_T,\nu^*t_T$ and
$t_T\vee\nu^*t_T\ne1_S$. A sentence code outside this union
is the code of a sentence $\varphi$ for which
\[
 T\nvdash\varphi \qquad\text{and}\qquad T\nvdash\neg\varphi .
\]
\end{proof}
\subsection{The associated recursion categories}

Write $\mathscr C_a=\Split(\mathcal E_a)$, and let
$t_a:\mathsf T_a\hookrightarrow S$ be the inclusion representing $T_a$. A sentence theory $u:U\hookrightarrow S$ in
$\mathcal D_a$ is understood to be closed under the field-language
deduction rules above.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:miller-associated-categories}
Let $a$ be a Miller sequence, and let $u:U\hookrightarrow S$ be a
consistent internal sentence theory extending $t_a$. The category
\[
 \mathscr C_a[U]=\Par(\mathcal D_a/U,\Mono)
\]
is a Turing category, and its internal theory
\[
 1_U\times u:U\times U\hookrightarrow U\times S
\]
is essentially incomplete. Its theorem and refutation domains are
inseparable. Let $\delta_u:S\rightharpoonup\Two$ be the partial
morphism with domain $u\vee\nu^*u$ taking the value true on $u$
and false on $\nu^*u$. Then
$1_U\times\delta_u:U\times S\rightharpoonup U\times\Two$
has no total extension in $\mathscr C_a[U]$.

If $u':U'\hookrightarrow S$ is another consistent internal
sentence theory and $u=u'i$ for $i:U\hookrightarrow U'$, then
postcomposition induces a fully faithful restriction functor
\[
 \Sigma_i:\mathscr C_a[U]\longrightarrow\mathscr C_a[U'].
\]
This functor is not essentially surjective when $i$ is proper.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:miller-theory-realization} supplies regularity,
disjoint stable finite coproducts, and the partial inverses of
monomorphisms. Lemma~\ref{lem:miller-parameterized-deduction}
supplies the syntax and finite derivations with parameters,
including the languages with nullary predicate symbols used in the
general construction.

Soundness in the real-field model of $T_a$ makes $t_a$ disjoint
from its refutation subobject. The total morphism
$\theta:\N\to S$, $\theta(n)=\ulcorner 2c_n<1\urcorner$,
reduces the inseparable pair
$1_{L_a},1_{R_a}$ to these subobjects, as in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:miller-incompleteness}.
Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness} therefore applies to
every consistent internal sentence theory extending $t_a$.
In particular, $u$ is essentially incomplete and its theorem and
refutation domains are inseparable.

The point $\lambda:1\to S$ selecting the code of $0=0$ factors through
$u$, since $T_a$ proves $0=0$. Theorem~\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness}
therefore gives essential incompleteness of $1_U\times u$ and excludes
a total extension of $1_U\times\delta_u$. A complementary separator in
the slice would give such an extension by assigning true and false to its
two summands. Lemma~\ref{lem:partial-slice-turing} gives the Turing
category, and Theorem~\ref{thm:theory-extension} gives the assertions
about $\Sigma_i$.
\end{proof}
\section{A recursion category from a three-point space}\label{sec:cosheaves}

We construct a recursion category $\mathscr R_X$ from set-valued
cosheaves in the sense of Curry~\cite[Definition~2.6]{CurryCosheaves}
on a three-point space $X$. A cosheaf on $X$ is determined up to isomorphism
by a diagram of shape $J=(1\leftarrow 0\to 2)$. Evaluating an internal propositional theory
of $\operatorname{Kar}(\mathscr R_X)$ at either endpoint gives a consistent theory.
The indices of its provable atoms and those of its refutable atoms
contain, respectively, the two members of a recursively inseparable pair.
In that endpoint language, every consistent extension with a computably
enumerable axiom set leaves an atom undecided. The internal first-order theory constructed
in Section~\ref{subsec:fork-first-order} restricts to this propositional
theory.

For a topological space $X$, let $\mathcal O(X)$ be the category
of open sets and inclusions. A \emph{set-valued cosheaf} is a
covariant functor $C:\mathcal O(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$ for which
every open cover $(O_\lambda)_\lambda$ of $O$ gives a coequalizer
\[
 \coprod_{\lambda,\mu} C(O_\lambda\cap O_\mu)
 \rightrightarrows \coprod_\lambda C(O_\lambda)
 \longrightarrow C(O).
\]
The two parallel morphisms are induced by the inclusions into the two
members of the cover; the empty cover requires
$C(\varnothing)=\varnothing$.
The \emph{Sierpi\'nski space} has two points and exactly three open
sets: the empty set, one singleton, and the whole space.

Let $X=\{a,b,c\}$ have opens
$\varnothing,\{c\},\{a,c\},\{b,c\},X$.
The open subspaces $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,c\}$ are Sierpi\'nski spaces
with common open singleton $\{c\}$. Thus $X$ is obtained by gluing
two copies of the Sierpi\'nski space along that singleton.
Its category of set-valued cosheaves is equivalent to
$\mathbf{Set}^{J}$, where $J$ has objects $0,1,2$ and nonidentity
morphisms $0\to1$ and $0\to2$.
The equivalence sends a cosheaf $C$ to the functor with values
$C(\{c\}),C(\{a,c\}),C(\{b,c\})$ at $0,1,2$, respectively,
and morphisms induced by the inclusions of these open sets.
The cosheaf value $C(X)$ is the pushout of
$C(\{a,c\})\leftarrow C(\{c\})\to C(\{b,c\})$
(Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-cosheaves}).

Use the category $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ of
Section~\ref{subsec:numerical-realization}. Its objects are pairs
$C=(m,C_0)$ with carrier $|C|=C_0$, and its morphisms are total
computable functions on the carriers. For a c.e.\ subset
$C_0\subseteq\N^m$, writing $C_0$ for the object $(m,C_0)$
abbreviates this pair. Membership, subset and image expressions,
and elementwise computations involving numerical objects refer
to their carriers.

Put $\mathcal E=\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}^J$.
An object is a covariant functor $Y:J\to\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$,
given by the objects $Y_j=Y(j)$, for $j=0,1,2$, and the
morphisms $r_i^Y=Y(0\to i):Y_0\to Y_i$, for $i=1,2$.
A morphism $f:Y\to Z$ is a natural transformation: its components
are morphisms $f_j:Y_j\to Z_j$ of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ satisfying
$r_i^Zf_0=f_i r_i^Y$.
A \emph{c.e.\ subfunctor} $D\subseteq Y$ has component objects
$D_j=(m_j,D_{j,0})$, where $Y_j=(m_j,Y_{j,0})$ and
$D_{j,0}\subseteq|Y_j|$ is c.e.\ for each $j\in\{0,1,2\}$.
The conditions $|r_i^Y|(|D_0|)\subseteq|D_i|$, for $i=1,2$,
define its morphisms $r_i^D:D_0\to D_i$ by restriction.
The component inclusions give a natural transformation $D\hookrightarrow Y$.
The underlying sets and functions define a functor
$\mathcal E\to\mathbf{Set}^J$. Composing with the quasi-inverse of
the cosheaf equivalence above assigns a set-valued cosheaf to each
object of $\mathcal E$ and a natural transformation to each morphism.

Put
$\mathcal A=\operatorname{Par}(\mathcal E,\operatorname{Mono})$.
Monomorphisms of $\mathcal E$ are componentwise injections.
Thus a partial morphism is equivalently a computably enumerable
subfunctor $D\subseteq Y$ together with a natural transformation
$D\to Z$. Its restriction is the partial identity on $D$, and its range is the
partial identity on the subfunctor of component images.
Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-structure} proves these assertions.

Define an object $V:J\to\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ of $\mathcal E$
by the following objects $V_j=V(j)$ and morphisms
$r_i^V=V(0\to i)$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universal-fork}
 \begin{gathered}
 V_0=\N^4,\qquad V_1=V_2=\N^2,\\
 r_i^V:V_0\to V_i,\qquad r_i^V(k,z,x_1,x_2)=(k,x_i)
 \quad(i=1,2).
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
For $A=(m,A_0)$ in $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$, put
$m(A)=m$. Thus $|A|\subseteq\N^{m(A)}$,
$m(V_0)=4$, and $m(V_1)=m(V_2)=2$.
Fix recursive numerical encodings of nonempty finite sequences of tuples,
\[
 \operatorname{code}_m:
 \coprod_{n\ge1}(\N^m)^n\xrightarrow{\cong}W_m\subseteq\N
 \qquad(m\ge0),
\]
where each $W_m$ is recursive and the length and entry operations
are recursive. For an object $A$ of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$, put
\[
 A^\#=\{\operatorname{code}_{m(A)}(a_1,\ldots,a_n):
                 n\ge1,\ a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A\}\subseteq W_{m(A)}.
\]
This is a c.e.\ numerical carrier. For each $Y\in\mathcal E$, let
$(Y^\#)_j=(Y_j)^\#$. Its morphism
$(Y^\#)(0\to i):(Y_0)^\#\to(Y_i)^\#$ applies $r_i^Y$ to each
entry of a word, for $i=1,2$.
Choose isomorphisms in $\mathcal E$
$V\cong V\times V$, $V\cong V+V$, and $V\cong V^\#$.
Together with their inverses, these form a \emph{frame} at $V$
\cite[Section 3]{Heller}.
Let $\mathscr R_X$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathcal A$
on the objects obtained from $V$ by finitely many applications of
the chosen binary restriction products, binary coproducts, and
nonempty-word formation.
The isomorphisms, constructed in Lemma~\ref{lem:fork-frames}, make
$\mathscr R_X$ isotypical.

Theorem~\ref{thm:fork-turing} constructs a Turing morphism
$\tau:V\times V\rightharpoonup V$ in $\mathcal A$.
For every object $Y$ of $\mathcal A$ and every morphism
$F:Y\times V\rightharpoonup V$ in $\mathcal A$, there is a
total morphism $p_F:Y\to V$ such that $\tau(p_F\times1_V)=F$.
By fullness this property holds in $\mathscr R_X$ when
$Y$ belongs to $\mathscr R_X$. Together with the inherited
prodominical structure, it makes $\mathscr R_X$ a recursion category.

Every object $Y$ of $\mathcal E$ admits a total morphism $s_Y:Y\to V$ in
$\mathcal A$ with a partial inverse $r:V\rightharpoonup Y$
such that $r s_Y=1_Y$ and $s_Y r=\bar r$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:fork-dominance}). Thus $V$ is a
\emph{universal object} of $\mathcal A$.
These embeddings give the equivalence
$\operatorname{Split}(\mathscr R_X)\simeq\mathcal A$
proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-recursion}.
Every idempotent in $\mathcal A$ splits through its image.
Corollary~\ref{cor:fork-karoubi} gives a restriction equivalence
$Q:\operatorname{Kar}(\mathscr R_X)\to\mathcal A$. We construct the
formula and derivation objects in $\mathcal E$, canonically isomorphic to
$\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal A)$.
A quasi-inverse to $Q$ transports them to the total category of
$\operatorname{Kar}(\mathscr R_X)$. At an endpoint $i$, the evaluation
of a transported object is given, up to the counit isomorphism, by
its original $i$th component.
\subsection{Complementary restriction idempotents and inseparability}

Let $e,e'$ be complementary restriction idempotents on $V$ in
$\mathscr R_X$. Write $\iota_C:C\hookrightarrow V$ and
$\iota_{C'}:C'\hookrightarrow V$ for the inclusions in $\mathcal E$
through which $e,e'$ split in $\mathcal A$.
The component carriers $C_j,C'_j$ are disjoint c.e.\ subsets whose union
is $V_j$ for each $j\in\{0,1,2\}$. Consequently the copairing
$\chi=[\iota_C,\iota_{C'}]:C+C'\to V$ has bijective components
$\chi_j:C_j+C'_j\to V_j$. Each inverse is
computable by running the membership searches for $C_j$ and $C'_j$ in
parallel and returning the element in the corresponding coproduct
summand. Naturality of $\chi$ gives
\[
 r_i^{C+C'}\chi_0^{-1}=\chi_i^{-1}r_i^V:V_0\longrightarrow C_i+C'_i
 \qquad(i=1,2).
\]
Thus these inverse components define $\chi^{-1}:V\to C+C'$ in
$\mathcal E$, proving that $\chi$ is an isomorphism.
For the injections $i_0,i_1:V\to V+V$, define
$\ell_e=[i_1\iota_C,i_0\iota_{C'}]\chi^{-1}:V\to V+V$.
It satisfies $\ell_e e=i_1e$ and $\ell_e e'=i_0e'$ and belongs to
$\mathscr R_X$ by fullness. The full inclusion
$I:\mathscr R_X\hookrightarrow\mathcal A$ is a range functor,
$I(1_V)\ne0$, and inverse images along total morphisms in $\mathcal A$ preserve
binary joins by Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-structure}.
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} therefore gives an inseparable
pair in $\mathscr R_X$.
The category $\mathscr R_X$ is not restriction-equivalent to the
recursion category of partial recursive functions
(Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-distinction}).
\subsection{Evaluation functors}

Let
$\mathcal K=\operatorname{Par}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}},\operatorname{Mono})$.
Its objects are c.e.\ numerical carriers, and its morphisms are partial
recursive functions with c.e.\ domains contained in their sources.
The functor
$\mathsf Q_{\mathrm{num}}:\operatorname{Split}(\mathrm{Rec})\to\mathcal K$
constructed in Proposition~\ref{prop:numerical-structure} is a
restriction equivalence.
For $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, component evaluation defines
\begin{equation}\label{eq:endpoint-functor}
 E_j:\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathcal K,\qquad
 E_j(Y)=Y_j,\qquad
 E_j(Y\xleftarrow{\iota_D}D\xrightarrow{f}Z)
   =(Y_j\xleftarrow{(\iota_D)_j}D_j\xrightarrow{f_j}Z_j).
\end{equation}
For the Turing morphism $\tau:V\times V\rightharpoonup V$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fork-turing}, write
$\tau_j=E_j(\tau):V_j\times V_j\rightharpoonup V_j$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:endpoint}
The covariant functors $E_j$ preserve restrictions, zeros, ranges,
binary restriction products and coproducts, and finite joins of
restriction idempotents.
For $i=1,2$, the Turing morphism
$\tau:V\times V\rightharpoonup V$ constructed in
Theorem~\ref{thm:fork-turing} is sent
to a Turing morphism on $\N^2$ in $\mathcal K$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Component evaluation preserves identities, monomorphisms, and
pullbacks in the total categories. Consequently \eqref{eq:endpoint-functor}
is independent of the representative span and preserves partial-map
composition. The stated operations are represented componentwise by
partial identities, empty sets, images, products, disjoint unions, and
finite unions, respectively.

Use the recursive bijection $\operatorname{encode}_2:\N^2\to\N$,
its inverse $\operatorname{decode}_2:\N\to\N^2$, and the acceptable numbering
$(\varphi_p)_{p\in\N}$ chosen in the construction of $\tau$ in
Appendix~\ref{app:fork-structure}. For $i=1,2$, the component $\tau_i$ is given by
\eqref{eq:fork-turing-endpoint}.
For a partial recursive map
$F:Z\times\N^2\rightharpoonup\N^2$ with c.e.\ carrier $Z$,
the parameter theorem gives a total recursive map $s:Z\to\N$ such that
\[
 \varphi_{s(z)}
 =\operatorname{encode}_2\circ F(z,-)\circ\operatorname{decode}_2
 :\N\rightharpoonup\N
 \qquad(z\in Z).
\]
Thus $z\mapsto(0,s(z)):Z\to\N^2$ is the required total parameter morphism.
\end{proof}

For $i\in\{1,2\}$, let $H_i:J\to\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$
have component $\{*\}$ at $i$ and empty components elsewhere.
For $Y\in\mathcal E$ and $y\in Y_i$, let $p_y:H_i\to Y$ be the total morphism
whose component at $i$ sends $*$ to $y$. Every total morphism
$H_i\to Y$ has this form for a unique $y\in Y_i$. A partial
morphism from $H_i$ is either total or zero, since $H_i$ has
two restriction idempotents. Postcomposition therefore defines
$\Phi_i:\mathcal A\to\Pfn$ by
\[
 \Phi_i(Y)=\operatorname{Tot}(\mathcal A)(H_i,Y),\qquad
 \Phi_i(f)(p)=fp\quad\hbox{when }fp\hbox{ is total}.
\]
If $fp$ is not total, it is zero, and every further composite
remains zero. If it is total, further postcomposition has exactly
the domain specified by the next partial function. This proves
$\Phi_i(gf)=\Phi_i(g)\Phi_i(f)$, and $\Phi_i(1_Y)(p)=p$.
Let $\lvert-\rvert:\mathcal K\to\Pfn$ send a c.e.\ numerical carrier to its
underlying set and a partial recursive morphism to the same partial
function. The bijections $p_y\mapsto y$ give a natural isomorphism
$\Phi_i\cong\lvert-\rvert\circ E_i$.
Indeed, $fp_y=p_{E_i(f)(y)}$ when $E_i(f)(y)$ is defined, and $fp_y=0$
otherwise.
For a restriction idempotent $e$ on $Y$, put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:probe-domain}
 |e|_i:=\{y\in Y_i:ep_y=p_y\}
       =\{y\in Y_i:E_i(e)(y)=y\}.
\end{equation}
This is the c.e.\ subset on which $E_i(e)$ is the partial identity.

The morphism $E_0(\tau)$ is not a Turing morphism. For the parameter
object $1$, its universal property would represent each partial recursive
$F:V_0\rightharpoonup V_0$ by a total point $1\to V_0$, using
$1\times V_0\cong V_0$. The total function $F:V_0\to V_0$ given by
$F(k,z,x_1,x_2)=(0,0,z,0)$ cannot equal $\tau_0(p,-)$ for any $p\in V_0$.
Let $D_\tau\hookrightarrow V\times V$ be the domain subfunctor of
$\tau$ constructed in Appendix~\ref{app:fork-turing}.
If $F=\tau_0(p,-)$, totality of $F$ gives $(p,x)\in D_{\tau,0}$
for every $x\in V_0$. Naturality of $D_\tau\to V$ then gives
\[
 r_1^V F(x)=\tau_1(r_1^Vp,r_1^Vx).
\]
The right-hand side is unchanged when only the $z$ coordinate
of $x=(k,z,x_1,x_2)$ changes, whereas the left-hand side is $(0,z)$.
\subsection{Propositional theories and component theorem sets}

Let $\zeta:V\to V+V$ be the coproduct isomorphism of
Lemma~\ref{lem:fork-frames}. At each component $j$, the map
$\zeta_j$ selects the summand according to the parity of the
first coordinate in $V_j$. Define complementary restriction idempotents
$\varepsilon^V_0,\varepsilon^V_1:V\rightharpoonup V$ by
\[
 \varepsilon^V_0=\zeta^{-1}(1_V+0_V)\zeta,\qquad
 \varepsilon^V_1=\zeta^{-1}(0_V+1_V)\zeta.
\]
Put $d=\tau\Delta_V:V\rightharpoonup V$. Let $A,B\subseteq V$ be the
c.e.\ subfunctors on which the restriction idempotents
$d^*\varepsilon^V_0,d^*\varepsilon^V_1$ are the partial identities
$1_A,1_B$, respectively. These idempotents are inseparable by
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} for the full inclusion
$\mathscr R_X\hookrightarrow\mathcal A$. They remain inseparable
in $\mathcal A$: fullness leaves the restriction idempotents on $V$, their order,
and their complements unchanged.
Write $A_j=A(j)$ and $B_j=B(j)$
for $j=0,1,2$. For $i\in\{1,2\}$, put $d_i=E_i(d)$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:endpoint},
\begin{align*}
 A_i&=\{x:d_i(x)\text{ is defined with even first coordinate}\},\\
 B_i&=\{x:d_i(x)\text{ is defined with odd first coordinate}\}.
\end{align*}
Let $\mathcal K_2$ be the full subcategory of $\mathcal K$ on the
objects obtained from $\N^2$ by the chosen binary restriction
products and coproducts. Every object of $\mathcal K_2$ is recursively
isomorphic to $\N^2$. The restriction products, coproducts, and
prodominical zero law restrict to this subcategory. By fullness,
$E_i\tau$ and the total parameter morphisms of
Proposition~\ref{prop:endpoint} belong to $\mathcal K_2$ whenever
their sources do. Thus $\mathcal K_2$ is a recursion category.

On $\mathcal K_2$, the underlying-set functor preserves
restrictions, zeros, and ranges, since it sends each morphism to its
underlying partial function. It also preserves the chosen products
and coproducts, so it is a range functor.
For complementary restriction idempotents $e,e':W\rightharpoonup W$
in $\mathcal K_2$, the construction in
Section~\ref{sec:numerical-incompleteness} gives a total recursive
morphism $\ell_e:W\to W+W$ with
$\ell_e e=i_1e$ and $\ell_e e'=i_0e'$.
It belongs to $\mathcal K_2$ by fullness. With the componentwise coproduct
identification, $E_i\zeta:\N^2\to\N^2+\N^2$ is a coproduct
isomorphism in $\mathcal K_2$.
Since the identity on $\N^2$ is nonzero and inverse images along
total morphisms in $\Pfn$ preserve unions,
Corollary~\ref{cor:source-conditionals} makes the partial identities
on $A_i,B_i$ inseparable in $\mathcal K_2$. A recursive separator
would define a complemented restriction idempotent on $\N^2$ in
this full subcategory. Hence $A_i,B_i$ are recursively inseparable.

The category $\mathcal E$ is regular with finite coproducts, and its
images are componentwise images (Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-total}).
Apply the propositional construction of
Appendix~\ref{app:propositional-theories} in this category, with atom
object $V$ and additional axioms determined by $A,B\subseteq V$.

For $j=0,1,2$, let $S_j$ be the set of finite rooted ordered formula trees
with constructors
\[
 \theta_j(x)\quad(x\in V_j),\qquad
 \nu_j(\varphi)\quad(\varphi\in S_j),\qquad
 \varphi\Rightarrow_j\psi\quad(\varphi,\psi\in S_j).
\]
The constructor images are pairwise disjoint. Recursive encodings with
recursive parsing make $S_j$ a recursive numerical carrier, since
$V_j$ is recursive. For $i=1,2$, replacing every atom label $x$ by
$r_i^V(x)$ and retaining the constructors gives a total recursive map
$\sigma_i:S_0\to S_i$. These maps define a functor
$S:J\to\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$. The constructors commute with
relabeling, so they define morphisms $\theta:V\to S$,
$\nu:S\to S$, and ${\Rightarrow}:S\times S\to S$ of $\mathcal E$.
Define $P:\mathcal E\to\mathcal E$ by
$P(Z)=V+Z+(Z\times Z)$ and
$P(f)=1_V+f+(f\times f)$. Its constructor algebra is
$\iota=[\theta,\nu,\Rightarrow]:P(S)\to S$.

\begin{proof}
At component $j$, evaluate a formula tree from its leaves to its root,
using the operations given by $\alpha_j:V_j+Z_j+Z_j^2\to Z_j$.
Induction proves termination, membership of the result in $Z_j$, and
the algebra equation. Evaluation is partial recursive and total on
$S_j$, so it defines a morphism $u_j:S_j\to Z_j$ of
$\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

Write $z_i=Z(0\to i):Z_0\to Z_i$. Naturality of $\alpha$
says that $z_i$ commutes with each constructor operation, with
$r_i^V$ applied to atom labels. Induction therefore gives
$z_i u_0=u_i\sigma_i$. Thus the $u_j$ form a morphism of
$\mathcal E$. Any algebra morphism agrees with these evaluations
on atoms and then on negations and implications by induction,
proving uniqueness.
\end{proof}

The logical axiom schemes define morphisms
$\Lambda_1,\Lambda_3:S^2\to S$ and $\Lambda_2:S^3\to S$.
For $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in S_j$, their components are
\begin{align*}
 \Lambda_{1,j}(\alpha,\beta)
   &=\alpha\Rightarrow_j(\beta\Rightarrow_j\alpha),\\
 \Lambda_{2,j}(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)
   &=(\alpha\Rightarrow_j(\beta\Rightarrow_j\gamma))
     \Rightarrow_j((\alpha\Rightarrow_j\beta)
                         \Rightarrow_j(\alpha\Rightarrow_j\gamma)),\\
 \Lambda_{3,j}(\alpha,\beta)
   &=(\nu_j\beta\Rightarrow_j\nu_j\alpha)
                         \Rightarrow_j(\alpha\Rightarrow_j\beta).
\end{align*}
The morphism
$[\theta|_A,\nu\theta|_B]:A+B\to S$ inserting the positive and negative
atomic axioms is monic: each component is
injective, because the constructors are
injective and the atom and negation constructors have disjoint images.
Its image is the subobject of signed axioms. Put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathrm{Ax}=S^2+S^3+S^2+A+B,\\
 \lambda=[\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2,\Lambda_3,\theta|_A,\nu\theta|_B]:
                 \mathrm{Ax}\longrightarrow S.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Each element of $\mathrm{Ax}_j$ specifies an axiom instance.
The morphism $\lambda_j$ gives its conclusion.

Write $\pi_1,\pi_2:S^2\to S$ for the projections and put
$\mu=\langle\pi_1,\Rightarrow\rangle:S^2\to S^2$.
For $h:Y\to S$ in $\mathcal E/S$, let $M(Y,h)$ be the pullback
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 M(Y,h)\arrow[r,"v_h"]\arrow[d,"w_h"'] &
 Y\times Y\arrow[d,"h\times h"]\\
 S\times S\arrow[r,"\mu"'] & S\times S.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
An element $(p_1,p_2,\alpha,\beta)$ of $M(Y,h)_j$ satisfies
$h_j(p_1)=\alpha$ and $h_j(p_2)=\alpha\Rightarrow_j\beta$.
The conclusion morphism is
$\kappa_h=\pi_2w_h:M(Y,h)\to S$. Define
\[
 \mathsf H:\mathcal E/S\longrightarrow\mathcal E/S,
 \qquad
 \mathsf H(Y,h)=
       (\mathrm{Ax}+M(Y,h),[\lambda,\kappa_h]).
\]
For a slice morphism $g:(Y,h)\to(Y',h')$, the pullback gives
$M(g):M(Y,h)\to M(Y',h')$ with
$v_{h'}M(g)=(g\times g)v_h$ and $w_{h'}M(g)=w_h$.
Put $\mathsf H(g)=1_{\mathrm{Ax}}+M(g)$; pullback uniqueness
proves the functor laws. The rule data of
Appendix~\ref{app:closed-subobjects} are
$R_0=\mathrm{Ax}$, $q_0=\lambda$, $R_1=0$, and
$R_2=S^2$, $p_2=\mu$, $q_2=\pi_2$; the morphism $p_0:R_0\to1$
is unique. Since $\mathcal E$ is extensive, the unary pullback
summand is initial, giving the displayed form of $\mathsf H$.

At component $j$, a derivation is a finite rooted ordered tree.
Each leaf is labeled by a member of $\mathrm{Ax}_j$ and concludes
its image under $\lambda_j$. Each nonleaf represents a modus-ponens
inference and has two children concluding $\alpha$ and
$\alpha\Rightarrow_j\beta$; it concludes $\beta$. Let
$\mathrm{Prf}_j$ be the carrier of these trees. Tree shape, logical
parameters, and premise matching are recursively decidable; the
finitely many positive and negative axiom labels require semidecision
of membership in $A_j$ and $B_j$. Dovetailing these tests shows that
$\mathrm{Prf}_j$ is c.e. Reading the conclusion gives a morphism
$c_{\mathrm p,j}:\mathrm{Prf}_j\to S_j$ of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

For $i=1,2$, relabel formula parameters by $\sigma_i$ and atomic
axiom labels by $r_i^V$, retaining the rule at each node. Since $A,B$ are
subfunctors, $r_i^V(A_0)\subseteq A_i$ and
$r_i^V(B_0)\subseteq B_i$. Relabeling therefore preserves axiom
leaves. Commutation of $\sigma_i$ with implication preserves premise
matching at modus-ponens nodes. The resulting morphisms
$\rho_i:\mathrm{Prf}_0\to\mathrm{Prf}_i$ satisfy
$c_{\mathrm p,i}\rho_i=\sigma_i c_{\mathrm p,0}$, by induction. They define an object
$\mathrm{Prf}$ of $\mathcal E$, and the $c_{\mathrm p,j}$ define
$c_{\mathrm p}:\mathrm{Prf}\to S$ in $\mathcal E$.

Forming a leaf and adjoining a modus-ponens root give morphisms
$\mathsf{leaf}:\mathrm{Ax}\to\mathrm{Prf}$ and
$\mathsf{mp}:M(\mathrm{Prf},c_{\mathrm p})\to\mathrm{Prf}$ in $\mathcal E$.
They are recursive on their carriers and commute with relabeling.
The injective implication constructor makes the consequent at a
modus-ponens node unique. The equations
$c_{\mathrm p}\,\mathsf{leaf}=\lambda$ and $c_{\mathrm p}\,\mathsf{mp}=\kappa_{c_{\mathrm p}}$ make
$\delta=[\mathsf{leaf},\mathsf{mp}]:\mathsf H(\mathrm{Prf},c_{\mathrm p})\to(\mathrm{Prf},c_{\mathrm p})$
an algebra in $\mathcal E/S$.

\begin{proof}
Evaluate a derivation from its leaves to its root using $\eta_j$.
At a leaf labeled by $\xi\in\mathrm{Ax}_j$, the value has
$h_j$-image $\lambda_j(\xi)$ because $\eta$ is a slice morphism.
If the children of a modus-ponens node conclude $\alpha$ and
$\alpha\Rightarrow_j\beta$, their evaluated values, together
with $\alpha,\beta$, belong to $M(Y,h)_j$. The corresponding
operation of $\eta_j$ returns a value with $h_j$-image $\beta$.
Induction proves termination and gives a partial recursive function
$u_j:\mathrm{Prf}_j\to Y_j$ total on its source carrier, with
$h_ju_j=c_{\mathrm p,j}$.

Naturality of $\eta$, $\lambda$, and the pullback projections
makes each evaluation step commute with relabeling. Induction gives
$Y(0\to i)u_0=u_i\rho_i$, so the $u_j$ form a morphism
$u:\mathrm{Prf}\to Y$ of $\mathcal E$. Its defining recursion
is the algebra equation. Any other algebra morphism agrees on
leaves and then on each modus-ponens node by induction, proving
uniqueness.
\end{proof}

For a restriction idempotent $t$ on $S$, let $D_t\subseteq S$
be the c.e. subfunctor on which $t$ is the partial identity. View
$c_{\mathrm p}$ as a total morphism of $\mathcal A$ and put $t_0=\ran(c_{\mathrm p})$.

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:least-theorem-subobject} to the regular
category $\mathcal E$ and the initial algebra of
Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-proof-initial}. It identifies the image
of $c_{\mathrm p}$ with the least subobject closed under these rules. Images
in $\mathcal E$ are componentwise, so its components are
$(D_{t_0})_j=c_{\mathrm p,j}(\mathrm{Prf}_j)\subseteq S_j$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image}, applied in
$\mathcal A=\Par(\mathcal E,\Mono)$, identifies its partial identity
with $t_0=\ran(c_{\mathrm p})$, and hence the image subfunctor with $D_{t_0}$.
The one-node positive and negative proofs give morphisms
$A\to\mathrm{Prf}$ and $B\to\mathrm{Prf}$ whose composites
with $c_{\mathrm p}$ are $\theta|_A$ and $\nu\theta|_B$. These factorizations
give the first two inequalities in \eqref{eq:atomic-inequalities}.

For consistency, fix $j$ and suppose derivations $p,p'$ conclude
$\varphi$ and $\nu_j\varphi$. Let $L\subseteq A_j$ be the finite
set of labels at positive leaves of either derivation. Assign truth
value $1$ precisely to atoms with labels in $L$, and value $0$ to
all other atoms. Extend this assignment by Boolean negation and
implication. Every positive leaf is true. Every negative leaf has
its label in $B_j$, disjoint from $A_j$ and hence from $L$, so it
is true. The three logical schemes are Boolean tautologies, and
modus ponens preserves truth. Induction on both derivations would
make $\varphi$ and its negation true, a contradiction. Thus
$(D_{t_0})_j\cap\nu_j^{-1}((D_{t_0})_j)=\varnothing$ at every component, which
is $t_0\nu^*t_0=0_S$ because restriction operations in
$\mathcal A$ are componentwise.
\end{proof}

Write $\sigma_i=S(0\to i):S_0\to S_i$ for $i=1,2$.
A compatible family of c.e.\ theory extensions consists of c.e.\ sets
$T_j\subseteq S_j$, for $j=0,1,2$, containing $(D_{t_0})_j$ and closed
under modus ponens, with $\sigma_i(T_0)\subseteq T_i$ for $i=1,2$.
These sets form a subfunctor $T\subseteq S$.
The family is consistent if each theory is consistent, that is,
$T_j\cap\nu_j^{-1}(T_j)=\varnothing$ for every $j$.
Each compatible family of consistent c.e.\ deductively closed extensions
determines a restriction idempotent $t_T:S\rightharpoonup S$, the partial
identity on its theorem subfunctor $T\subseteq S$.
It satisfies $t_0\le t_T$ and $t_T\nu^*t_T=0_S$.
All three theories are complete precisely when
$t_T\vee\nu^*t_T=1_S$, since the $j$th component of $\nu^*t_T$
is the partial identity on $\nu_j^{-1}(T_j)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:cosheaf-observation}
Fix $i\in\{1,2\}$. Let $T\subseteq S$ be a compatible family of
consistent c.e.\ theory extensions as above, and let
$t_T:S\rightharpoonup S$ be its partial identity. The total morphism $E_i\theta$ induces the function
$\theta_i:|V_i|=\N^2\to |S_i|$ on carriers. Define
\[
 P_{i,T}=\{x\in\N^2:\theta_i(x)\in T_i\},\qquad
 N_{i,T}=\{x\in\N^2:\nu_i(\theta_i(x))\in T_i\}.
\]
The restriction idempotents $t_T,\nu^*t_T$ are inseparable in $\mathcal A$.
The sets $P_{i,T},N_{i,T}$ are disjoint c.e.\ subsets of $\N^2$ satisfying
$A_i\subseteq P_{i,T}$ and $B_i\subseteq N_{i,T}$.
They are recursively inseparable. The assignment
$T\mapsto(\omega\times\omega,P_{i,T},N_{i,T})$,
with the identity of $\omega\times\omega$ for extension inclusions, is a
covariant functor from the poset of these families, ordered by componentwise
inclusion, to $\operatorname{Pair}(\mathrm{Rec})$.
The theory with theorem set $T_i$ is incomplete.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The category $\mathcal A$ has restriction zeros and joins of restriction idempotents
preserved by inverse images along total morphisms. Its restriction idempotents $1_A,1_B$ are inseparable,
and \eqref{eq:atomic-inequalities} gives the hypotheses of
Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness}. Hence $t_T,\nu^*t_T$ are
inseparable.

The atom morphism $E_i\theta:\N^2\to S_i$ is total recursive.
The component theorem and refutation sets $|t_T|_i$ and $|\nu^*t_T|_i$
are c.e.; their inverse images under the total recursive map
$E_i\theta$ are therefore c.e. Consistency and preservation of meets and
zero make them disjoint. Applying $E_i$ to
\eqref{eq:atomic-inequalities} and using $t_0\le t_T$ gives
the two inclusions. A recursive separator would consequently
separate $A_i,B_i$, which is impossible.
If $P_{i,T}\cup N_{i,T}=\N^2$, simultaneous enumeration of these
disjoint c.e.\ sets would decide membership in $P_{i,T}$ and hence
separate the pair. Take $x\in\N^2\setminus(P_{i,T}\cup N_{i,T})$.
By the definitions of the two inverse images,
\[
  \theta_i(x)\notin T_i,\qquad \nu_i\theta_i(x)\notin T_i .
\]
Thus an atomic sentence is undecided at endpoint $i$.

If $T\subseteq T'$, monotonicity gives inclusions of both component
sets, so the identity of $\omega\times\omega$ is the required pair morphism.
The functor laws follow from the identity maps.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $U\subseteq S_i$ be the deductive closure of such an axiom set.
The finite proof calculus makes $U$ computably enumerable, and
$U$ contains $(D_{t_0})_i$.
Set $T_i=U$ and $T_j=(D_{t_0})_j$ for $j\ne i$.
This family is consistent. Since $D_{t_0}$ is a subfunctor and
$T_i$ contains its $i$th component, the family is compatible.
Theorem~\ref{thm:cosheaf-observation} therefore makes $U$ incomplete.
\end{proof}

\subsection{First-order theories in the functor category}
\label{subsec:fork-first-order}

Let $N_\Delta=\Delta\N$ be the constant functor on $J$ with value
$\N$ and identity transition morphisms. We use $N_\Delta$ as the
object of variables. For an object $D$ of $\mathcal E$, consider
the first-order language with nullary predicate symbols labelled by
$D$, equality, and no other nonlogical symbols. Its terms are variables.

\begin{proof}
The formula constructor endofunctor is
\[
 K_D(Y)=N_\Delta^2+D+Y+Y^2+N_\Delta\times Y.
\]
For $f:Y\to Y'$, set
$K_D(f)=1_{N_\Delta^2}+1_D+f+(f\times f)+(1_{N_\Delta}\times f)$.
Its five summands represent equality, atoms, negation, implication,
and universal quantification. At each component, finite numerical
tree codes form a c.e.\ carrier. Membership in the label carrier
$D_j$ is semidecidable.
For $i=1,2$, relabel each atomic label by $D(0\to i)$ and retain
the variable names and constructors. This defines the transition
morphisms of a formula object $F_D$.

Given an algebra $\alpha:K_D(Y)\to Y$, evaluate its finite trees
from the leaves to the root using the components of $\alpha$.
This is partial recursive and total on each formula carrier.
Naturality of $\alpha$ makes evaluation commute with transitions,
and induction on the trees gives the algebra equation and
uniqueness. If an algebra has a parameter in an object $Z$ of
$\mathcal E$, retain that parameter at every evaluation step.
The same induction proves the parameterized initiality equation
and uniqueness in $\mathcal E/Z$.

Finite lists of variables and their operations are formed
componentwise, with identity transitions on variable names.
Equality of variables is decidable because the variable object
is $N_\Delta$. The occurrence-list and substitution constructions
of Proposition~\ref{prop:categorical-substitution} therefore apply.
Their recursive clauses commute with transitions, since the
atomic predicates are nullary and their relabelling does not
change variable names. In particular, empty occurrence lists
define the sentence subobject of $F_D$.

Write $S_D\hookrightarrow F_D$ for the sentence inclusion and let
$A\hookrightarrow S_D$ be an axiom subobject. Use the seven schemes
and two rules of Appendix~\ref{app:first-order-derivations}. At component
$j$, parse a proposed derivation and its rule parameters. Check the
tree form, premise codes, and substitution and free-variable conditions.
For every predicate label $d$ occurring in a formula parameter, run the
test for $d\in D_j$, including at logical axiom leaves. For each
nonlogical axiom leaf also test its sentence for membership in $A_j$.
These finitely many semidecisions succeed together exactly on the
derivation carrier, so that carrier is computably enumerable. Relabelling preserves
each logical scheme and rule and carries nonlogical axiom leaves to nonlogical
axiom leaves because the axioms form a subfunctor.

Evaluation of derivation trees in an algebra for the inference
endofunctor is total on their carriers. Its algebra equation is
proved by induction on the last rule. Naturality of the algebra
operations makes the evaluations a natural transformation.
Induction also gives uniqueness. For $Z\in\mathcal E$ and an axiom
subobject $A\hookrightarrow Z\times S_D$, the conclusion of a tree
at component $j$ is $(z,\varphi)\in Z_j\times (F_D)_j$. Its nodes
retain $z$, and its nonlogical leaves test $(z,\psi)\in A_j$.
Thus the conclusion morphism $c_{Z,A}:P_{Z,A}\to Z\times F_D$
and the inference algebra lie over $Z\times F_D$. For any other
algebra with carrier $h:Y\to Z\times F_D$, evaluation is the unique
algebra morphism $u:P_{Z,A}\to Y$ with $hu=c_{Z,A}$. This gives the initial algebra for the inference endofunctor on
$\mathcal E/(Z\times F_D)$, equivalently on the slice of $\mathcal E/Z$
over $\pi_1:Z\times F_D\to Z$.
\end{proof}

Take $D=V$. Write $F_{\mathrm f}$ for the formula object,
$s_{\mathrm f}:S_{\mathrm f}\hookrightarrow F_{\mathrm f}$ for
its sentence inclusion, and $\theta_{\mathrm f}:V\to S_{\mathrm f}$
for its atomic constructor. The propositional formula
object is $S$. Preserving atoms, negation, and implication defines
a monomorphism $j:S\hookrightarrow S_{\mathrm f}$.
Let $T_{\mathrm p}=D_{t_0}\hookrightarrow S$ be the
propositional theory of Theorem~\ref{thm:fork-proof-presentation}.
Let $T_{\mathrm f}^F\hookrightarrow F_{\mathrm f}$ be the
formula theory generated by the positive atoms from $A$ and the
negative atoms from $B$, and put
$T_{\mathrm f}=s_{\mathrm f}^*T_{\mathrm f}^F$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:fork-first-order-conservative}
The theory $T_{\mathrm f}$ is consistent and essentially
incomplete in $\mathcal A$. Its restriction to the propositional
language is $T_{\mathrm p}$, that is,
\[
 j^*T_{\mathrm f}=T_{\mathrm p}.
\]
At either endpoint $i=1,2$, every consistent extension of
$(T_{\mathrm f})_i$ in its first-order language with a c.e.\ axiom set
is incomplete.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The components
$(0,0,0,0)$, $(0,0)$, and $(0,0)$ give a global element of $V$.
Let $p_*$ be its propositional atom and put
$\top=(p_*\Rightarrow p_*)$. Define a morphism
$r:F_{\mathrm f}\to S$ by the following clauses, writing $P_v$
for the first-order atom with label $v$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 r(P_v)&=\theta(v),& r(x=y)&=\top,\\
 r(\neg\varphi)&=\nu r(\varphi),&
 r(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)&=r(\varphi)\Rightarrow r(\psi),\\
 r(\forall x\,\varphi)&=r(\varphi).
\end{aligned}
\]
The clauses commute with transitions and satisfy
$r s_{\mathrm f}j=1_S$. Induction on formulas gives
\[
 r(\varphi[x:=y])=r(\varphi)
\]
whenever the substitution is admissible.

The subobject $r^*T_{\mathrm p}$ contains the generating positive
and negative atoms. It is closed under modus ponens, and erasing
quantification makes it closed under generalization. The first
three logical schemes are sent to the corresponding
propositional schemes. The remaining four schemes are sent to
\[
 H\Rightarrow H,\qquad
 (H\Rightarrow K)\Rightarrow(H\Rightarrow K),\qquad
 \top,\qquad
 \top\Rightarrow(H\Rightarrow H).
\]
Each has a finite propositional derivation, uniformly in $H,K$.
For example, the first two propositional schemes give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &H\Rightarrow((H\Rightarrow H)\Rightarrow H),\\
 &H\Rightarrow(H\Rightarrow H),\\
 &\bigl(H\Rightarrow((H\Rightarrow H)\Rightarrow H)\bigr)
   \Rightarrow
   \bigl((H\Rightarrow(H\Rightarrow H))
                   \Rightarrow(H\Rightarrow H)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Two applications of modus ponens yield $H\Rightarrow H$.
Substituting $H\Rightarrow K$ and $p_*$ for $H$ gives the second
formula and $\top$, respectively. The first
propositional scheme and modus ponens applied to $H\Rightarrow H$ give
$\top\Rightarrow(H\Rightarrow H)$.
Leastness of the generated formula theory proves
\[
 T_{\mathrm f}^F\le r^*T_{\mathrm p}.
\]
The inclusion $j$ preserves the signed axioms, the three propositional
schemes, and modus ponens, so $T_{\mathrm p}\le j^*T_{\mathrm f}$.
Put $k=r s_{\mathrm f}:S_{\mathrm f}\to S$. Restricting the formula
inclusion to sentences gives $T_{\mathrm f}\le k^*T_{\mathrm p}$.
Since $kj=1_S$, this gives $j^*T_{\mathrm f}\le T_{\mathrm p}$.
Writing $\nu_{\mathrm f}$ for sentence negation, we have
$k\nu_{\mathrm f}=\nu k$, and hence
\[
 T_{\mathrm f}\wedge\nu_{\mathrm f}^*T_{\mathrm f}
 \le k^*(T_{\mathrm p}\wedge\nu^*T_{\mathrm p})=\bot .
\]

Let $U\hookrightarrow S_{\mathrm f}$ be a consistent closed extension of
$T_{\mathrm f}$. The positive and negative axioms give
\[
 A\leq \theta_{\mathrm f}^{*}U,\qquad
 B\leq \theta_{\mathrm f}^{*}\nu_{\mathrm f}^{*}U .
\]
If $U$ were complete, $U$ and $\nu_{\mathrm f}^{*}U$ would be
complementary. Their inverse images under $\theta_{\mathrm f}$
would separate $A$ and $B$, contrary to their inseparability.
This is Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness} in $\mathcal A$.

For the endpoint assertion, let $U_i$ be the deductive closure
of a consistent c.e.\ set of first-order axioms, and suppose
$(T_{\mathrm f})_i\subseteq U_i$. The inverse image $j_i^*U_i$ is a
consistent c.e.\ propositional theory extending
$(T_{\mathrm p})_i$. Completeness of $U_i$ would imply
completeness of $j_i^*U_i$, since $j_i$ preserves negation.
This contradicts Corollary~\ref{cor:cosheaf-essential-incompleteness}.
\end{proof}
\subsection{Categories associated with theory extensions}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:fork-associated-theories}
Let $t:T_{\mathrm f}\hookrightarrow S_{\mathrm f}$ be the
first-order theory above, and let
$u:U\hookrightarrow S_{\mathrm f}$ be any consistent internal
sentence theory with $t=ui$ for a monomorphism
$i:T_{\mathrm f}\hookrightarrow U$. Then
\[
 \mathcal A[T_{\mathrm f}]=\Par(\mathcal E/T_{\mathrm f},\Mono),
 \qquad
 \mathcal A[U]=\Par(\mathcal E/U,\Mono)
\]
are Turing categories, and postcomposition gives the fully
faithful functor
\[
 \Sigma_i:\mathcal A[T_{\mathrm f}]\longrightarrow\mathcal A[U]
\]
of Theorem~\ref{thm:theory-extension}. It is not essentially
surjective when $i$ is not an isomorphism. The theory
\[
 1_U\times u:U\times U\hookrightarrow U\times S_{\mathrm f}
\]
is essentially incomplete in $\mathcal A[U]$. Its theorem and
refutation domains are inseparable there.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Propositions~\ref{prop:fork-total} and
\ref{prop:fork-structure} identify $\mathcal E$ as regular and
extensive and $\mathcal A$ as its split partial-map category.
Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-recursion} identifies
$\mathcal A\simeq\Split(\mathscr R_X)$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-first-order-realization} supplies the
parameter-stable syntax and deduction required by the general
theorem. The global sentence $j(\top)$ is a logical theorem, so
there is a total morphism $\lambda_U:1\to U$ with $u\lambda_U=j(\top)$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-first-order-conservative} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:domain-incompleteness} show that every such
$u$ is essentially incomplete and that its theorem and
refutation domains are inseparable in $\mathcal A$. If the constant
domains had a separator in the slice, its inverse image along
$\langle \lambda_U !_{S_{\mathrm f}},1_{S_{\mathrm f}}\rangle:
 S_{\mathrm f}\to U\times S_{\mathrm f}$ would separate $u$ and
$\nu_{\mathrm f}^*u$ in $\mathcal A$.
Theorems~\ref{thm:theory-extension} and
\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness} give the assertions about the
comparison functor and essential incompleteness.
\end{proof}

We construct the sentence object from initial algebras of syntax and
variable lists that are stable under parameters. Given an axiom
subobject, we construct the generated sentence theory as the image
of the conclusion morphism for derivations ending in sentences.

\subsection{Categorical hypotheses and notation}
\label{app:categorical-hypotheses}

For list objects, we use the parameterized recursion property studied by
Cockett~\cite[Lemma 2.2 and Definition 2.3]{CockettLists}.
Its formulation by pullback into slices is
recalled by Maietti~\cite[Definition 2.4 and the following paragraph]{MaiettiLists}.

Let $\mathcal D$ be a regular category with finite coproducts.
Thus $\mathcal D$ has finite limits, every morphism factors as a
regular epimorphism followed by a monomorphism, and regular
epimorphisms are stable under pullback. A regular epimorphism is a
coequalizer; the monic part of the factorization is the image.
For the construction of first-order syntax, assume also that finite
coproducts are disjoint and stable under pullback. In particular,
a morphism into $X+Y$ decomposes its source as the coproduct of its
two inverse images.

Composition is $gf=g\circ f$. Finite products and coproducts are
chosen and parenthesized to the left. Rebracketing uses the canonical
associativity isomorphisms determined by their projections or injections;
terminal factors are removed by the canonical product unit isomorphisms.
For $X\in\mathcal D$, write $X^0=1$, $X^1=X$, and
$X^{n+1}=X^n\times X$ for $n\geq1$.
For $f:X\to Y$, the morphism $f^n:X^n\to Y^n$ is the corresponding
product morphism, with $f^0=1_1$ and $f^1=f$.

Put $\Two=1+1$, with injections
$\mathbf{f},\mathbf{t}:1\to\Two$. Pulling this coproduct back along
$\pi_1:\Two\times\Two\to\Two$ decomposes $\Two\times\Two$ into two copies of
$\Two$. Decomposing each copy as $1+1$ gives the isomorphism
\[
 \gamma=[\langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{f}\rangle,
          \langle\mathbf{f},\mathbf{t}\rangle,
          \langle\mathbf{t},\mathbf{f}\rangle,
          \langle\mathbf{t},\mathbf{t}\rangle]:
          1+1+1+1\xrightarrow{\cong}\Two\times\Two.
\]
Define $\neg_2=[\mathbf{t},\mathbf{f}]:\Two\to\Two$ and
$\wedge_2,\vee_2:\Two\times\Two\to\Two$ by
\[
 \wedge_2=[\mathbf{f},\mathbf{f},\mathbf{f},\mathbf{t}]\gamma^{-1},
 \qquad
 \vee_2=[\mathbf{f},\mathbf{t},\mathbf{t},\mathbf{t}]\gamma^{-1}.
\]
These morphisms make $\Two$ a Boolean algebra object in $\mathcal D$.
Distributivity expresses each finite power $\Two^n$ as a
coproduct of $2^n$ copies of $1$, indexed by the ordered choices of
$\mathbf{f}$ or $\mathbf{t}$ in each coordinate. These
coproduct injections are jointly epimorphic. On each summand the
copairings give the ordinary Boolean operations on the two truth values.
Hence every Boolean algebra identity holds as an equality of morphisms.

For $p:X\to\Two$, let $[p=\mathbf{t}]\hookrightarrow X$ and
$[p=\mathbf{f}]\hookrightarrow X$ be the pullbacks along $p$ of
$\mathbf{t}:1\to\Two$ and $\mathbf{f}:1\to\Two$, respectively.
Denote these inclusions by $i_{\mathbf{t}}$ and $i_{\mathbf{f}}$.
The coproduct hypotheses give the isomorphism
$\delta_p=[i_{\mathbf{t}},i_{\mathbf{f}}]:
[p=\mathbf{t}]+[p=\mathbf{f}]\xrightarrow{\cong}X$.
For branches $f,g:X\to Y$, define the conditional by
\[
 \mathsf{if}(p;f,g)=
 [f i_{\mathbf{t}},g i_{\mathbf{f}}]\delta_p^{-1}:X\to Y.
\]
It is the unique morphism $h:X\to Y$ satisfying
$h i_{\mathbf{t}}=f i_{\mathbf{t}}$ and
$h i_{\mathbf{f}}=g i_{\mathbf{f}}$.

We use variables to abbreviate projections from a product.
An expression built from them denotes a composite of morphisms on
that product. An equation between such expressions is an equality
of morphisms with that common source. A morphism $c:1\to Y$ used
on a source $X$ denotes $c!_X:X\to Y$.

Fix an object $V\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal D)$ and a morphism
$\epsilon:V\times V\to\Two$ in $\mathcal D$ such that the square
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 V\arrow[r,"{!_V}"]\arrow[d,hook,"\Delta_V"'] &
 1\arrow[d,hook,"\mathbf{t}"]\\
 V\times V\arrow[r,"\epsilon"'] & \Two
\end{tikzcd}
\]
is a pullback. Thus $V$ is equipped with decidable equality:
its diagonal is a complemented subobject of $V\times V$, with
complement given by the pullback of $\mathbf{f}:1\to\Two$
along $\epsilon$.
For $0\leq k\leq d$, fix objects
$\Sigma_k,\Pi_k\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal D)$ to index the
$k$-ary function and relation constructors, respectively.
Here $d$ is a fixed nonnegative integer. Equality is a logical symbol.

Under the identification $\mathcal D\simeq\mathcal D/1$, pullback
along $!_P:P\to1$ sends $X$ to $\pi_1:P\times X\to P$ and $f$ to
$1_P\times f$. For an endofunctor $K$ on $\mathcal D^r$ built from
finite products, coproducts, and constants, form $K_P$ on
$(\mathcal D/P)^r$ using slice products and coproducts and replacing
each constant $X$ by $!_P^*X$. Pullback preserves finite products
and, by the coproduct hypotheses, finite coproducts. Applied
componentwise, it thus gives the natural isomorphism in the composite
\[
 \iota_P:K_P(!_P^*A)\xrightarrow{\sim} !_P^*(KA)
          \xrightarrow{!_P^*\iota} !_P^*A
\]
for each $K$-algebra $\iota:KA\to A$. An initial $K$-algebra is
\emph{stable under parameters} if $\iota_P$ is initial for every
$P\in\mathcal D$.

\subsection{Terms, formulas, and free variables}
\label{app:first-order-syntax}

Initial many-sorted algebras are used to specify abstract syntax by
Goguen, Thatcher, Wagner, and Wright~\cite[Section 2]{GTWW}.
Goguen and Burstall~\cite[Section 4]{GoguenBurstall} apply this method
to the term and sentence sorts of logical languages.
Here the signature objects, syntax objects, and constructor morphisms
lie in $\mathcal D$.

Initial-algebra accounts of binding and substitution are developed by
Fiore, Plotkin, and Turi~\cite[Sections 2--4]{FPT} and by
Gabbay and Pitts~\cite[Section 6]{GabbayPitts}.
Katsumata~\cite[Section 2, Example 1(3)]{Katsumata} gives a first-order
instance with a quantifier. These treatments identify expressions up to
renaming of bound variables. The syntax defined below retains variable
names, and formula substitution is defined on an admissibility subobject.

Define $K:\mathcal D^2\to\mathcal D^2$ by
$K(X,Y)=\bigl(K_1(X,Y),K_2(X,Y)\bigr)$, where
\begin{align}
 K_1(X,Y)&=V+\coprod_{k=0}^{d}\Sigma_k\times X^k,
                                                        \label{eq:term-functor}\\
 K_2(X,Y)&=X^2+\coprod_{k=0}^{d}\Pi_k\times X^k
                  +Y+Y^2+V\times Y.                    \label{eq:formula-functor}
\end{align}
On a morphism $(f,g):(X,Y)\to(X',Y')$, use
$1_V$, $1_{\Sigma_k}\times f^k$, $f^2$,
$1_{\Pi_k}\times f^k$, $g$, $g^2$, and $1_V\times g$ on
the respective summands. Product and coproduct laws give the
functor laws.

The syntax constructors are the following morphisms in $\mathcal D$:
\begin{gather*}
 \eta:V\to\Tm,\qquad f_k:\Sigma_k\times\Tm^k\to\Tm,\\
 {\mathsf{eq}}:\Tm^2\to\Fm,\qquad
 r_k:\Pi_k\times\Tm^k\to\Fm,\\
 \neg:\Fm\to\Fm,\qquad
 {\Rightarrow}:\Fm^2\to\Fm,\qquad
 {\forall}:V\times\Fm\to\Fm.
\end{gather*}
The morphism $\eta$ is the variable constructor.
The quantifier constructor $\forall$ is indexed
by $V$; its binding behaviour is specified by the free-variable and
substitution morphisms constructed below.
For every $K$-algebra $\alpha:K(X,Y)\to(X,Y)$ there is a unique
$(u,v):(\Tm,\Fm)\to(X,Y)$ making the square
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 K(\Tm,\Fm)\arrow[r,"\iota"]\arrow[d,"{K(u,v)}"'] &
 (\Tm,\Fm)\arrow[d,"{(u,v)}"]\\
 K(X,Y)\arrow[r,"\alpha"'] & (X,Y)
\end{tikzcd}
\]
commute. The same property holds in every slice with parameters.
For a subalgebra inclusion $m:B\hookrightarrow(\Tm,\Fm)$,
initiality gives an algebra morphism $h:(\Tm,\Fm)\to B$.
Then $mh=1$ by uniqueness, and $hm=1$ by monicity. The same
argument applied to $\iota_P$ gives induction in the slice over $P$.

List initiality with parameters gives concatenation
$+\!+:W^2\to W$, membership $\mem:V\times W\to\Two$, and
deletion $\del:V\times W\to W$ by
\begin{align*}
 \nil+\!+w&=w,&
 \cons(y,w)+\!+w'&=\cons(y,w+\!+w'),\\
 \mem(x,\nil)&=\mathbf{f},&
 \mem(x,\cons(y,w))&=\epsilon(x,y)\vee_2\mem(x,w),\\
 \del(x,\nil)&=\nil,&
 \del(x,\cons(y,w))&=
 \mathsf{if}\bigl(\epsilon(x,y);\del(x,w),
                         \cons(y,\del(x,w))\bigr).
\end{align*}
Write $[x]=\cons(x,\nil)$.
Parameterized list induction gives the identities
\begin{align*}
 \mem(x,w+\!+w')&=\mem(x,w)\vee_2\mem(x,w'),\\
 \mem(x,\del(y,w))&=\neg_2\epsilon(x,y)\wedge_2\mem(x,w).
\end{align*}
In the deletion step for $\cons(z,w)$, the diagonal pullback identifies
$y$ with $z$ on $[\epsilon(y,z)=\mathbf t]$. On the other fiber, a
head equal to $x$ is distinct from $y$.

Give $(W,W)$ the $K$-algebra defined by singleton lists at variables,
ordered concatenation at function and relation symbols and equality,
the identity at negation, concatenation at implication, and deletion
at quantification. The unique morphism from the initial $K$-algebra to this algebra
defines $\FV_{\Tm}:\Tm\to W$ and $\FV_{\Fm}:\Fm\to W$ by
\begin{align*}
 \FV_{\Tm}(\eta x)&=[x],&
 \FV_{\Tm}(f_k(s,\vec t))&=\FV_{\Tm}(t_1)+\!+\cdots+\!+\FV_{\Tm}(t_k),\\
 \FV_{\Fm}(\mathsf{eq}(u,t))&=\FV_{\Tm}(u)+\!+\FV_{\Tm}(t),&
 \FV_{\Fm}(r_k(s,\vec t))&=\FV_{\Tm}(t_1)+\!+\cdots+\!+\FV_{\Tm}(t_k),\\
 \FV_{\Fm}(\neg\varphi)&=\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi),&
 \FV_{\Fm}(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)&=\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi)+\!+\FV_{\Fm}(\psi),\\
 \FV_{\Fm}(\forall x\,\varphi)&=\del(x,\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi)).&&
\end{align*}
An empty concatenation is $\nil$. These are lists of free-variable
occurrences; repetitions are retained.

Negation restricts to $
u:S	o S$ by the equation for
$\FV_{\Fm}(
eg\varphi)$. Existential quantification is the derived morphism
$\exists=
eg\circ orall\circ(1_V	imes
eg):V	imes\Fm	o\Fm$.

\subsection{Admissible substitution}
\label{app:substitution}

To construct substitution of one term for one variable, we retain
the original expression together with the recursive result; compare
Gabbay and Pitts~\cite[proof of Corollary 6.7]{GabbayPitts}. Put $E=V\times\Tm$, with projections
$x:E\to V$ and $t:E\to\Tm$. For an object $Y$, write
$O(Y)=1+Y$, with injections $\fail_Y:1\to O(Y)$ and
$\ok_Y:Y\to O(Y)$. A morphism $g:Y\to Z$ induces
$O(g)=1_1+g$. For a binary morphism $h:Y^2\to Y$, let
$\widehat h:O(Y)^2\to O(Y)$ restrict to $\ok_Yh$ on the
$Y\times Y$ summand and to $\fail_Y$ on the other three summands.
Define $\widehat\forall:V\times O(\Fm)\to O(\Fm)$ by
$\fail_{\Fm}\,!_{V\times1}$ on $V\times1$ and $\ok_{\Fm}\forall$ on
$V\times\Fm$.
Distributivity of products over coproducts defines these morphisms.

In $(\mathcal D/E)^2$, use the carriers
\[
 X_T=E\times(\Tm\times\Tm)\longrightarrow E,
 \qquad
 X_F=E\times(\Fm\times O(\Fm))\longrightarrow E.
\]
The first projection of each pair is the original expression.
Define a $K_E$-algebra as follows, retaining the same parameter
$(x,t)$ in every operation. At a variable $v$, the pair is
$(\eta v,\mathsf{if}(\epsilon(v,x);t,\eta v))$.
At a function symbol, apply its constructor separately to the
original term components and the substituted term components.
At equality and relation symbols, reconstruct the original formula
and apply $\ok_{\Fm}$ to the formula formed from the substituted
term components. At negation and implication, reconstruct the
original formula and apply $O(\neg)$ or
$\widehat{\Rightarrow}$ to the result components.

Put $X_{\forall}=V\times\Fm\times E$, with coordinates $(y,\varphi,x,t)$,
and define the quantifier test $\chi_{\forall}:X_{\forall}\to\Two$ by
\[
 \chi_{\forall}(y,\varphi,x,t)=
 \neg_2\mem(x,\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi))
 \vee_2\neg_2\mem(y,\FV_{\Tm}(t)).
\]
At the quantifier the input is $(x,t,y,\varphi,z)$ in
$E\times V\times\Fm\times O(\Fm)$. The test uses the projection
$(x,t,y,\varphi,z)\mapsto(y,\varphi,x,t)$ to $X_{\forall}$. The original
component is $\forall y\,\varphi$ and the result component is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantifier-fold}
 \mathsf{if}\left(\epsilon(y,x);
   \ok_{\Fm}(\forall y\,\varphi),
   \mathsf{if}\bigl(\chi_{\forall}(y,\varphi,x,t);
          \widehat\forall(y,z),\fail_{\Fm}\bigr)\right).
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:categorical-substitution}
Parameterized initiality uniquely determines morphisms
$a_T:\Tm\times E\to\Tm$ and
$b_F:\Fm\times E\to O(\Fm)$.
Admissibility and formula substitution are defined by the pullback
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 \Adm\arrow[r,"a_F"]\arrow[d,hook,"i_{\Adm}"'] &
 \Fm\arrow[d,hook,"\ok_{\Fm}"]\\
 \Fm\times E\arrow[r,"b_F"'] & O(\Fm).
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The monomorphism $i_{\Adm}$ is complemented.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The unique $K_E$-algebra morphism into $(X_T,X_F)$ has the original
expression and its substitution value as its two components. Composing this algebra morphism with the
projections to the original components gives an endomorphism of the
initial $K_E$-algebra, hence the identity. The result components,
after interchanging the parameter
and syntax factors, are $a_T$ and $b_F$. The pullback defines
$i_{\Adm}$ and $a_F$; the coproduct hypotheses make $i_{\Adm}$ complemented.
\end{proof}

Both $\forall\times1_E$ and the projection
$\pi=\langle\pi_{\Fm},\pi_E\rangle$ map $X_{\forall}$ to $\Fm\times E$.
Let $D_=$ and $D_{\ne}$ be the true and false fibers of $\epsilon(y,x)$
in $X_{\forall}$. Equation~\eqref{eq:quantifier-fold} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:admissibility-subobjects}
 (\forall\times1_E)^*\Adm=D_=\;\vee\;
    (D_{\ne}\wedge [\chi_{\forall}=\mathbf{t}]\wedge \pi^*\Adm).
\end{equation}
Here meet is pullback intersection, and the disjoint join is the
coproduct inclusion into $X_{\forall}$. On $D_=$ the substitution
result is $\forall y\,\varphi$. If $i:Z\hookrightarrow X_{\forall}$
represents the second summand, its inclusion in $\pi^*\Adm$ induces
$\widetilde\pi:Z\to\Adm$ with $i_{\Adm}\widetilde\pi=\pi i$.
The result on $Z$ is $\forall\langle y\circ i,a_F\widetilde\pi\rangle$.
Thus quantification binds its named variable and prevents capture
of free occurrences of the replacement term.

Write $\varphi[x:=t]$ on $\Adm$, and $u[x:=t]$ for
$a_T(u,x,t)$. Define
\[
 e_T=\langle\pi_{\Tm},\pi_V,\eta\pi_V\rangle:
          \Tm\times V\to\Tm\times E,
 \qquad
 e_F=\langle\pi_{\Fm},\pi_V,\eta\pi_V\rangle:
          \Fm\times V\to\Fm\times E.
\]
Identity substitution satisfies $a_Te_T=\pi_{\Tm}$ and
$b_Fe_F=\ok_{\Fm}\pi_{\Fm}$; the second equality also states
admissibility. For substitution at
an absent variable, use the subobjects
\begin{align*}
 N_T&=[\mem(x,\FV_{\Tm}(u))=\mathbf{f}]
                            \hookrightarrow\Tm\times E,\\
 N_F&=[\mem(x,\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi))=\mathbf{f}]
                            \hookrightarrow\Fm\times E.
\end{align*}
On $N_T$, $a_T$ is the term projection. On $N_F$, $b_F$ is
$\ok_{\Fm}$ composed with the formula projection, so substitution
is admissible and fixes the formula.

These term and formula statements follow simultaneously by
parameterized induction. Atomic steps use the term equations;
the negation step uses $O(\neg)$ and the implication step uses
$\widehat{\Rightarrow}$. At a quantifier with equal variable names,
\eqref{eq:quantifier-fold} gives $\ok_{\Fm}(\forall y\,\varphi)$.
For identity substitution with distinct names,
$\FV_{\Tm}(\eta x)=[x]$ and $\mem(y,[x])=\epsilon(y,x)=\mathbf f$ give
$\chi_{\forall}(y,\varphi,x,\eta x)=\mathbf t$.
For an absent variable with distinct names, the deletion identity
transfers the absence condition to the body. In both cases the
induction hypothesis identifies the value of the second branch with
$\ok_{\Fm}(\forall y\,\varphi)$.

\subsection{Inference rules and deductively closed subobjects}
\label{app:closed-subobjects}

Aczel~\cite[Propositions 1.1.4 and 1.4.5]{Aczel} describes finitary
inductive closure by the conclusions of finite proofs. We express the
rule presentation in a slice category.
Let $\mathcal D$ be regular with finite coproducts, and fix an object
$F$ and an integer $N\geq0$. For $0\leq n\leq N$, morphisms
$p_n:R_n\to F^n$ and $q_n:R_n\to F$ specify the ordered premises
and conclusions of the rule instances $R_n$.
The nullary rule instances specify axioms.
For an object $q:Q\to F$ of the slice category $\mathcal D/F$,
form the pullback
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
 B_n(Q,q)\arrow[r,"{b_{n,q}}"]\arrow[d,"{a_{n,q}}"'] &
 Q^n\arrow[d,"q^n"]\\
 R_n\arrow[r,"p_n"'] & F^n.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Put
\[
 H(Q,q)=\left(\coprod_{n=0}^N B_n(Q,q),\kappa_q\right),\qquad
 \kappa_q=[q_na_{n,q}]_{n=0}^N.
\]
Here $B_0(Q,q)\cong R_0$ since $Q^0=F^0=1$ and $q^0=1_1$.
For a slice morphism $h:(Q,q)\to(Q',q')$, define $B_n(h)$ by
$a_{n,q'}B_n(h)=a_{n,q}$ and
$b_{n,q'}B_n(h)=h^n b_{n,q}$.
Pullback uniqueness proves the identity and composition laws, so
$H(h)=\coprod_nB_n(h)$ defines an endofunctor of $\mathcal D/F$.

\begin{definition}\label{def:deductively-closed}
A subobject $m:T\hookrightarrow F$ is closed under these rules if
there is a morphism $\alpha:\coprod_nB_n(T,m)\to T$ with
$m\alpha=\kappa_m$. Equivalently, $(T,m)$ admits an $H$-algebra
structure in $\mathcal D/F$. When $F$ and the rule morphisms specify
a logical calculus, such a subobject is a deductively closed theory
of formulas for that calculus.
\end{definition}

The algebra structure is unique because $m$ is monic. Its nullary
part includes all axioms, and its other parts express closure under
the inference rules. An inclusion of closed subobjects is
an algebra morphism, by composing with the target monomorphism.

The image construction below is an instance of Wi\ss{}mann's lifting of a
