factorization system to algebras for an endofunctor preserving its left
class~\cite[Lemma 3.6]{Wissmann}.

\begin{proof}
Factor $c=me$ with $e:P\twoheadrightarrow T$ regular epic and
$m:T\hookrightarrow F$ monic. The endofunctor $H$ preserves
regular epimorphisms: finite products preserve them in a regular
category, each $B_n(e)$ is a pullback of $e^n$, and finite coproducts
preserve coequalizers. Thus $H(e)$ is regular epic.

Writing $|H(P,c)|$ for the underlying object of the slice object,
the equations $c\delta=\kappa_c$ and
$\kappa_mH(e)=\kappa_c$ give the commuting square
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 \lvert H(P,c)\rvert\arrow[r,"e\delta"]\arrow[d,two heads,"H(e)"'] &
 T\arrow[d,hook,"m"]\\
 \lvert H(T,m)\rvert\arrow[r,"\kappa_m"']\arrow[ur,dashed,"\alpha"] & F.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Since $m$ is monic, $e\delta$ coequalizes the kernel pair of $H(e)$.
The regular epimorphism $H(e)$ is its kernel-pair coequalizer, so
there is a unique diagonal $\alpha$. In particular, $m\alpha=\kappa_m$,
so the image is closed. If $u:U\hookrightarrow F$ is another
closed subobject, initiality gives an algebra morphism
$v:(P,c)\to(U,u)$, hence $uv=c$. The image factorization gives
a unique $w:T\to U$ with $uw=m$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{First-order theories}
\label{app:first-order-derivations}

Continue with the syntax structure of
Definition~\ref{def:categorical-syntax} and its substitution.
Put $F=\Fm$. The propositional axiom schemes are those of
H\'ajek and Pudl\'ak~\cite[0.10, p.~7]{HP}:
\begin{align}
 &\varphi\Rightarrow(\psi\Rightarrow\varphi),
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-one}\\
 &(\varphi\Rightarrow(\psi\Rightarrow\chi))
   \Rightarrow((\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)
   \Rightarrow(\varphi\Rightarrow\chi)),
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-two}\\
 &(\neg\psi\Rightarrow\neg\varphi)
   \Rightarrow(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi).
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-three}
\end{align}
The named-variable quantifier axioms follow
Hirst and Hirst~\cite[Sections 2.11--2.12]{HH}. For equality, we use
their reflexivity and substitutivity principles with terms as
parameters~\cite[Section 3.1]{HH}:
\begin{align}
 &(\forall x\,\varphi)\Rightarrow\varphi[x:=t],
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-instantiation}\\
 &\forall x(\varphi\Rightarrow\psi)
       \Rightarrow(\varphi\Rightarrow\forall x\,\psi),
                                                        \label{eq:hilbert-distribution}\\
 &t=t,                                                   \label{eq:hilbert-reflexivity}\\
 &(u=t)\Rightarrow
       (\varphi[x:=u]\Rightarrow\varphi[x:=t]).           \label{eq:hilbert-equality}
\end{align}
Each scheme denotes a morphism from its parameter object to $F$.
For the first three these objects are $F^2,F^3,F^2$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-instantiation}, use the pullback of
$i_{\Adm}:\Adm\hookrightarrow F\times V\times\Tm$ along the
permutation $V\times F\times\Tm\to F\times V\times\Tm$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-distribution}, use
$[\mem(x,\FV_{\Fm}(\varphi))=\mathbf{f}]
\hookrightarrow V\times F^2$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-reflexivity}, use $\Tm$.
For \eqref{eq:hilbert-equality}, intersect the pullbacks of $i_{\Adm}$
along
\[
 (x,\varphi,u,t)\longmapsto(\varphi,x,u),\qquad
 (x,\varphi,u,t)\longmapsto(\varphi,x,t)
\]
from $V\times F\times\Tm^2$ to $F\times E$.
Let $L$ be the coproduct of these seven parameter objects and
$\lambda:L\to F$ their copairing.

Fix an axiom subobject $i_A:A\hookrightarrow S$. Define rule objects
and their premise and conclusion morphisms by
\begin{gather*}
 R_0=L+A,\quad p_0:R_0\to1,\quad q_0=[\lambda,ji_A],\\
 R_1=V\times F,\quad p_1=\pi_F:R_1\to F,
             \quad q_1=\forall:R_1\to F,\\
 R_2=F^2,\quad p_2=\langle\pi_1,\Rightarrow\rangle:R_2\to F^2,
             \quad q_2=\pi_2:R_2\to F.
\end{gather*}
These are axiom introduction, generalization, and modus ponens.
Let $H_A:\mathcal D/F\to
\mathcal D/F$ be the resulting inference endofunctor.

Suppose these initial derivation algebras exist for every axiom
subobject of $S$. A \emph{sentence theory} is a subobject
$u:U\hookrightarrow S$ through which $c_{U,S}$ factors.
Since $T_{U,S}$ is the image of $c_{U,S}$, this condition is
$T_{U,S}\leq U$. Axiom introduction gives the reverse inclusion.
Theorem~\ref{thm:first-order-reflection} therefore identifies $T_{A,S}$
as the least sentence theory containing $A$.

\begin{lemma}[Regular images and ranges]\label{lem:range-regular-image}
Let $\mathcal S$ be a restriction category with ranges in which every
restriction idempotent splits. Suppose $\mathcal D=\Tot(\mathcal S)$
is regular, and let $f:X\to Y$ have regular-image factorization
$f=me$ in $\mathcal D$, with $e:X\twoheadrightarrow I$ and
$m:I\hookrightarrow Y$.
If $m$ has a partial inverse $r:Y\rightharpoonup I$ in $\mathcal S$,
then $\ran(f)=mr=\bar r$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The restriction idempotent $mr=\bar r$ satisfies $mrf=mrme=f$.
Since $\ran(f)$ is the least restriction idempotent fixing $f$,
$\ran(f)\leq mr$. For the reverse inequality, let $a:Y\rightharpoonup Y$
be any restriction idempotent with $af=f$. Choose a splitting
$a=i_a s_a$, where $i_a:Y_a\to Y$ is total, $s_a:Y\rightharpoonup Y_a$,
and $s_a i_a=1_{Y_a}$. Then $f=i_a(s_a f)$, and $s_a f:X\to Y_a$ is
total since $\overline{s_a f}=\overline{i_a s_a f}=\bar f=1_X$.
The morphism $i_a$ is monic in $\mathcal D$, so the universal property
of the regular image gives a unique $u:I\to Y_a$ with $i_a u=m$.
Since $a i_a=i_a$, we have $am=m$ and $a(mr)=mr$. Thus $mr\leq a$.
Taking $a=\ran(f)$ gives $mr\leq\ran(f)$.
\end{proof}

The relation between split ranges and factorizations through restriction
monomorphisms is developed in Cockett, Guo, and
Hofstra~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{CGHRangeI}.
The additional conditions for these to be regular-image factorizations
are given in \cite[Section 3.16 and Proposition 3.17]{CGHRangeII}.

Since $\mathcal D$ is regular, $\Par(\mathcal D,\Mono)$ is a
split restriction category with ranges
\cite[Theorem 4.5 and Section 4.11]{CGHRangeI}; its total subcategory
is canonically isomorphic to $\mathcal D$.
The sentence theory is represented in this category by
\[
 t_A=[S\xleftarrow{m_A}T_{A,S}\xrightarrow{m_A}S]:S\rightharpoonup S,
 \qquad m_A:T_{A,S}\hookrightarrow S.
\]
Every monomorphism in $\mathcal D$ has a partial inverse in this
partial-map category. Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image} therefore
gives $t_A=\ran(c_{A,S})$.
If instead $\mathcal D=\Tot(\Split(\mathcal R))$ for a restriction
category $\mathcal R$ whose restriction splitting has ranges, require
$m_A$ to have a partial inverse
$r_A:S\rightharpoonup T_{A,S}$ in $\Split(\mathcal R)$.
The same lemma gives $\ran(c_{A,S})=m_A r_A=\bar r_A$.

In Lemma~\ref{lem:range-regular-image}, a range-preserving
restriction functor $G:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S'$ sends
$m:I\to Y$ and $r:Y\rightharpoonup I$ to a splitting of the
range of $G(f):G(X)\to G(Y)$, since
\[
 G(m)G(r)=G(\ran(f))=\ran(G(f)),\qquad G(r)G(m)=1_{G(I)}.
\]

\subsection{Propositional theories}
\label{app:propositional-theories}

Let $\mathcal D$ be regular with finite coproducts, fix an atom
object $V\in\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal D)$, and suppose
$G(Z)=V+Z+Z^2$ has an initial algebra
$S$ with constructors $\theta:V\to S$, $\nu:S\to S$, and
${\Rightarrow}:S^2\to S$. For an axiom subobject
$i_A:A\hookrightarrow S$, let $L=S^2+S^3+S^2$ and let
$\lambda:L\to S$ be given by
\eqref{eq:hilbert-one}--\eqref{eq:hilbert-three}, with $\nu$ for
negation. Use $R_0=L+A$, $q_0=[\lambda,i_A]$, and $R_1=0$.
The unary rule imposes no closure condition. Indeed, its premise and
conclusion are the unique morphism $0\to S$, so the pullback
projection $b_{1,q}:B_1(Q,q)\to Q$ satisfies $q b_{1,q}=q_1a_{1,q}$
for every $q:Q\to S$. The binary rule has $R_2=S^2$, premise morphism
$p_2=\langle\pi_1,\Rightarrow\rangle:S^2\to S^2$, and conclusion
morphism $q_2=\pi_2:S^2\to S$.
If the resulting inference endofunctor has an initial algebra,
Theorem~\ref{thm:least-theorem-subobject} constructs the least
subobject of $S$ containing the axioms and closed under these rules.
Its partial identity belongs to $\Par(\mathcal D,\Mono)$.
In particular, subobjects $i_+:A_+\hookrightarrow V$ and
$i_-:A_-\hookrightarrow V$ specify positive and negative atomic
axioms by the image of
$[\theta i_+,\nu\theta i_-]:A_++A_-\to S$. For a generalized
index $x:Z\to A_-$ the corresponding negative axiom is the
composite $\nu\theta i_-x:Z\to S$.
\section{The three-point cosheaf construction}\label{app:fork-structure}
\subsection{Cosheaves and functor categories}

Write $O_0=\{c\}$, $O_1=\{a,c\}$, and $O_2=\{b,c\}$ for the nonempty
proper opens of $X$. Morphisms of the set-valued cosheaves defined in
Section~\ref{sec:cosheaves} are natural transformations.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:fork-cosheaves}
Restriction to $O_0,O_1,O_2$ defines an equivalence
$\operatorname{CoSh}(X,\mathbf{Set})\simeq\mathbf{Set}^{J}$,
where $J=(1\leftarrow0\to2)$. A quasi-inverse sends a diagram
$Y_1\xleftarrow{r_1^Y}Y_0\xrightarrow{r_2^Y}Y_2$ to the cosheaf
with value $Y_j$ at $O_j$ and $Y_1\amalg_{Y_0}Y_2$ at $X$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $F:\mathcal O(X)\to\mathbf{Set}$ satisfy $F(\varnothing)=\varnothing$.
Every cover of $O_j$ contains $O_j$. A cover of $X$ that omits $X$
contains both $O_1$ and $O_2$. Each of its members lies in $O_1$
or $O_2$, so a cocone on the cover is determined
by its maps on $O_1$ and $O_2$ agreeing on $O_0=O_1\cap O_2$.
Thus the remaining cosheaf condition is that the canonical map
\[
 F(O_1)\amalg_{F(O_0)}F(O_2)\longrightarrow F(X)
\]
be a bijection.

Extend $Y$ by sending $O_i\subseteq X$ to the coprojection
$\iota_i^Y:Y_i\to Y_1\amalg_{Y_0}Y_2$ for $i=1,2$. A morphism $f:Y\to Z$ of diagrams consists of functions
$f_j:Y_j\to Z_j$ satisfying $f_i r_i^Y=r_i^Z f_0$ for $i=1,2$.
It induces the unique map
\[
 f_X:Y_1\amalg_{Y_0}Y_2\longrightarrow Z_1\amalg_{Z_0}Z_2,
 \qquad f_X\iota_i^Y=\iota_i^Z f_i\quad(i=1,2).
\]
Uniqueness gives preservation of identities and composition.
Restriction of this extension recovers the original diagram and
its morphisms. For a cosheaf $F$, the comparison from the extension
of its restriction to $F$ is the identity on the proper opens and
the canonical bijection above at $X$. Naturality at $X$ follows
from the equations for $f_X$.
\end{proof}

For an object $Y$ of $\mathcal E$, the pushout has a
quotient presentation on the disjoint union $Y_1+Y_2$: identify
$(1,r_1^Yy)$ with $(2,r_2^Yy)$ for every $y\in Y_0$ and take the
equivalence relation $\sim_Y$ generated by these pairs. Enumerate the
generating pairs in both directions and the diagonal on $Y_1+Y_2$.
Finite paths in these edges enumerate $\sim_Y$.
For $f:Y\to Z$ in $\mathcal E$, the component at $X$ of the associated
cosheaf morphism is
\[
 (Y_1+Y_2)/{\sim_Y}\longrightarrow (Z_1+Z_2)/{\sim_Z},\qquad
 [(i,y)]\longmapsto [(i,f_i(y))]\quad(i=1,2).
\]
Indeed, $f_i r_i^Y=r_i^Z f_0$, so each generating pair maps to a
generating pair.

Products and subobjects are taken in $\mathcal E$. The cosheaf
associated with $Y\times Z$ has value
$(Y_1\times Z_1)\amalg_{Y_0\times Z_0}(Y_2\times Z_2)$ at $X$.
This need not be the product of the values at $X$ of
the cosheaves associated with $Y$ and $Z$. Write $0$, $1$, and $2$
for empty, singleton, and two-element numerical carriers, respectively.
For example,
the object $H=(1\leftarrow0\to1)$ of $\mathcal E$ satisfies
$H\times H\cong H$,
and the cosheaf associated with $H$ has two elements at $X$,
whereas the Cartesian square of that set has four.
Likewise $H\to(1\leftarrow1\to1)$ is a monomorphism in $\mathcal E$,
although the associated cosheaf morphism has component $2\to1$ at $X$.
We use regularity and regular images as in
Appendix~\ref{app:categorical-hypotheses}.
Finite coproducts are \emph{extensive} when, for every finite family
$(Y_k)_k$, copairing defines an equivalence
\[
 \prod_k(\mathcal E/Y_k)\longrightarrow
 \mathcal E/\Bigl(\coprod_kY_k\Bigr).
\]

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:fork-total}
The categories $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ and
$\mathcal E=\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}^J$ have finite limits and
finite coproducts. The category $\mathcal E$ is regular and
extensive. Its monomorphisms are componentwise injections, and its
regular images are the componentwise c.e.\ images.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Proposition~\ref{prop:numerical-structure} gives finite limits,
disjoint pullback-stable finite coproducts, regular images, and
computable sections of surjections in $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

Limits and finite coproducts in $\mathcal E$ are formed
componentwise. Their universal morphisms are natural because their
components are uniquely determined by the corresponding numerical
universal properties. For a natural transformation $f:Y\to Z$,
the equations $r_i^Zf_0=f_i r_i^Y$ show that its component images
form a subfunctor of $Z$.
For a componentwise surjection $q:Y\to Z$, a natural transformation
$u:Y\to W$ coequalizing its kernel pair descends componentwise.
If $v_jq_j=u_j$ are the descended morphisms, then
\[
 r_i^Wv_0q_0=r_i^Wu_0=u_i r_i^Y
 =v_iq_i r_i^Y=v_i r_i^Zq_0.
\]
Surjectivity of $q_0$ gives $r_i^Wv_0=v_i r_i^Z$, so the
descent is a natural transformation. These image factorizations are stable
under pullback because the corresponding assertion holds in
each component. They give regularity of $\mathcal E$.

The three objects of $\mathcal E$
\[
 H_0=(1\leftarrow1\to1),\qquad
 H_1=(1\leftarrow0\to0),\qquad
 H_2=(0\leftarrow0\to1)
\]
detect component elements: total morphisms $H_j\to Y$ are in bijection
with elements of $Y_j$. Each testing morphism $H_j\to Y$ has computable components because every
nonempty component of $H_j$ is a singleton.
If a morphism of $\mathcal E$ is monic,
testing it on these morphisms proves that each component is injective.
The converse follows by cancelling those component injections.
An injective morphism of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ has a partial recursive inverse
on its c.e.\ image, obtained by preimage search.

Finally, for a morphism $Y\to A+B$, the inverse images of the two
coproduct summands form c.e.\ subfunctors $Y^A,Y^B$ and give an
isomorphism $Y^A+Y^B\cong Y$. Morphisms over $A+B$ restrict uniquely to morphisms
over $A$ and $B$, and two such morphisms combine uniquely by
copairing. This proves the slice equivalence expressing extensivity.
\end{proof}

units.tex: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:fork-structure}
The category $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Par}(\mathcal E,
\operatorname{Mono})$ is a split prodominical restriction category
with binary restriction products, restriction coproducts, weak
choice, and ranges satisfying the agreement law. The range of a morphism
represented by $Y\hookleftarrow D\xrightarrow{v}Z$ is the partial
identity on the regular image of $v$.
Joins of restriction idempotents are partial identities on finite
unions of their subfunctors, and inverse image along every partial
morphism preserves binary meets and finite joins. Ranges commute with products and
are stable under pullback along total morphisms.
\end{proposition}

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
\begin{proof}
Replace the monic leg of a representing span by its image
inclusion, using its computable inverse on that image. A partial
morphism $f:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ is then represented by a c.e.\ subfunctor
$D_f\subseteq Y$ and a natural transformation $D_f\to Z$.
For $j\in\{0,1,2\}$, write $f_j:Y_j\rightharpoonup Z_j$ for the
partial recursive function with domain $(D_f)_j$ whose restriction
to $(D_f)_j$ is the $j$-component of this natural transformation.
Use the same convention for other partial morphisms.
If $g:Z\rightharpoonup W$ has domain subfunctor $D_g$, the domain of $gf$
at component $j$ is
\[
 \{y\in(D_f)_j:f_j(y)\in(D_g)_j\},
\]
and its value there is $g_j(f_j(y))$. These carriers are c.e.\
and form a subfunctor by naturality. This is the
pullback composition of the representing spans. Associativity
and identities follow from these domain and value formulas.

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
The restriction $\bar f$ is the partial identity on $D_f$.
The restriction axioms reduce componentwise to the corresponding
identities of partial functions. Every restriction idempotent
splits through its domain subfunctor: the inclusion is total,
and its partial inverse is the identity with that domain.
Empty domains give restriction zeros. The restriction product
uses componentwise Cartesian products. For $f:W\rightharpoonup Y$
and $g:W\rightharpoonup Z$, the projection equations determine the pairing by
\[
 (D_{\langle f,g\rangle})_j=(D_f)_j\cap(D_g)_j,\qquad
 \langle f,g\rangle_j(w)=(f_j(w),g_j(w))
 \quad(w\in (D_f)_j\cap(D_g)_j).
\]
Coproducts use disjoint unions of carriers. The domain of a partial copairing is
the disjoint union of the two domains. A product with an empty domain
is empty, which proves the prodominical zero law.

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
The component images $f_j((D_f)_j)$ form a c.e.\ subfunctor
$I_f\subseteq Z$. Its partial identity satisfies $1_{I_f}f=f$.
If a restriction idempotent $e$ on $Z$ satisfies $ef=f$, its domain
contains $f_j((D_f)_j)$ at each $j$. Thus $1_{I_f}\leq e$, and
$\ran(f)=1_{I_f}$. For $g,h:Z\rightharpoonup W$ with
$gf=hf$, choose a preimage of each $z\in(I_f)_j$. Equality of the two partial composites shows
that $g_j$ is defined at $z$ exactly when $h_j$ is, and their
values there agree. Hence $g\ran(f)=h\ran(f)$, including
equality of domains.

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
For a total $u:W\to Z$, the projection
$D_f\times_Z W\to W$ has component image
$u_j^{-1}(f_j((D_f)_j))$. Thus its range is $u^*\ran(f)$,
which is the asserted pullback law. The image of a product
of two representing morphisms is the product of their images, giving
$\ran(f\times g)=\ran(f)\times\ran(g)$.
Intersections and finite unions of domain subfunctors are again
c.e.\ subfunctors; their partial identities give the meets and joins
of the corresponding restriction idempotents. For a restriction idempotent
$e$ on $Z$ with domain subfunctor $D_e$, the inverse image $f^*e$
has component carrier
\[
 \{y\in(D_f)_j:f_j(y)\in(D_e)_j\}.
\]
This formula proves preservation of binary meets and finite joins,
including the empty join.

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
Suppose that $p:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ is a partial monomorphism
and let $D_p$ be its domain subfunctor. If two elements of $(D_p)_j$
have the same image, their corresponding total morphisms
$H_j\to D_p\to Y$ have equal composites with $p$.
Partial monicity makes the original morphisms equal, since their
images lie in $D_p$. Thus each $p_j$ is injective on $(D_p)_j$.
Preimage search gives recursive inverse components on $I_p$;
they form a natural transformation by injectivity and naturality of
the representing morphism $D_p\to Z$.
The resulting partial morphism $p^\dagger:Z\rightharpoonup Y$ has
domain $I_p$ and satisfies $pp^\dagger=\overline{p^\dagger}$ and
$pp^\dagger p=p$.
This proves weak choice.
\end{proof}

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
\subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
\begin{proof}
Let $Y$ be an object of $\mathcal E$. For $y\in Y_0$, take the
finite subfunctor $D\subseteq Y$ with
\[
 D_0=\{y\},\qquad D_1=\{r_1^Yy\},\qquad D_2=\{r_2^Yy\}.
\]
The partial identity on $D$ is connected: in any partition of $D$
into two disjoint subfunctors, the part containing $y$ in component
$0$ must contain its images in components $1$ and $2$, and hence
must equal $D$. The partial identity on a singleton subfunctor
in component $i\in\{1,2\}$, with the other components empty,
is connected as well.

units.subsection: \subsection{Partial maps, ranges, and connected restriction idempotents}
units.tex:
Suppose that partial morphisms $f,g:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ agree
after composition with every connected restriction idempotent.
Restriction to the
finite subfunctor generated by $y\in Y_0$ detects whether
$f_0$ and $g_0$ are defined at $y$, and compares their values
when defined. Partial identities on singleton subfunctors in
components $1$ and $2$ do the same for $f_1,g_1$ and $f_2,g_2$.
Thus all three component partial functions agree, proving $f=g$.
\end{proof}
\subsection{A universal object and a frame}

Let $V$ be the object of $\mathcal A$ defined in
\eqref{eq:universal-fork}.

\begin{proof}
For $j=0,1,2$, choose a recursive injection $c_j:Y_j\to\N$
with a partial recursive inverse on its image, using a tuple
coding of the ambient finite power. Define
\[
 s_{Y,i}(y_i)=(0,c_i(y_i))\quad(i=1,2),\qquad
 s_{Y,0}(y)=(0,c_0(y),c_1(r_1^Yy),c_2(r_2^Yy)).
\]
These maps are total and injective, and satisfy
$r_i^Vs_{Y,0}=s_{Y,i} r_i^Y$ for $i=1,2$.
Their images form a c.e.\ subfunctor $I\subseteq V$. The inverses
$s_{Y,j}^{-1}:I_j\to Y_j$ are computable and satisfy
$r_i^Y s_{Y,0}^{-1}=s_{Y,i}^{-1}r_i^I$. They define a partial morphism
$r:V\rightharpoonup Y$ with $rs_Y=1_Y$ and $s_Y r=\bar r$, the partial
identity on $I\subseteq V$.
\end{proof}

For $Y\in\mathcal E$, let $Y^\#$ be the object of nonempty words
defined in Section~\ref{sec:cosheaves}.
For a partial morphism $f:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ of $\mathcal A$
with domain subfunctor $D_f$, define
$f^\#:Y^\#\rightharpoonup Z^\#$ to have, at component $j$, domain
\[
 \{\operatorname{code}_{m(Y_j)}(y_1,\ldots,y_n):
          n\ge1,\ y_1,\ldots,y_n\in(D_f)_j\}\subseteq(Y^\#)_j.
\]
Its component at $j$ decodes a sequence, applies $f_j$ to every
entry, and encodes the resulting sequence in $(Z_j)^\#$.
These assignments preserve identities and composition and define
a functor $(-)^\#:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$.
Concatenation and singleton insertion give morphisms
$\mu_Y:Y^\#\times Y^\#\to Y^\#$ and $\eta_Y:Y\to Y^\#$
in $\mathcal E$.
For an internal semigroup $(M,\mu)$ in $\mathcal E$, with
associative multiplication $\mu:M\times M\to M$, and a morphism
$f:Y\to M$, multiplication of the $f$-images of the entries gives
the unique semigroup morphism $\widehat f:Y^\#\to M$ satisfying
$\widehat f\eta_Y=f$.

Fix a recursive pairing bijection
$\pi:\N^2\to\N$. For $n\ge1$ choose tuple bijections
$\operatorname{encode}_n:\N^n\to\N$ and their inverses
$\operatorname{decode}_n:\N\to\N^n$, both computable uniformly in $n$.
Encode a nonempty word $(k_1,\ldots,k_n)$ by
$\pi(n-1,\operatorname{encode}_n(k_1,\ldots,k_n))$.

\begin{proof}
For the product isomorphism, decode each of $k,z,x_1,x_2$ into a
pair using $\pi^{-1}$. Send $(k,z,x_1,x_2)$ to the resulting pair
of four-tuples. At component $i\in\{1,2\}$, decode $(k,x)$ into
the resulting pair of two-tuples. The naturality equations hold
coordinatewise, and coordinatewise pairing gives the inverse.

For the coproduct isomorphism, write $k=2q+t$ with
$t\in\{0,1\}$. Send a tuple with first coordinate $k$ to
summand $t$, replace $k$ by $q$, and retain its remaining
coordinates. This rule is the same at all three components.
The inverse replaces $q$ in summand $t$ by $2q+t$.

For the word isomorphism, decode $k$ as the nonempty word
$(k_1,\ldots,k_n)$. Apply $\operatorname{decode}_n$ to $z,x_1,x_2$
to obtain $(z_j)_j,(x_{1,j})_j,(x_{2,j})_j$, respectively. Send $(k,z,x_1,x_2)$ to the numerical code
\[
 \operatorname{code}_4
 ((k_1,z_1,x_{1,1},x_{2,1}),\ldots,(k_n,z_n,x_{1,n},x_{2,n}))
 \in(V^\#)_0.
\]
At endpoint $i$, the input is $(k,x_i)$. The same decodings give
\[
 \operatorname{code}_2((k_1,x_{i,1}),\ldots,(k_n,x_{i,n}))\in(V^\#)_i.
\]
These maps form a natural transformation. To invert them, decode
the sequence, recover the word of first coordinates, and apply
the tuple encodings to the remaining coordinate sequences.
These inverses are total recursive.
\end{proof}
\subsection{A Turing morphism}\label{app:fork-turing}

We construct a Turing morphism $\tau:V\times V\rightharpoonup V$
in $\mathcal A$ by giving a monomorphism $D_\tau\hookrightarrow V\times V$
and a natural transformation $D_\tau\to V$.

We use an acceptable numbering
$\varphi:\N\times\N\rightharpoonup\N$ of the partial recursive
functions and write $\varphi_p(t)=\varphi(p,t)$.
The specialization property of this numbering is the following:
if $m\geq0$, $n\geq1$, and
$G:\N^m\times\N^n\rightharpoonup\N$ is partial recursive,
there is a total recursive map $s:\N^m\to\N$ such that
\[
 \varphi_{s(y)}(\operatorname{encode}_n x)\simeq G(y,x).
\]
Here $\simeq$ means equality of partial values,
including simultaneous undefinedness. The case $m=0$ is a
constant program index. This is the $s$-$m$-$n$ theorem.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:fork-turing}
The object $V$ of
$\mathcal A=\operatorname{Par}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}^J,
\operatorname{Mono})$ admits a Turing morphism
$\tau:V\times V\rightharpoonup V$: for every object $Y$ of
$\mathcal A$ and every morphism $F:Y\times V\rightharpoonup V$
in $\mathcal A$, there is a total morphism
$p_F:Y\to V$ such that $\tau(p_F\times1_V)=F$.
At component $i\in\{1,2\}$, this Turing morphism is given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fork-turing-endpoint}
 \tau_i((k,p),(\ell,x))
 =\operatorname{decode}_2
     \varphi_p(\operatorname{encode}_2(\ell,x)).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $i=1,2$, let $D_{\tau,i}\subseteq V_i\times V_i$ be the c.e.\ set
on which the numerical computation in
\eqref{eq:fork-turing-endpoint} halts, and define
$\tau_i:V_i\times V_i\rightharpoonup V_i$ with domain $D_{\tau,i}$
by that equation. The first coordinate $k$
of the parameter has no effect on this computation.

At component $0$, write the parameter as
$P=(k,p_0,p_1,p_2)\in V_0$ and the input as
$x=(\ell,x_0,x_1,x_2)\in V_0$.
Define partial recursive maps $\psi_j:V_0\times V_0\rightharpoonup V_j$
for $j=0,1,2$ by the following parallel computations:
\begin{align*}
 \psi_0(P,x)&\simeq
   \operatorname{decode}_4
      \varphi_{p_0}(\operatorname{encode}_4 x),\\
 \psi_i(P,x)&\simeq
   \operatorname{decode}_2
      \varphi_{p_i}(\operatorname{encode}_2(\ell,x_i))
      \qquad(i=1,2).
\end{align*}
Let $D_{\tau,0}\subseteq V_0\times V_0$ consist of those pairs $(P,x)$
for which all three computations halt and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fork-turing-check}
 \psi_i(P,x)=r_i^V \psi_0(P,x)\qquad(i=1,2).
\end{equation}
Define $\tau_0:V_0\times V_0\rightharpoonup V_0$ with domain
$D_{\tau,0}$ by $\tau_0(P,x)=\psi_0(P,x)$.
Dovetailing the three computations and checking equality of their
numerical outputs enumerates $D_{\tau,0}$ and computes $\tau_0$ on it.

If $(P,x)\in D_{\tau,0}$, then
$(r_i^V P,r_i^V x)=((k,p_i),(\ell,x_i))\in D_{\tau,i}$.
Thus $D_\tau=(D_{\tau,0},D_{\tau,1},D_{\tau,2})$ is a c.e.\ subfunctor of $V\times V$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:fork-turing-check} gives
\[
 r_i^V\tau_0(P,x)
   =\tau_i(r_i^V P,r_i^V x)
 \qquad((P,x)\in D_{\tau,0}).
\]
The restrictions $\tau_j|_{D_{\tau,j}}:D_{\tau,j}\to V_j$, for $j=0,1,2$,
therefore form a morphism $D_\tau\to V$ in $\mathcal E$.
Together with the inclusion $D_\tau\hookrightarrow V\times V$,
they define the required partial morphism $\tau$.

Now let $F:Y\times V\rightharpoonup V$ be any partial morphism.
Choose its representation by a c.e.\ subfunctor
$D\subseteq Y\times V$ and a morphism $D\to V$ in
$\mathcal E$. Its components are the restrictions
$F_j|_{D_j}:D_j\to V_j$, where $j=0,1,2$.
Let $d_j=m(V_j)$, so $d_0=4$ and $d_1=d_2=2$.
For each component define a partial recursive numerical function
\[
 G_j:\N^{m(Y_j)}\times\N^{d_j}\rightharpoonup\N
\]
as follows. On input $(y,x)$, wait until $(y,x)$ appears in an
enumeration of $D_j$; then compute $F_j(y,x)$ and return its
$\operatorname{encode}_{d_j}$-code. This function has domain
exactly $D_j$.
Specialization gives total recursive maps
$s_j:\N^{m(Y_j)}\to\N$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fork-specialization}
 \operatorname{decode}_{d_j}
   \varphi_{s_j(y)}(\operatorname{encode}_{d_j}x)
 \simeq F_j(y,x),
 \qquad\text{with domain }D_j.
\end{equation}

Define the component maps of $p_F:Y\to V$ by
\begin{align*}
 p_{F,i}(y_i)&=(0,s_i(y_i)) &&(i=1,2),\\
 p_{F,0}(y)&=(0,s_0(y),s_1(r_1^Yy),s_2(r_2^Yy)).
\end{align*}
These maps are recursive and total on their respective carriers:
the maps $s_j$ are total on the ambient numerical powers and the
maps $r_i^Y$ are total on $Y_0$. Moreover,
$r_i^Vp_{F,0}(y)=(0,s_i(r_i^Yy))=p_{F,i}(r_i^Yy)$,
so $p_F$ is a natural transformation in $\mathcal E$, hence total in
$\mathcal A$.

At component $i\in\{1,2\}$, equations
\eqref{eq:fork-turing-endpoint} and
\eqref{eq:fork-specialization} show that the partial function
\[
 (y_i,v_i)\longmapsto\tau_i(p_{F,i}(y_i),v_i)
 :Y_i\times V_i\rightharpoonup V_i
\]
has domain $D_i$ and agrees there with $F_i$.
At component $0$, fix $(y,x)\in Y_0\times V_0$.
If $(y,x)\in D_0$, the computation $\psi_0(p_{F,0}(y),x)$ returns $F_0(y,x)$.
Since $D$ is a subfunctor,
$(r_i^Yy,r_i^Vx)\in D_i$ for $i=1,2$.
The computations $\psi_i(p_{F,0}(y),x)$, for $i=1,2$, consequently
halt, and naturality of the morphism $D\to V$ gives
\[
 F_i(r_i^Yy,r_i^Vx)=r_i^VF_0(y,x).
\]
Both tests in \eqref{eq:fork-turing-check} succeed, so
$\tau_0(p_{F,0}(y),x)=F_0(y,x)$.
Conversely, if $\tau_0(p_{F,0}(y),x)$ is defined, the computation
$\psi_0(p_{F,0}(y),x)$ has halted. Equation~\eqref{eq:fork-specialization}
then implies $(y,x)\in D_0$.
Thus $\tau(p_F\times1_V)=F$, with equality of domains and values
at each component.
\end{proof}
\subsection{The recursion category and its splitting}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:fork-recursion}
Let $\mathscr R_X$ be the full subcategory of $\mathcal A$
whose objects are obtained from $V$ by finitely many applications
of the chosen binary products, binary coproducts, and nonempty-word formation.
Then $\mathscr R_X$ is a recursion category. Its inclusion
into $\mathcal A$ is a range functor, and its restriction
splitting is equivalent to $\mathcal A$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The isomorphisms of Lemma~\ref{lem:fork-frames}, applied inductively,
show that every object of $\mathscr R_X$ is isomorphic to $V$.
The binary restriction products, coproducts, and prodominical
zero law restrict from $\mathcal A$ to this full subcategory.
The Turing morphism of Theorem~\ref{thm:fork-turing} has
source $V\times V$ and target $V$ in the subcategory.
Its total parameter morphisms for objects of $\mathscr R_X$ belong
to $\mathscr R_X$ by fullness. Hence it retains its Turing
universal property there, proving that $\mathscr R_X$ is a
recursion category.

By fullness, the restriction idempotents on each object of $\mathscr R_X$
are the same as in $\mathcal A$. Hence the least $e$ satisfying $ef=f$
is the same in both categories. The inclusion preserves restrictions,
ranges and the chosen coproducts, so it is a range functor.

For a restriction idempotent $e$ on an object $Y$ of $\mathscr R_X$,
write $\iota_e:D_e\to Y$ and $r_e:Y\rightharpoonup D_e$ for its
domain inclusion and partial inverse. Send $(Y,e)$ to $D_e$
and a morphism $f:(Y,e)\rightharpoonup(Z,d)$, represented by
$f:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ satisfying $f=dfe$, to
$r_d f \iota_e:D_e\rightharpoonup D_d$.
The equations $\iota_er_e=e$ and $r_e\iota_e=1_{D_e}$ show that
identities and composition are preserved. Conversely, send a
partial map $g:D_e\rightharpoonup D_d$ to $\iota_d g r_e$.
This morphism belongs to $\mathscr R_X$ by fullness and satisfies
$d(\iota_d g r_e)e=\iota_d g r_e$. The two assignments are inverse on
each hom-set, so the functor is fully faithful.
It preserves restrictions, since
$\overline{r_d f \iota_e}=r_e\bar f \iota_e$.
For every $Z\in\mathcal A$, Lemma~\ref{lem:fork-dominance}
provides a restriction monomorphism $s_Z:Z\to V$ with partial inverse
$s_Z^\dagger:V\rightharpoonup Z$. The domain subfunctor of
$s_Zs_Z^\dagger$ is isomorphic to $Z$,
so the functor is essentially surjective.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $p:Y\rightharpoonup Y$ satisfy $p^2=p$, and let
$D\subseteq Y$ be its domain subfunctor. For $j=0,1,2$, put
$I_j=p_j(D_j)\subseteq Y_j$. These sets are c.e., and naturality
of $p:D\to Y$ gives $r_i^Y(I_0)\subseteq I_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Thus $I\subseteq Y$ is an object of $\mathcal E$.
Let $\iota_I:I\to Y$ be the inclusion, and let
$r:Y\rightharpoonup I$ have domain $D$ and component functions $p_j$.
The equation $p^2=p$ implies that $I_j\subseteq D_j$ and that
$p_j$ fixes every element of $I_j$. Hence $\iota_I r=p$ and $r\iota_I=1_I$.

For each idempotent $e:Y\rightharpoonup Y$ in $\mathscr R_X$, write
$I_e$ for its image subfunctor and
$\iota_e:I_e\to Y$, $r_e:Y\rightharpoonup I_e$ for the splitting just
constructed. Define
$Q:\operatorname{Kar}(\mathscr R_X)\to\mathcal A$ by
$Q(Y,e)=I_e$ and
$Q(f)=r_d f \iota_e:I_e\rightharpoonup I_d$ for
$f:(Y,e)\rightharpoonup(Z,d)$.
The equations $\iota_er_e=e$ and $r_e\iota_e=1_{I_e}$ prove the functor
laws. As in Proposition~\ref{prop:fork-recursion}, the inverse
assignment on hom-sets is $g\mapsto \iota_d g r_e$, so $Q$ is fully faithful.
For $f:(Y,e)\rightharpoonup(Z,d)$, restriction preservation follows from
$\overline{r_d f \iota_e}=r_e\bar f e \iota_e$, since $e$ fixes its image
and $f=dfe$ takes values in the image of $d$.
Every object of $\mathcal A$ is isomorphic to the image of a restriction
idempotent on $V$, so this functor is essentially surjective.
\end{proof}

Use the restriction equivalence
\[
 \mathsf Q_{\mathrm{num}}:\Split(\mathrm{Rec})
       \longrightarrow\mathcal K_{\mathrm{rec}}
       =\operatorname{Par}(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}},\operatorname{Mono})
\]
constructed in Proposition~\ref{prop:numerical-structure}.
Sending a total morphism of $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{rec}}$ to its underlying
function gives the isomorphism
$\Tot(\mathcal K_{\mathrm{rec}})\cong\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$.
Under this identification, restriction to total categories gives the
equivalence $F:\mathcal B_{\mathrm{rec}}\to\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$
of that proposition.

Decidable equality on $V$ has the meaning fixed in
Appendix~\ref{app:categorical-hypotheses}: it is a morphism
$\epsilon:V\times V\to\Two$ in $\mathcal E$ whose inverse image
of $\mathbf t:1\to\Two$ is the diagonal subfunctor.

\begin{proof}
The terminal object of $\mathcal E$ is the constant functor at a singleton.
A subobject with empty component $0$ has independently empty or
singleton components $1$ and $2$, giving four subobjects. A
subobject with singleton component $0$ must also have singleton
components $1$ and $2$, giving one more. Thus its subobject order has five elements, whereas
the terminal singleton of $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$ has two.
An equivalence of the asserted restriction categories would induce
an equivalence of their restriction splittings, hence of their
total categories $\mathcal E$ and $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{rec}}$.
Equivalences preserve terminal objects and their subobject orders,
so this is impossible.

Suppose that $\epsilon$ decides equality on $V$. The functor $1+1$
is constant and sends both nonidentity morphisms of $J$ to
identity functions. Choose distinct $u,v\in V_0$ differing only
in their $z$ coordinate. Then $r_1^Vu=r_1^Vv$, so
$\epsilon_1(r_1^Vu,r_1^Vv)=\mathbf t_1(*)$.
Naturality gives $\epsilon_0(u,v)=\mathbf t_0(*)$, contrary to $u\ne v$.
\end{proof}

\section{Necessity of section lifting for inseparability}
\label{app:lifting-counterexample}

The lifting hypothesis in Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison} cannot be
omitted, even for a faithful range functor that preserves restriction
products and reflects zero morphisms. We construct a source category
containing the partial identities on a nonrecursive set $A\subseteq\N$
and its complement. In the target category of partial functions, the
codiagonal restricted to $A^c$ in the left summand and $A$ in the right
has a section $\N\to\N+\N$. Its value at $n$ lies in the right summand
exactly when $n\in A$. Every total source morphism is recursive in the
chosen codings, so reading the output summand of a lift would decide
membership in $A$. This example disproves
\cite[Theorem~4.1]{Lengyel2006} as stated.

Fix an acceptable numbering $(\varphi_e)_{e\in\N}$ of the ordinary
partial recursive functions $\N\rightharpoonup\N$. For a partial
numerical function $f$, write $f(x)\mathord\downarrow$ when $f$ is
defined at $x$. Put $K=\{e:\varphi_e(e)\mathord\downarrow\}$.
The set $K$ is not recursive.
Fix the standard enumeration of finite oracle-machine programs. For an
oracle $B\subseteq\N$, let $W_m^B$ be the domain of program $m$ run with oracle $B$.
Fix a recursive bijective pairing function
$\langle-,-\rangle:\N^2\to\N$, with projections $\pi_0,\pi_1$.

The objects of $\mathcal C_K$ are generated from $\N$ by binary
products and disjoint unions. For each such object $X$, let
$\gamma_X:X\to\N$ be the coding bijection obtained from the identity
on $\N$, the pairing function for products, and the even and odd
tags for disjoint unions. A morphism $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ with domain
$D_f$ is a partial function such that $\gamma_X(D_f)$ is c.e.\ relative
to $K$ and $\gamma_Y f\gamma_X^{-1}$ has an ordinary partial recursive
extension. Write $f_0:X\rightharpoonup Y$ for such an extension in the
chosen codings. Two morphisms are equal if their graphs are equal. The total morphisms of $\mathcal C_K$ are exactly
the total functions $f:X\to Y$ for which
$\gamma_Y f\gamma_X^{-1}:\N\to\N$ is recursive.
Let $F:\mathcal C_K\to\Pfn$ be the inclusion.

On $\N$, the morphisms are precisely the functions
\[
 f_{e,m}(x)\simeq
 \begin{cases}
  \varphi_e(x),&x\in W_m^K,\\
  \text{undefined},&x\notin W_m^K.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here $\simeq$ includes simultaneous undefinedness: the domain
is $W_m^K\cap\operatorname{dom}(\varphi_e)$. Every morphism has this
form by taking an index of its extension and an oracle index of its
domain.
\Needspace{18\baselineskip}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:missing-lift}
The category $\mathcal C_K$ is a prodominical recursion category with
binary restriction coproducts and ranges. The functor $F$ is a faithful range functor, preserves restriction products and
reflects zero morphisms, and $F(1_{\N})\ne0$. Inverse images along
total morphisms in its target preserve binary joins of restriction idempotents.
There are a Turing morphism
$\tau_K:\N\times\N\rightharpoonup\N$ and an isomorphism
$b:\N\to\N+\N$ for which the restriction idempotents
\[
 a_0=(b\tau_K\Delta_{\N})^*(1_{\N}+0_{\N}),\qquad
 a_1=(b\tau_K\Delta_{\N})^*(0_{\N}+1_{\N})
\]
are separated by the partial identities on $A$ and $A^c$ for some
nonrecursive set $A\subseteq\N$. Both partial identities belong to
$\mathcal C_K$, and $D_{a_0}\subseteq A$, $D_{a_1}\subseteq A^c$.
There exists a partial function $s:\N\rightharpoonup\N+\N$ with
\[
 s^{-1}(i_0(\N))=A^c,\qquad s^{-1}(i_1(\N))=A.
\]
For every such $s$, there is no morphism
$\ell:\N\rightharpoonup\N+\N$ in $\mathcal C_K$ with $F(\ell)=s$.
Moreover, there are parallel morphisms in $\mathcal C_K$
with disjoint restriction idempotents and no common upper bound in
the restriction order, although finite joins of restriction idempotents
exist.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ and $g:Y\rightharpoonup Z$ have
ordinary partial recursive extensions $f_0,g_0$. Their composite has
extension $g_0f_0$ and domain $D_{gf}=D_f\cap f_0^{-1}(D_g)$.
This domain is c.e.\ relative to $K$: enumerate $D_f$, compute the
corresponding $f_0$-values, and test for their appearance in the
enumeration of $D_g$, using dovetailing. Identities and associativity
are inherited from partial functions. Restriction is the partial
identity on $D_f$, which has the identity as an extension.
Empty partial functions give restriction zeros.

For $f:X\rightharpoonup Y$ and $g:X\rightharpoonup Z$, the
restriction pairing $\langle f,g\rangle:X\rightharpoonup Y\times Z$
has domain $D_f\cap D_g$ and ordinary partial recursive extension
$\langle f_0,g_0\rangle$. For $u:X\rightharpoonup Z$ and
$v:Y\rightharpoonup Z$, the copairing $[u,v]:X+Y\rightharpoonup Z$
has domain $D_u+D_v$ and extension $[u_0,v_0]$. These domains are
c.e.\ relative to $K$. The projections and injections are recursive,
so the restriction product and coproduct of partial functions have
their universal properties in $\mathcal C_K$. Product with a zero morphism is zero, and the chosen
recursive coding isomorphisms make the category isotypical.

The set $f(D_f)$ is c.e.\ relative to $K$: enumerate $D_f$ and run
$f_0$ on its elements. The partial identity on this image belongs to
$\mathcal C_K$ and is its range. Leastness and the agreement law
hold for partial functions: equality after $f$ gives equality on
every value in its image, including equality of definedness.
Ranges commute with restriction products because images of products
of partial functions are products of images. Restriction idempotents
are the partial identities on the subsets c.e.\ relative to $K$;
their order corresponds to inclusion, and their finite joins are
partial identities on unions.

Define $\tau_K:\N\times\N\rightharpoonup\N$ by
$\tau_K(\langle e,m\rangle,x)\simeq f_{e,m}(x)$.
Its domain is c.e.\ relative to $K$, uniformly in all three
variables, and it has the ordinary partial recursive extension
$(\langle e,m\rangle,x)\mapsto\varphi_e(x)$.
To prove its Turing property, let
$v:\N\times\N\rightharpoonup\N$ be a morphism, with ordinary
partial recursive extension $v_0:\N\times\N\rightharpoonup\N$ and
domain $D_v$ c.e.\ relative to $K$. Specializing the ordinary program
for $v_0$ gives a total recursive function $t:\N\to\N$ such that
$\varphi_{t(z)}(x)\simeq v_0(z,x)$.
For oracle programs, let $\operatorname{spec}(m,z)$ be the index of the program that,
on input $x$, computes $\langle z,x\rangle$ and runs program $m$
on that input with the same oracle. The function $\operatorname{spec}:\N^2\to\N$ is
total recursive and satisfies, for every oracle $B\subseteq\N$,
\[
 x\in W_{\operatorname{spec}(m,z)}^B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \langle z,x\rangle\in W_m^B.
\]
Choose an oracle-machine index $m_v$ with
$W_{m_v}^K=\{\langle z,x\rangle:(z,x)\in D_v\}$.
Then $W_{\operatorname{spec}(m_v,z)}^K=\{x:(z,x)\in D_v\}$.
Thus $r(z)=\langle t(z),\operatorname{spec}(m_v,z)\rangle$ defines a total
morphism $r:\N\to\N$ of $\mathcal C_K$, and
$v=\tau_K(r\times1_{\N})$, with equality of domains and values.
For $w:X\times\N\rightharpoonup\N$, apply this construction to
$v=w(\gamma_X^{-1}\times1_{\N})$. The parameter for $w$ is
$r\gamma_X:X\to\N$, since
$\tau_K((r\gamma_X)\times1_{\N})=v(\gamma_X\times1_{\N})=w$.
Hence $\tau_K$ is a Turing morphism.

The functor $F$ is faithful and preserves restrictions, zeros,
ranges, binary restriction products, and coproducts. It also reflects
zero morphisms. Inverse images along total morphisms in $\Pfn$ preserve unions,
and $F(1_{\N})\ne0$.

Use the total recursive isomorphism
\[
 b:\N\longrightarrow\N+\N,\qquad
 b(2n)=i_0(n),\quad b(2n+1)=i_1(n).
\]
Put $d=\tau_K\Delta_{\N}:\N\rightharpoonup\N$ and
$a_0=(bd)^*(1_{\N}+0_{\N})$,
$a_1=(bd)^*(0_{\N}+1_{\N})$.
For $q\in\N$, write
$p(q)\simeq\varphi_{\pi_0(q)}(q)$. These restriction idempotents
are the partial identities on the sets
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_{a_0}&=\{q:q\in W_{\pi_1(q)}^K,
                    \ p(q)\mathord\downarrow\text{ with an even value}\},\\
 D_{a_1}&=\{q:q\in W_{\pi_1(q)}^K,
                    \ p(q)\mathord\downarrow\text{ with an odd value}\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Let $A=\{q:p(q)\mathord\downarrow\text{ with an even value}\}$.
This is an ordinary c.e.\ set and is decidable relative to $K$.
For the latter assertion, uniformly construct a program that ignores
its input, simulates $p(q)$, and halts precisely when the output is
even; membership of its index in $K$ decides membership of $q$ in $A$.
Thus $A$ and $A^c$ are c.e.\ relative to $K$, and their partial
identities are complementary restriction idempotents in $\mathcal C_K$.
They separate $a_0,a_1$ because
$D_{a_0}\subseteq A$ and $D_{a_1}\subseteq A^c$.

The set $A$ is not recursive. Choose an ordinary
total recursive function $h:\N\to\N$ such that $\varphi_{h(n)}$
ignores its input, simulates $\varphi_n(n)$, and returns $0$ if that
simulation halts. For every $n,m\in\N$,
\[
 n\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \langle h(n),m\rangle\in A.
\]
For a subset $B$ of a set $Y$, write $1_B:Y\rightharpoonup Y$ for
the partial identity on $B$. The source morphism
$p_A=\nabla_{\N}(1_{A^c}+1_A):\N+\N\rightharpoonup\N$
is a partial injection. Its unique section $s_A:\N\to\N+\N$ in $\Pfn$ is
\[
 s_A(n)=
 \begin{cases}
  i_1(n),&n\in A,\\
  i_0(n),&n\notin A.
 \end{cases}
\]
This section is total and satisfies $s_A^{-1}(i_1(\N))=A$.
Since $i_1(\N)$ is recursive in the fixed coproduct coding and
$A$ is not recursive, $s_A$ is not recursive.
If it had a preimage under $F$, that source morphism would
be total and hence ordinary total recursive, a contradiction.
In fact, take $P=F(1_A)$ and $N=F(1_{A^c})$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison}. For any
$s:\N\rightharpoonup\N+\N$ with
$s^{-1}(i_0(\N))=A^c$ and $s^{-1}(i_1(\N))=A$,
these inverse images cover $\N$, so $s$ is total. Here the coproduct
comparison $\chi_{\N,\N}$ is the identity on the tagged union. A source
lift $\ell$ would therefore be a total recursive function. Let
$\operatorname{tag}:\N+\N\to\N$ send $i_j(k)$ to $j$ for $j=0,1$.
Then $\operatorname{tag}\,\ell$ would be the characteristic function of
$A$: its value is $1$ exactly on $s^{-1}(i_1(\N))=A$.
This contradicts the nonrecursiveness of $A$.

The morphisms $i_1 1_A$ and $i_0 1_{A^c}$ belong to
$\mathcal C_K$: they have the total recursive extensions $i_1$
and $i_0$, respectively. Their domains are disjoint. Any common
upper bound would agree with the first morphism on $A$ and the second
on $A^c$. It would therefore be the total function $s_A$, which
is not a source morphism. Thus no such upper bound exists.
\end{proof}

The target $\Pfn$ is split because each partial identity splits through
its domain. Singleton partial identities are connected and jointly
epimorphic, so the target is locally connected. For a partial
monomorphism $p:X\rightharpoonup Y$, testing on maps $1\to X$
shows that $p$ is injective on $D_p$. Define $s:Y\rightharpoonup X$
on $p(D_p)$ by $s(p(x))=x$ for $x\in D_p$. Then
$ps=1_{p(D_p)}=\bar s$ and $psp=p$, as weak choice requires.
For every $u:\N\rightharpoonup\N$ in $\mathcal C_K$, the Turing
property applied to $u\pi_2$, where $\pi_2(z,x)=x$, gives a total parameter
$r_u:\N\to\N$ with $\tau_K(r_u\times1_{\N})=u\pi_2$.
This is the weak Turing hypothesis,
and $F(1_{\N})\ne0$. Nevertheless $1_A$ and $1_{A^c}$ separate
the diagonal pair in $\mathcal C_K$. The earlier proof
\cite[p.~11]{Lengyel2006} chooses a Turing index for $b^{-1}f$, where
$f$ is the section of the restricted codiagonal. Here the corresponding
target endomorphism is $F(b)^{-1}s_A:\N\to\N$. A source morphism
$u:\N\rightharpoonup\N$ with $F(u)=F(b)^{-1}s_A$ would give a lift
$\ell=bu:\N\rightharpoonup\N+\N$, since $F(bu)=s_A$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:missing-lift} excludes such a lift.
\section{Faithful model interpretations and theory extension}\label{app:faithful-family}

Fix a consistent theory $T\supseteq\PA$.
Let $\mathcal M_T$ be the set of all structures for the language of
arithmetic with underlying set $\N$ that satisfy $T$.
Completeness and
the downward L\"owenheim--Skolem theorem imply
$\mathcal M_T\ne\varnothing$: every model of $T$ is infinite, and a
countably infinite model can be transported to the carrier $\N$.

Define the product category
$\mathcal D_T=\prod_{M\in\mathcal M_T}\Pfn$.
An object is a family of sets $A=(A_M)_M$. A morphism
$f:A\rightharpoonup B$ is a family
$(f_M:A_M\rightharpoonup B_M)_M$. Composition and the
restriction, range, restriction-product, and coproduct operations are coordinatewise.
The functors of Proposition~\ref{prop:model} combine to give
$F_T:S_T\to\mathcal D_T$, defined by $F_T(X)=(X_M)_M$ and
$F_T([e]_T)=(F_M[e]_T)_M$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:faithful}
The functor $F_T$ is faithful and preserves restrictions, zeros, binary
restriction products and coproducts, ranges, and finite joins of
restriction idempotents. The category
$\mathcal D_T$ is split and locally connected, satisfies weak choice,
and has inverse images preserving binary joins of restriction
idempotents. Moreover,
$F_T(1_\omega)\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Preservation follows coordinatewise from Proposition~\ref{prop:model}.
Suppose $[e]_T,[f]_T:X\rightharpoonup Y$ are distinct. By
\eqref{eq:uniform}, $T$ does not prove the sentence
$\forall x\forall y\,(G_e(x,y)\leftrightarrow G_f(x,y))$.
Its negation is therefore consistent with $T$.
Completeness and downward L\"owenheim--Skolem give
$M\in\mathcal M_T$ in which the two graphs differ. Hence
$F_M([e]_T)\ne F_M([f]_T)$, so $F_T([e]_T)\ne F_T([f]_T)$.

A restriction idempotent in $\mathcal D_T$ is a family of partial
identities on subsets. Its splitting uses those subsets as the
coordinate sets. For $M\in\mathcal M_T$ and $x\in A_M$, let $e_{M,x}$ be the
partial identity on $\{x\}$ at $M$ and zero elsewhere.
Every idempotent below $e_{M,x}$ is zero or $e_{M,x}$, since a subset
of $\{x\}$ is empty or all of $\{x\}$. Hence $e_{M,x}$ is connected.
For $f,g:A\rightharpoonup B$, equality
$fe_{M,x}=ge_{M,x}$ means $f_M(x)$ and $g_M(x)$ are both undefined
or are defined and equal. If these equations hold for every $M,x$,
then $f_M=g_M$ for every $M$, whence $f=g$.
This proves local connectedness.

Let $p:A\rightharpoonup B$ be a partial monomorphism. If
$p_M(x)=p_M(x')$ is defined, take the family with a singleton at $M$
and the empty set elsewhere. The two total maps from this family to $A$
selecting $x,x'$ have equal composites with $p$. Their composites with
$\bar p$ are therefore equal, so $x=x'$. The inverses of the coordinate
injections, defined on their images, form a section of $p$.
Inverse images commute with unions coordinatewise. Since
$\mathcal M_T$ and each $X_M$ are nonempty, $F_T(1_X)\ne0$ for
every object $X$, in particular for $X=\omega$.
\end{proof}

For consistent computably enumerable $T\supseteq\PA$, the source $S_T$
is not locally connected \cite[Corollary 4.4, pp.~657--658]{DPM}.

For an inclusion $T\subseteq T'$ of consistent theories, the quotient
functor $\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}:S_T\to S_{T'}$ fixes objects and sends
$[e]_T$ to $[e]_{T'}$. Every $T$-proof of graph equivalence is a
$T'$-proof. Composition uses the same program index in both quotients,
and the range formula $R_e(y)=\exists x\,G_e(x,y)$ depends only on $e$.
The functor preserves restrictions, zeros, ranges, binary restriction
products and coproducts, and satisfies $\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}(\tau_T)=\tau_{T'}$.
Since $\mathcal M_{T'}\subseteq\mathcal M_T$, restriction of families
defines the projection
$\pi_{T,T'}:\mathcal D_T\to\mathcal D_{T'}$. Fixing the assignments
$X\mapsto X_M$ once for each arithmetic structure gives a strictly
commuting square:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 S_T \arrow[r,"\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}"] \arrow[d,"F_T"'] &
 S_{T'} \arrow[d,"F_{T'}"]\\
 \mathcal D_T \arrow[r,"\pi_{T,T'}"'] & \mathcal D_{T'}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
On a morphism $[e]_T$, both composites have, at every
$M\in\mathcal M_{T'}$, the partial function defined by interpreting
$G_e$ in $M$. For $T\subseteq T'\subseteq T''$, the quotient
functors satisfy $\mathsf{quot}_{T',T''}\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}=\mathsf{quot}_{T,T''}$, and the coordinate
projections satisfy
$\pi_{T',T''}\pi_{T,T'}=\pi_{T,T''}$.
The identity cases follow from the same definitions.
\subsection{Inseparable pairs under theory extension}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:pair}
Let $T\supseteq\PA$ be consistent.
Fix a Turing morphism $\tau:\omega\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$ in $S_T$.
Choose an isomorphism $b_0:\omega\to\omega+\omega$ in $S_{\PA}$ and put
$b=\mathsf{quot}_{\PA,T}(b_0)$. Define
\[
 d=\tau\Delta_\omega,\qquad
 a_0=(bd)^*(1_\omega+0_\omega),\qquad a_1=(bd)^*(0_\omega+1_\omega).
\]
Then $a_0,a_1$ are inseparable in $S_T$. For every consistent
extension $T'\supseteq T$, their images under $\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}$ form the
inseparable pair defined by the same formulas in $S_{T'}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:model-pair} gives the first assertion, since
$\mathcal M_T\ne\varnothing$.
Write $\mathsf{quot}=\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}$. Given
$f:X\times\omega\rightharpoonup\omega$ in $S_{T'}$, its program
index represents a morphism $\tilde f$ of the same type in $S_T$ with
$\mathsf{quot}(\tilde f)=f$. Choose a total $g:X\to\omega$ in $S_T$
with $\tilde f=\tau(g\times1_\omega)$. Then $\mathsf{quot}(g)$ is
total and $f=\mathsf{quot}(\tau)(\mathsf{quot}(g)\times1_\omega)$.
Thus $\mathsf{quot}(\tau)$ is Turing in $S_{T'}$. Since
$\mathsf{quot}$ preserves the operations defining $a_0,a_1$,
Corollary~\ref{cor:model-pair} applied to $T'$ gives inseparability
of their images.
\end{proof}

The morphism $F_T(\tau_T)$ is not a Turing morphism in $\mathcal D_T$.
Fix $M\in\mathcal M_T$ and put
$t=F_M(\tau_T):|M|\times|M|\rightharpoonup |M|$.
Define $h:|M|\rightharpoonup|M|$ to have constant value $0^M$ on
the domain
\[
 \operatorname{dom}(h)=\{x\in|M|:(x,x)\notin\operatorname{dom}(t)\}.
\]
Let $\mathbf1$ be the family of singleton sets. Take the morphism
$\mathbf1\times F_T\omega\rightharpoonup F_T\omega$ whose
$M$-coordinate is $h$ under $1\times|M|\cong|M|$, and whose other
coordinates are zero. A Turing factorization with a total parameter
$\mathbf1\to F_T\omega$ would give an $m\in|M|$ with
$h(x)\simeq t(m,x)$ for every $x$. At $x=m$, equality of domains and the
definition of $h$ give
\[
 (m,m)\in\operatorname{dom}(t)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m\in\operatorname{dom}(h)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (m,m)\notin\operatorname{dom}(t).
\]

The restriction lattices of $\mathcal D_T$ are Boolean, so every image
of a disjoint source pair has a separator. Lemma~\ref{lem:switch}
supplies lifts for sections associated with complementary restriction
idempotents of $S_T$.
\subsection{Provability of numeral instances}

Suppose in addition that $T$ is computably enumerable.
For a restriction idempotent
$c=[C]_T$ on $\omega$, define the subset of the standard natural numbers
\begin{equation}\label{eq:observation}
 E_T(c)=\{n\in\N:T\vdash C(\bar n)\}.
\end{equation}
Proof enumeration makes $E_T(c)$ computably enumerable, and
\eqref{eq:domain-order} makes it independent of the representative.
Thus $E_T$ maps the restriction idempotents on $\omega$ in $S_T$
to $\mathcal P(\N)$. It preserves order, finite meets, top and
bottom. For a consistent c.e.\ extension $T'\supseteq T$, every
$T$-proof is also a proof from $T'$, so
$E_T(c)\subseteq E_{T'}(\mathsf{quot}_{T,T'}c)$. For $n\in\N$ choose a constant-function index
$\operatorname{const}(n)$ for which
$\PA\vdash\forall x\forall y\,
(G_{\operatorname{const}(n)}(x,y)\leftrightarrow y=\bar n)$, and put
$\kappa_n=[\operatorname{const}(n)]_T:\omega\to\omega$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:faithful-observation}
 n\in E_T(c)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c\kappa_n=\kappa_n
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_T(c)F_T(\kappa_n)=F_T(\kappa_n).
\end{equation}
The composition formula makes
$G_{\operatorname{comp}(j_C,\operatorname{const}(n))}(x,y)$
$T$-provably equivalent to $C(\bar n)\land y=\bar n$, which gives
the first equivalence.
The second follows from faithfulness of $F_T$. In the product
category the last equality holds exactly when
$M\models C(\bar n)$ for every $M\in\mathcal M_T$.
\subsection{The theory of the standard model}

Put $T=\operatorname{Th}(\N)$. Both $S_T$ and $\mathrm{Rec}$ have
the terms in $\mathsf O$ as objects. On a morphism $[e]_T:X\rightharpoonup Y$,
standard interpretation gives $\varphi_e:|X|\rightharpoonup|Y|$ as in
Section~\ref{subsec:numerical-realization}.
For each pair of objects $X,Y$ it gives a bijection
\[
 S_T(X,Y)\longrightarrow\mathrm{Rec}(X,Y),\qquad
 [e]_T\longmapsto\varphi_e .
\]
Indeed, the inverse sends a partial recursive function to the class
of any program computing it on its indicated type. Two such programs
represent the same class because their graph equality in
\eqref{eq:uniform} is true in $\N$, hence belongs to $T$.
Standard interpretation preserves identities and composition.
These bijections therefore give an isomorphism of categories with
the indicated common objects.
By Corollary~\ref{cor:pair}, $S_T$ has an inseparable pair although
$T=\operatorname{Th}(\N)$ is complete.
\section{Reading the Lean proofs}\label{app:reading-lean-proofs}

\newcommand{\CEIproof}[3]{\href{https://github.com/flengyel/CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/blob/cei-v72-palomar-v3/Lean/#1.lean\##2}{#3}}
\newcommand{\CEIregistration}{\href{https://palomar-registry.org/entry.html?id=PALOMAR-2026-11-22-000009&version=3}{PALOMAR-2026-11-22-000009, version~3}}
\subsection{Restriction and extension of an interpretation}

Let $(X,a,b)$ be an object of $\mathsf{Pair}_c(\mathcal D)$ and
$(P,T)$ a consistent theory in $\mathsf{FO}_V(\mathcal D)$.
The bijection of Theorem~\ref{thm:free-first-order-adjunction} is
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{FO}_V(\mathcal D)}(\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}(X,a,b),(P,T))
 \cong
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathsf{Pair}_c(\mathcal D)}((X,a,b),J_{\mathrm{FO}}(P,T)).
\]
Given a translation $\sigma:\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}(X,a,b)\to(P,T)$, \texttt{restrict}
takes its sentence morphism $\sigma_S:S_X\to S_P$ and composes it with
the atomic sentence morphism $\theta_X:X\to S_X$. For every
$x:W\to X$, the atom with index $x$ is $\theta_Xx:W\to S_X$ and
its translation is $\sigma_S\theta_Xx:W\to S_P$. Lean writes
$\sigma_S\theta_X$ as $\theta_X\mathbin{\gg}\sigma_S$.
Conversely, \texttt{extend} takes an assignment $f:X\to S_P$ satisfying
$a\leq f^*T$ and $b\leq f^*(\nu_P^*T)$, where $\nu_P$ denotes negation.
The interpretation $\widehat f$ sends each variable to its variable term
in $P$ and each generating predicate to the closed sentence assigned by $f$.
Substitution fixes these sentences.
Induction on formulas shows that the interpretation commutes with
admissible substitution. The inequalities
put the translated axioms in $T$. Closure under deduction gives
$\widehat f_!T_{a,b}\leq T$.

In \texttt{homEquiv}, extending the restriction of $\sigma$ recovers
$\sigma$ by uniqueness of the interpretation on generators. Restricting
$\widehat f$ recovers $f$ by its defining equation
$\widehat f_S\theta_X=f$. Restriction of the identity on
$\Sigma_{\mathrm{FO}}(X,a,b)$ gives the unit $\theta_X$. Extension of the
identity on $J_{\mathrm{FO}}(P,T)$ gives the counit, which interprets the
predicate indexed by a sentence $\varphi$ as $\varphi$
itself.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46SignedFirstOrderAdjunction}{L27-L56}{The hom-set bijection}
and \CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46SignedFirstOrderAdjunction}{L58-L91}{its naturality, unit and counit}.}
\subsection{Separators and complete extensions}

Let $i_a:X_a\hookrightarrow X$ and $i_b:X_b\hookrightarrow X$ represent
disjoint subobjects $a,b$. In Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-first-order-incompleteness},
$T_{a,b}$ is the least sentence theory containing the images of
$\theta_X i_a$ and $\nu_X\theta_X i_b$. Suppose that $T_{a,b}$ is consistent and $(a,b)$ is inseparable.
If a consistent closed extension $U$ of $T_{a,b}$ were complete, its
theorem and refutation subobjects $U$ and $\nu_X^*U$ would be
complementary in $S_X$. Pullback along $\theta_X$ gives complementary
subobjects of $X$, and the signed axioms give the two inequalities
\[
   a\leq\theta_X^*U,\qquad b\leq\theta_X^*(\nu_X^*U).
\]
Thus the two inverse images would separate $a$ and $b$.

Conversely, a separator defines $d:X\to 1+1$ with value true on $a$
and false on $b$. Interpret the predicates by $d$, equality by true,
and $\forall v\,\varphi$ by the value of $\varphi$. The logical axioms
are true and the rules preserve truth, so the true sentences form a
closed theory, \texttt{booleanTheory}. It contains the signed axioms
and hence $T_{a,b}$. Boolean negation interchanges true and false, so
the theory is consistent and complete. This extension rules out
essential incompleteness of $T_{a,b}$.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46SignedSubobjectIncompleteness}{L43-L75}{The two implications}
and \CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46SignedBooleanExtension}{L28-L74}{the Boolean extension}.
For the subobject formulation of Corollary~\ref{cor:signed-first-order-incompleteness}
and the Boolean-assignment theorem, see \CEIregistration{} and the corresponding
\CEIproof{CEIPalomar/Solution}{L83-L110}{Lean declarations}.}
\subsection{One valuation for two derivations}

The consistency assertion in Lemma~\ref{lem:arithmetic-signed-theory}
concerns the theory $t_{\pm}$ generated by the arithmetic diagonal pair. Fix a
model $M\models\PA$. Suppose $p,q$ code derivations in $M$ from the
signed calculus with conclusions $\varphi,\neg\varphi$, respectively.
The definition \texttt{jointSupport} concatenates the lists of positive
axiom labels from $p$ and $q$. Write $L$ for the resulting list in $M$.
In the predicate category of $\PA$, let $N$ be the number object and
$j^{\pm}:S^{\pm}\hookrightarrow\Fm^{\pm}$ the sentence inclusion of
the signed language. With $\theta^{\pm}:N\to S^{\pm}$ its atomic
sentence morphism, the valuation satisfies
\[
  v:\List N\times\Fm^{\pm}\longrightarrow\Two,
  \qquad v(\ell,j^{\pm}\theta^{\pm}x)=\mem(x,\ell).
\]
Interpreting $v$ in $M$ with the same $L$ for both derivations
makes every positive axiom leaf true. If $\neg P_n$ is a negative
axiom leaf, disjointness of the diagonal domains excludes $n$ from $L$,
so $\neg P_n$ is true as well.

The logical schemes are true, and modus ponens and generalization preserve
truth. Induction in $M$ therefore gives truth of both conclusions for the
same $L$, even for derivations of nonstandard length. But Boolean
negation gives the conclusions of $p$ and $q$ opposite truth values. The
valuation uses only the axiom leaves of $p$ and $q$; a separator
must assign the prescribed values on both entire diagonal domains. Since the argument holds in
every model of $\PA$, first-order completeness gives a proof in $\PA$
that no two derivations in the signed calculus conclude a formula and its
negation.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46ArithmeticSignedContradiction}{L32-L56}{The common list},
\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46ArithmeticSignedContradiction}{L85-L92}{the contradiction},
and \CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46ArithmeticSignedConsistencyPA}{L45-L64}{provability in PA}.
For the existential consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:arithmetic-signed-theory},
see \CEIregistration. The
\CEIproof{CEIPalomar/Solution}{L114-L145}{Lean proof} uses the two diagonal
subobjects in the predicate category of $\PA$ as its witness.}
\subsection{The lift of a conditional}

In Theorem~\ref{thm:comparison}, let $F:\mathscr R\to\mathcal A$ be
the range functor and let $a_0,a_1$ be the inverse images of the two
summand domains under $h=b\tau\Delta_U:U\rightharpoonup U+U$.
The disjoint domains $P,N$ on $FU$ satisfy $F(a_0)\leq P$ and
$F(a_1)\leq N$. The conditional $s:FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$ has
summand inverse images $N,P$, in that order.

Let $\chi_{U,U}:FU+FU\to F(U+U)$ be the coproduct isomorphism. Given
a lift $\ell:U\rightharpoonup U+U$ with $F\ell=\chi_{U,U}s$,
\texttt{turing\_diagonal} supplies a total
$g:U\to U$ with $hg=\ell g$. Set
$H=\chi_{U,U}^{-1}Fh:FU\rightharpoonup FU+FU$. Applying $F$ to $hg=\ell g$
gives $H(Fg)=s(Fg)$. Taking inverse images of the two summand domains
along this common morphism gives
\[
 (Fg)^*N=(Fg)^*F(a_0)\leq (Fg)^*P,\qquad
 (Fg)^*P=(Fg)^*F(a_1)\leq (Fg)^*N.
\]
The inequalities give $(Fg)^*P=(Fg)^*N$. Since $P$ and $N$ are disjoint
and inverse image preserves meets and zero, both inverse images are zero.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46Comparison}{L35-L89}{The two inverse images under $Fg$}.}

In Proposition~\ref{prop:missing-lift} the output summand of the total
conditional decides membership in a nonrecursive set. The inclusion
functor preserves the underlying partial function, so any source lift
would be defined everywhere. Every total source morphism in this example
is recursive. A lift would therefore decide the set
recursively.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/OracleMissingLift}{L89-L103}{Nonexistence of the lift}.}

units.subsection: \subsection{Evaluation of a theory in the slice}
units.tex: \subsection{Evaluation of a theory in the slice}

units.subsection: \subsection{Evaluation of a theory in the slice}
units.tex:
Let $u:U\hookrightarrow S$ be the consistent theory of
Theorem~\ref{thm:associated-incompleteness}, and let $W$ be a closed
extension of its constant family $B_U(u)$. The chosen logical theorem
gives a point $\lambda_U:1\to U$. Let $\operatorname{ev}:\mathcal D/U\to\mathcal D$
take the pullback along $\lambda_U$ and then its domain in $\mathcal D$.
Let $B:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D/U$ be the restriction of $B_U$ to total morphisms. Write
$\varepsilon:\operatorname{ev}B\cong 1_{\mathcal D}$ for the projection isomorphism and
$j:S\hookrightarrow\Fm$ for the sentence inclusion. The definition
\texttt{evaluationTheory} pairs the subobject
$W_0=(\varepsilon_S^{-1})^*\operatorname{ev}(W)\hookrightarrow S$ with its proof of closure.

units.subsection: \subsection{Evaluation of a theory in the slice}
units.tex:
Let $C(W)\hookrightarrow B(\Fm)$ be the formula subobject generated
by $W$ in the slice. Its evaluation lies over $\operatorname{ev}(B\Fm)$. Put
$C_0=(\varepsilon_{\Fm}^{-1})^*\operatorname{ev}(C(W))\hookrightarrow\Fm$.
Since $(Bj)^*C(W)=W$, preservation of pullbacks by $\operatorname{ev}$ and naturality
$\operatorname{ev}(Bj)\varepsilon_S^{-1}=\varepsilon_{\Fm}^{-1}j$ give $j^*C_0=W_0$. Evaluating the rule
operations and transporting them along $\varepsilon$ makes $C_0$ closed under
the rules. Thus $C_0$ contains the axioms $W_0$ and admits the map
from the initial algebra of their derivations. It follows that
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(W_0)=j^*C(W_0)\le j^*C_0=W_0 .
\]
Axiom introduction gives the reverse inclusion. If $W$ were consistent and complete, so would be $W_0$,
since evaluation preserves the finite limits, images and coproducts
defining these conditions. Evaluating $B_U(u)\leq W$ gives $u\leq W_0$
under $\varepsilon_S:\operatorname{ev}(BS)\cong S$. Thus a complete consistent closed extension in
the slice would give one in the base. Conversely, taking the constant
family of such an extension in the base gives one in the
slice.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46AssociatedClosedTheories}{L68-L111}{Closure under evaluation and the two implications}.}
\subsection{A uniform choice of independent sentences}

In Theorem~\ref{thm:uniform-independent-sentences},
$E=(\omega,1_\omega)$ is the number object and $S$ the arithmetic sentence
object in $\mathcal B=\Tot(\Split(S_{\PA}))$. Let $\Gamma_e$ consist
of the axioms of $\PA$ and the sentences on whose codes program $e$
halts. The Turing property gives a total morphism $g:\omega\to\omega$
in $S_{\PA}$. Composing its image $I(g):E\to E$ with the diagonal
sentence morphism $\theta:E\to S$ gives one morphism
$q=\theta I(g)$ for all $e$. For $e\in\N$, put $n=F_{\N}(g)(e)$.
Then $(G_{\N}q)(e)=\ulcorner\alpha(\bar n)\urcorner$, where
$\alpha(x)$ asserts that the diagonal computation at $x$ has an even output.

Suppose $\Gamma_e$ is consistent. If it proves $\alpha(\bar n)$,
the proof search selects the odd summand at $(e,n)$. The diagonal
identity puts $n$ in the odd diagonal domain, whence
$\PA\vdash\neg\alpha(\bar n)$. If $\Gamma_e$ proves
$\neg\alpha(\bar n)$, the even summand gives
$\PA\vdash\alpha(\bar n)$. Both alternatives contradict consistency
because $\Gamma_e$ extends $\PA$.\footnote{\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46ArithmeticUniformIndependent}{L116-L128}{The diagonal output and the sentence code}
and \CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46ArithmeticUniformIndependent}{L184-L218}{the two excluded derivations and the uniform morphism}.}

units.tex: \subsection{Finite proofs and the theorem domain for a Miller sequence}

units.subsection: \subsection{Finite proofs and the theorem domain for a Miller sequence}
units.tex:
In Lemma~\ref{lem:miller-parameterized-deduction}, let $P$ be the
parameter object and let $A\hookrightarrow P\times S$ specify the
axioms. A derivation with parameter $w$ has conclusion $(w,\varphi)$.
Here $S$ is the sentence object and $\Fm$ the formula object.
For the inference endofunctor $H$ on
$\mathcal D_a/(P\times\Fm)$, write $\delta:H(D_A,c_A)\to(D_A,c_A)$
for the algebra of finite derivations. Given an algebra
$\beta:H(Q,q)\to(Q,q)$ in this slice, its interpretation of derivations
is the unique $\widehat\beta:D_A\to Q$ satisfying
\[
     q\widehat\beta=c_A,\qquad \widehat\beta\delta=\beta H(\widehat\beta).
\]
The first equation fixes both the parameter and the conclusion. The
second determines $\widehat\beta$ at each leaf and at each application of an
inference rule. A logical axiom leaf at $w$ carries an instance of a
logical scheme. A nonlogical axiom leaf with sentence $\psi$ at $w$
requires $(w,\psi)\in A$.\footnote{%
\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46MillerParameterizedDeduction}{L97-L126}{The inference algebra and the two equations}
and \CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46MillerParameterizedDeduction}{L130-L151}{initiality for every axiom subobject}.}

units.subsection: \subsection{Finite proofs and the theorem domain for a Miller sequence}
units.tex:
For Theorem~\ref{thm:miller-incompleteness}, let $\Gamma$ be the
$\mathcal E_a$-semidecidable set of axiom codes for an extension
of $T_a$. Let $c_\Gamma:\mathrm{Prf}_\Gamma\to S$ take a derivation
whose conclusion is a sentence to its conclusion. In the numerical
presentation of $S$, write $s_\varphi$ for the point representing
a closed formula $\varphi$ and $D_\Gamma$ for the domain of the
partial identity $\ran(c_\Gamma)$. The comparison with finite Hilbert
proofs gives
\[
  s_\varphi\in D_\Gamma
    \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Gamma\vdash\varphi .
\]
The comparison of proof objects preserves conclusions and inference
rules. For an arbitrary axiom monomorphism $m:Z\hookrightarrow S$,
let $\Gamma_m$ be the set of sentence words encoding its image in the
numerical presentation. Write $i_{\Gamma_m}:A_{\Gamma_m}\hookrightarrow S$
for the axiom subobject reconstructed from these words.
The isomorphism $u:Z\xrightarrow{\cong}A_{\Gamma_m}$ satisfies
$i_{\Gamma_m}u=m$. Relabelling axiom leaves by $u$ preserves their
sentences; initiality extends this relabelling to derivations, preserving
conclusions. Relabelling by $u^{-1}$ gives the reverse inclusion of
sentence-conclusion images in $S$. Thus the displayed equivalence applies to $m$
with $\Gamma=\Gamma_m$. Pullback of this theorem domain along
$\nu:S\to S$ gives the refutation domain.\footnote{%
\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46MillerCanonicalProofComparison}{L155-L178}{Preservation of conclusions and inference rules},
\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46MillerTheoryDomainApplication}{L59-L98}{the equivalence with finite provability}, and
\CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46MillerCanonicalAxiomIncompleteness}{L139-L192}{recovery of the axiom subobject and conclusion image}.
See also \CEIproof{CategoricalEssentialIncompleteness/V46MillerCanonicalAxiomIncompleteness}{L327-L342}{inseparability and the independent sentence}.}
